> रुपादानानर्हत्वात् । नान्यत्किंचन मिषत् । ऐ. आ. २-४.१ । इति श्रुतेश्चेत्यभिप्रायः ।
> यतो यस्मादधिष्ठानादारंभणाच्च विश्वचक्षाः सर्वद्रष्टा विश्वकर्मा परमेश्वरो
> भूमिं जनयन्वर्तते तथा द्यां दिवं व्यौर्णोत् व्यवृणोत् सृष्टवान् महिना
> स्वमहत्त्वेन । किं स्विदासीदिति ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

This Ṛk, beginning किं स्वित् (*kiṃ svit*), is the anuvākyā for the offering of the omentum (vapā) of the animal belonging to the Viśvedevas. It is also stated in the sūtra: किं स्विदासीदधिष्ठानं यो नः पिता जनिता (*kiṃ svidāsīdadhiṣṭhānaṃ yo naḥ pitā janitā*) (Ā. 3-8).

Sāyaṇa says that in the previous mantra it was stated that at the time of dissolution the Lord withdrew the world, and afterwards, when the desire to create arose, created everything and entered it. Here an objection is raised: since for him, who is without a second, there could be no support, no material cause of the world and the like, creation is not possible. In the world, a potter who wishes to make a pot takes his stand on some place such as a house, and with earth as the material and with implements such as the wheel produces the pot. In the same way, for Īśvara, at the time of producing heaven and earth, which are the support of the world, what was the support? What was there? Nothing, is the meaning. Likewise, what was the आरंभणं (*āraṃbhaṇaṃ*) of those two, that is, that by which a thing is begun, the material cause? What could that be? That also was not, is the meaning. Even if it were possible, how was it? Would it itself be being or non-being? Neither is tenable. If it were being, there would be a breach of non-duality. If it were non-being, it could not be the material of heaven and earth, which consist of being. The scripture too says that nothing else existed (Ai. Ā. 2-4.1): such is the intention. Out of which support and which material the all-seeing Viśvakarman, the Supreme Lord, has been producing the earth, and likewise disclosed (made) heaven, by his own greatness: that is the question; what was it?

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- यतः (*yataḥ*)—from which support and original cause
- विश्वचक्षा (*viśvacakṣā*)—all-seeing
- विश्वकर्मा (*viśvakarmā*)—the Lord of the worlds
- भूमिं (*bhūmiṃ*)—the earth
- जनयन् (*janayan*)—producing
- महिना (*mahinā*)—by his greatness
- द्यां (*dyāṃ*)—the whole heaven-world
- व्यार्णोत् (*vyārṇot*)—did he create

### Printed p. 198

- अधिष्ठानं (*adhiṣṭhānaṃ*)—the support for the creation of this world
- किं स्वित् आसीत् (*kiṃ svit āsīt*)—what was there
- आरंभणं (*āraṃbhaṇaṃ*)—the original cause for the production
- कतमत् स्वित् (*katamat svit*)—what was it
- कथा आसीत् (*kathā āsīt*)—in what manner was it

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The all-seeing Lord of the worlds, producing the earth and creating the whole heaven-world by his greatness: from what support and original cause did he do so? What was the support for the creation of this world? What was the original cause of its production? What was its manner? What was its nature?

##### English translation
What was the station ? what was the material ? how was (it done) ?
so that the beholder of all, Vishwakarman (was) generating and disclosed

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

When the offering of the omentum in the animal sacrifice made for the Viśvedevas is performed, this Ṛk beginning किं स्वित् (*kiṃ svit*) is to be recited as the anuvākyā mantra; this is set forth by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra किं स्विदासीदधिष्ठानं यो नः पिता जनिता । (*kiṃ svidāsīdadhiṣṭhānaṃ yo naḥ pitā janitā |*) (Ā. 3-8).

In the previous Ṛk the nature of the dissolution of the world was stated; after some time the Supreme Lord wished to create again, created accordingly, and afterwards it was said that the Supreme Self entered all the moving and unmoving things that had been created. It has also been stated that before creation only the Brahman substance existed and that nothing else existed. It is known to everyone in worldly practice that, if a thing is to be made, three things are absolutely necessary: the place in which to make it, the original material, and the person who makes it. Since at the time of dissolution the Supreme Lord alone existed and no other thing existed, this Ṛk states how this creation could be possible.

If an example is given, it will be easier to understand the matter well. Suppose a potter makes a pot. A place is needed for making the pot. The original material needed for the pot, that is, clay, is needed. The instruments, the wheel, water and a stick, are needed. The maker, that is, the potter, who can make the pot by using all these with his intelligence, is needed. Only if all this exists is it possible to make the pot; otherwise it is not. Now at the time of dissolution the Supreme Self, who is the maker for creation, was indeed there. But where was the place? Where were the original material (Raw Materials) needed for the creation of the world, and the instruments? There was none of them. Yet the Supreme Self created the world. The seer examines this in this Ṛk by way of question and answer and explains how creation took place.

### Printed p. 199

अधिष्ठानं किं स्वित् आसीत् (*adhiṣṭhānaṃ kiṃ svit āsīt*)—at the time of the creation of the world, what was the support for the creation of this world? Since the heaven and earth that we now see, that is, the three worlds, earth, atmosphere and heaven, did not exist then, standing where, and how, did the Supreme Self make these worlds? That is, there was then no support at all for the creation of the worlds.

आरंभणं कतमत्स्वित् (*āraṃbhaṇaṃ katamatsvit*)—besides this, what was the original material (Raw Materials) needed for it at the beginning of making a thing? There was none. By original material is meant that, for making a pot, clay is the original material; for making cloth, cotton is the original material; for making vessels, metal is the original material; for making tables, chairs, cots and the like, wood (the tree) is the original material, and so on. This being so, what original material was there at that time for making this heaven and earth? There was none.

कथा आसीत् (*kathā āsīt*)—as said above, when neither place nor original material existed, the seer asks how this work of creation came about. In the Upaniṣads and other works it is said: असद्वा इदमग्र आसीत् । ततो वै सदजायत (*asadvā idamagra āsīt | tato vai sadajāyata*). That is, before creation there was non-being (asat), that which is nothing; from it being (sat), existence or the state, came into being, it is said. If a thing called being existed before creation and the world was created from it (from that original material), then the Supreme Self and being would be two things. If there are two things, where is non-duality? Therefore that is not right. Well, if non-being alone existed, how is it possible for heaven and earth, which are called being, to arise from non-being (from the void)? That is, the question naturally arises: how is it possible to create a new thing when there is nothing? According to what modern scientists say, "Nothing can be lost or nothing can be created": no thing can be completely destroyed, and likewise no new thing can be made without the help of an original material. This statement is a point to be noted especially in the principles of the Vedānta. On the basis of this very statement the nature of the creation, continuance and dissolution of the world is explained with discussion in the Vedānta principles, that is, in the Upaniṣads and the like. We shall explain all those in another context. Therefore it is stated here that neither being nor non-being was of help to the Supreme Self in the work of creation.

If so, यतो भूमिं जनयन् विश्वकर्मा विद्यामौर्णोत् (*yato bhūmiṃ janayan viśvakarmā vidyāmaurṇot*): how did Viśvakarman, the Supreme Lord, produce this heaven and earth? Thus the seer asks. In answer to this,

### Printed p. 200

महिना विश्वचक्षाः (*mahinā viśvacakṣāḥ*), the last sentence, he says there itself. That is, Viśvakarman has created this world by his great majesty. Here the word विश्वचक्षाः (*viśvacakṣāḥ*) is a qualifying word describing the unfathomable majesty of Viśvakarman. This Supreme Lord is one who can see, that is, can know, everything. Because he himself has been transformed into all moving and unmoving things, or because he has entered all created things as the inner controller and is the impeller of the movements of beings, there is nothing that is not seen or not known to this Supreme Lord, that is, to Viśvakarman. Therefore it should be understood that here the qualifying words विश्वचक्षाः (*viśvacakṣāḥ*) and महिना (*mahinā*), describing the unfathomable majesty of Viśvakarman, have been used. What would be understood of the nature of his majesty merely by saying "the great majesty of Viśvakarman"? What is the nature of that majesty? Is it possible for that majesty to be in others also? The seer has described these matters in detail in the next Ṛk.

If the creation of the world made by Īśvara is examined from the worldly point of view, a question naturally arises. The instruments and materials needed for worldly creation are not found here. For example, a potter who wishes to make a pot (ghaṭa) must have such instruments and materials as अधिष्ठान (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and आरंभण (*āraṃbhaṇa*). Adhiṣṭhāna means a place necessary for the making of the pot. Ārambhaṇa means the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa). For the making of a pot, clay is the material cause (the potter is the efficient cause, nimitta-kāraṇa). Just as a pot is not possible without clay, so the creation of the world is not possible without a material cause. Īśvara (Prajāpati, Viśvakarman: it has been stated above that all these are synonyms), at the time of dissolution, as the performer of the sacrifice in the form of withdrawal, offers the whole world as an oblation in this sacrifice, and after the complete dissolution he alone remains. While he remains without a second, the wish to create (sisṛkṣā) arises in him. Then there is neither a support in the form of a place (adhiṣṭhāna) needed for creation nor a material cause. The objection how the creation of the world is possible is natural here. Therefore in this Ṛk the question is asked in this way.

From which adhiṣṭhāna and ārambhaṇa has Īśvara (Viśvakarman) created heaven and earth? What is the nature of this material cause? That is the question. If there were any material cause at all, what would its nature be? Apart from Īśvara there was no other existing substance. For the making of a world that consists of being, an ārambhaṇa that consists of being is absolutely necessary. From a thing of the form of non-being it is not possible to make a world of the form of being.

### Printed p. 201

नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः । उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽंतस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः ॥ (*nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ | ubhayorapi dṛṣṭo 'ṃtastvanayostattvadarśibhiḥ ‖*) (Bha. Gī. 2-16)**NOTE**

From a principle of the form of non-existence, a principle of the form of existence does not arise. Without a thing of the form of existence, nothing arises. As existence cannot come about from a mere absence of everything, so how can the creation of a world of the form of being come about when there is nothing? This is the second question. If there is no proof that Īśvara alone remains after the dissolution, with nothing else, then, as was stated in the Ṛk above, य इमा विश्वा भुवनानि जुह्वत् (*ya imā viśvā bhuvanāni juhvat*). Moreover:

आत्मा ना इदमेक एवाग्र आसीत् नान्यत् किंचन मिषत् (*ātmā nā idameka evāgra āsīt nānyat kiṃcana miṣat*) (Ai. Ā. 2-4-1)

सदेव सोम्य इदमग्र आसीत् । एकमेवाद्वितीयं (*sadeva somya idamagra āsīt | ekamevādvitīyaṃ*) (Chā. U. 6-2-1)

प्रजापतिर्ह ना इदमग्र एवास (*prajāpatirha nā idamagra evāsa*) (Śa. Brā. 2-2-4-1)

Such śruti sentences establish the absence of the world and the non-duality of Īśvara. Even though there is non-duality, another question arises. The question is whether this single principle is of the form of being or of the form of non-being. Sentences such as नासदासीन्नो सदासीत् (*nāsadāsīnno sadāsīt*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-129-1) state that there was neither non-being nor being, but only that darkness pervaded. The answer to the question how a world of the form of being could arise from a state in which neither of the two existed will have to be given when that Ṛk is explained. But in some other places it is stated precisely that Īśvara, who is of the form of being, is the cause of the world. For example:

तद्भैक आहुरसदेवेदमग्र आसी नेकमेवाद्वितीयं तस्मादसतः सज्ञायत (*tadbhaika āhurasadevedamagra āsī nekamevādvitīyaṃ tasmādasataḥ sajñāyata*) (Chā. U. 6-2-1)

Before creation there was no thing of the form of being at all. Only non-being existed. There are also śruti sentences which say that from it the world of the form of being was produced. This is another prior position (pūrvapakṣa). If it is asked what the authority for this is:

असद्वा इदमग्र आसीत् । ततो वै सदजायत (*asadvā idamagra āsīt | tato vai sadajāyata*) (Tai. U. 2-7)

Before creation there was only a principle of the form of non-being. From this non-being the world of the form of being came into existence. Afterwards the activity of the world began. This is stated clearly in the Taittirīya Upaniṣad. The same idea is also stated in the Chāndogya, saying,

### Printed p. 202

आदित्यो ब्रह्मेत्यादेशस्तस्योपव्याख्यानमसदेवेदमग्र आसीत् । तत्सदासीत्तत्समभवत्तदांडं निरवर्तत.... .... .... ॥ (*ādityo brahmetyādeśastasyopavyākhyānamasadevedamagra āsīt | tatsadāsīttatsamabhavattadāṃḍaṃ niravartata.... .... .... ‖*) (Chā. U. 3.19-1)

"The sun is Brahman": this is the teaching which states the settled conclusion. Its explanation is as follows. In the beginning, from the absence of the form of non-being, existence of the form of being arose. It grew, increased and was transformed into the form of an egg. If it is said that sentences of this kind are the authority, then in the same Chāndogya this view is refuted. As the answer to the prior position stated in the sentence 6-2-1 quoted above, in the sentence that follows it the settled conclusion is stated in this way:

कुतस्तु खलु सोम्येवं स्यादिति होवाच कथमसतः सज्जायेतेति । सत्त्वेव सोम्येदमग्र आसीदेकमेवाद्वितीयं ॥ ( (*kutastu khalu somyevaṃ syāditi hovāca kathamasataḥ sajjāyeteti | sattveva somyedamagra āsīdekamevādvitīyaṃ ‖ (*) (Bhā. U. 6-2-2)**NOTE**

"My child, how could this be? How could a thing of the form of being arise from non-being? What existed before was nothing other than the principle of the form of being, one, without a second." Thus the settled conclusion has been stated precisely: that only such a principle of the form of being existed.

In the present context it also becomes possible to answer the question how a world of the form of being came about from a state of the form of non-existence. From the worldly point of view, non-existence (abhāva) can be said to be of four kinds. Abhāva means absence. This absence is of four kinds. First:

1) अत्यंताभावः (*atyaṃtābhāvaḥ*): that which is pure void. For example, the son of a barren woman. This shows an absolutely contrary state. The state of the world at the time of dissolution does not have this kind of absolute non-existence. It has been dissolved in Īśvara in a form so subtle that it does not appear to the eye of the world. Second:

2) प्रागभावः (*prāgabhāvaḥ*): non-existence is not pure void. It means only that something is not there in that state before it has arisen. That is, it means that the capacity of nature and the power to come to light are there (potentiality). As an example of this there is a section in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad itself. The example that shows this prior non-existence is:

न्यग्रोधफलमत आहरेतीदं भगव इति भिंदीति भिन्नं भगव इति किमत्र पश्यसीत्यण्व इवेमा धाना भगव इत्यासामंगैकां भिंधीति भिन्ना भगव इति किमत्र पश्यसीति न किंचन भगव इति ॥ (*nyagrodhaphalamata āharetīdaṃ bhagava iti bhiṃdīti bhinnaṃ bhagava iti kimatra paśyasītyaṇva ivemā dhānā bhagava ityāsāmaṃgaikāṃ bhiṃdhīti bhinnā bhagava iti kimatra paśyasīti na kiṃcana bhagava iti ‖*) (Bhā. U. 6-12-1)

### Printed p. 203

The teacher tells the pupil to bring the fruit of a banyan tree, and the pupil brought it. (One of the tall and wide-spreading trees such as the banyan and the fig.) Then, when told to press that fruit, he was startled. When told to see what was in it, he said that it contained minute seeds. When told to break even that small seed, he broke it. When told to see what was in it, he said, "Nothing, sir."

तं होवाच यं वै सोम्येतमणिमानं न निभालयस एतस्य वै सोम्येषोऽणिम्म एवं महान्यग्रोधस्तिष्ठति श्रद्धत्त्व सोम्येति । (*taṃ hovāca yaṃ vai somyetamaṇimānaṃ na nibhālayasa etasya vai somyeṣo 'ṇimma evaṃ mahānyagrodhastiṣṭhati śraddhattva somyeti |*) (Chā. U. 6-12-2)

"My child, after breaking the minute seed you cannot see the still more minute essence that is in it. But it is from this essence, which does not fall within your sight, that the very lofty and widely spreading banyan tree stands grown. In the same way,

स य एषोऽणिमैतदात्ममिदं सर्वं तत्सत्यं स आत्मा तत्त्वमसि श्वेतकेतो .... .... .... ॥ (*sa ya eṣo 'ṇimaitadātmamidaṃ sarvaṃ tatsatyaṃ sa ātmā tattvamasi śvetaketo .... .... .... ‖*) (Chā. U. 6-12.3)

"My child, this world, which has the vastness of the universe, lay hidden in the minute thing that does not come within your sight. The essential power that expands this world was in that minute thing." When he teaches thus, the teacher shows the prior non-existence of the world. In this form there was non-existence of the world, but there was no absolute non-existence.

3) Third, प्रध्वंसाभावः (*pradhvaṃsābhāvaḥ*): non-existence after having existed before. This has a beginning. It has no end. There is a pot. After it is broken the pot is no longer there.

4) Fourth, अन्नोन्याभावः (*annonyābhāvaḥ*): a pot is not a cloth. A cloth is not a pot, and so on. In the present context this explanation is unnecessary.

Thus (prior non-existence) non-existence does not mean absolute non-existence. It must be understood that the world was hidden in a subtle form and not in a gross form. But since it was merged in Īśvara, it was not a thing different from him but was united in him. Therefore there was no sense of distinction that Īśvara is one thing and the world another. For that very reason it is stated: प्रजापतिर्ह ना इदमग्र एवास (*prajāpatirha nā idamagra evāsa*) and so on. Just as the essence of the banyan seed, which is subtler than an atom, has the power to hold the whole wonderful tree within itself, so Īśvara, who is smaller than an atom, can hold the whole universe within himself. This power is indicated by the word महिना (*mahinā*).

### Printed p. 204

In the present Ṛk also, in the very putting of the question in the form of the prior position, the word महिना (*mahinā*), which indicates the greatness of Īśvara, has been used. The great deeds of Īśvara do not fall under worldly practices and measures. This word indicates that great deeds are possible by mere resolve alone. The greatness that is indicated by this word used in the present Ṛk is this:

अणोरणीयान्महतो महीयानात्मास्य जंतोर्निहितं गुहायां । (*aṇoraṇīyānmahato mahīyānātmāsya jaṃtornihitaṃ guhāyāṃ |*) (Kaṭh. U. 2-20)**NOTE**

एष स आत्मांतर्हृदयेऽणीयान् व्रीहेर्वा यवाद्वा, सर्षपाद्वा श्यामाकाद्दा श्यामाकतंडुलाद्दा एष आत्मांतर्हृदये ज्यायान्पृथिव्या ज्यायानंतरीक्षाः ष्ट्रियान्वितो ज्यायानेभ्यो लोकेभ्यः । (*eṣa sa ātmāṃtarhṛdaye 'ṇīyān vrīhervā yavādvā, sarṣapādvā śyāmākāddā śyāmākataṃḍulāddā eṣa ātmāṃtarhṛdaye jyāyānpṛthivyā jyāyānaṃtarīkṣāḥ ṣṭriyānvito jyāyānebhyo lokebhyaḥ |*) (Bhā. U. 3-14-2)

The very Īśvara who, after creation, is described as having entered the whole created world and pervaded it as the inner controller of all (अवरान् आ विवेश (*avarān ā viveśa*), 10-81-1), his greatness is described in the Upaniṣads and other works in this way. Īśvara is smaller than an atom. He is of a form subtler than that. He lies hidden in a subtle form in all hearts, which are like caves. This Īśvara of subtle form is greater than the earth. He is greater than the atmosphere. He is greater than the heaven-world. He is smaller than the smallest. He is more than all the worlds. This is his greatness: he has the power to hold all the worlds hidden within himself.

तवेजति तन्नैजति तद्दूरे तद्वदंतिके । तदंतरस्य सर्वस्य तदु सर्वस्यास्य बाह्यतः ॥ (*tavejati tannaijati taddūre tadvadaṃtike | tadaṃtarasya sarvasya tadu sarvasyāsya bāhyataḥ ‖*) (Īśa. U. 5)**NOTE**

Īśvara is of the nature of movement, and likewise unmoving. He is at a very distant place, and likewise he is hidden within all things and also beyond them. These are not contrary qualities of Īśvara. These qualities, which seem contrary to the view of the world, come into harmony in him.

Therefore for Īśvara, who consists of being and non-being and is also beyond them, at the time of the creation of the world he himself is the adhiṣṭhāna, he himself is the ārambhaṇa, the created world is he himself, and the creator is he himself. That is his greatness. This is what is stated by the words महिना विश्वचक्षाः (*mahinā viśvacakṣāḥ*). What the purport of the word विश्वचक्षाः (*viśvacakṣāḥ*) is will be explained in the Special Topics of the next Ṛk.

### Printed p. 205

#### Ṛk 3

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> वि॒श्वत॑श्चक्षुरु॒त वि॒श्वतो॑मुखो वि॒श्वतो॑बाहुरु॒त वि॒श्वतः॑ स्पात् ।  
> सं बा॒हुभ्यां॒ धम॑ति॒ सं पत॑त्त्रै॒र्दार्वा॒भूमी॑ ज॒नय॑न्दे॒व एकः॑ ॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> सिश्वतःचक्षुः । उत । विश्वतःमुखः । विश्वतःबाहुः । उत । विश्वतःपात् ।  
> सं । बाहुभ्यां । धमति । सं । पतत्रैः । द्यावाभूमिा इति । जनयन् । देवः एकः॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> अनया सर्वात्मकत्वेन कुलालादिविलक्षणत्वादधिष्ठानाद्यभावेऽपि स्रष्टुं
> रक्कोतीत्याह । विश्वतश्चक्षुः सर्वतो व्याप्तचक्षुः । उतापि च विश्वतो मुखः । तथा
> निश्वतो बाहुः । उतापि च विश्वतस्सात् । स एवंविधः परमेश्वरः स्वस्मिंस्त्रैलोक्यमुत्पादयतीत्यर्थः । कथमिति उच्यते । बाहुभ्यां दिवं सं धमति । धमतिर्गतिकर्मा ! सम्यक् प्रेरयति । तथा पतत्रैर्गमनशीलैः पादैः पृथिवीं सं धमतीति ।
> उभयोरेव श्रवणं प्राधान्याभिप्रायं । एवं द्यावाभूमी जनयन् दिवं च
> पृथिवीं चोत्पादयन्नेवो द्योतमानः स्वयंप्रकाशः परमेश्वर एकोऽसहाय
> एव वर्तते ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa says that by this Ṛk, because he is all-pervading and unlike the potter and the like, he states that Īśvara is able to create even without a support and the like. He is विश्वतश्चक्षुः (*viśvataścakṣuḥ*), with eyes spread everywhere; उत (*uta*), and also विश्वतो मुखः (*viśvato mukhaḥ*), with faces everywhere; likewise विश्वतो बाहुः (*viśvato bāhuḥ*), with arms everywhere; and also विश्वतस्सात् (*viśvatassāt*), with feet everywhere. Such a Supreme Lord produces the three worlds in himself, is the meaning. How? It is said: with his arms he सं धमति (*saṃ dhamati*) the heaven. The root धमति (*dhamati*) has the sense of motion; he sets it properly in motion. Likewise with पतत्रैः (*patatraiḥ*), that is, with his feet, which are given to going, he sets the earth in motion. The mention of both is meant to show their importance. Thus, producing heaven and earth, the Supreme Lord, shining and self-luminous, exists alone, without any helper.**NOTE**

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- विश्वतश्चक्षुः (*viśvataścakṣuḥ*)—one who has eyes spread everywhere
- उत (*uta*)—and
- विश्वतोमुखः (*viśvatomukhaḥ*)—one who has faces everywhere
- विश्वतोबाहुः (*viśvatobāhuḥ*)—one who has arms spread everywhere
- उत (*uta*)—and
- विश्वतस्सात् (*viśvatassāt*)—Īśvara, who has feet extended in every direction
- बाहुभ्यां (*bāhubhyāṃ*)—with his arms
- सं धमति (*saṃ dhamati*)—sets the heaven-world in motion
- पतत्रैः (*patatraiḥ*)—with his moving feet
- सं (*saṃ*)—sets the earth in motion
- द्यावाभूमी (*dyāvābhūmī*)—heaven and earth
- जनयन् (*janayan*)—producing
- एकः (*ekaḥ*)—without a helper (without a second)
- देवः (*devaḥ*)—shining and abiding

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Īśvara, who has eyes spread everywhere, faces everywhere, arms spread everywhere and feet extended in every direction, sets the heaven-world in motion with his arms.

### Printed p. 206

He sets the earth in motion with his moving feet. Producing heaven and earth, he shines without a second.

##### English translation
Having eyes everywhere, and having a face everywhere, having arms
everywhere, and having feet everywhere, he traverses (heaven) with his
arms, (earth) with his swift-moving (feet), and exists a god without com-
panion generating heaven and earth.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In this Ṛk the great nature of Viśvakarman (Parameśvara) is described. The idea in this Ṛk is indicated in the first Ṛk of the 90th sūkta of this same maṇḍala, in the Ṛk सहस्रशीर्षा पुरुषः (*sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*). In place of the word विश्वतः (*viśvataḥ*) in this Ṛk, the word सहस्र (*sahasra*) is used there. The meanings of these two words are the same; there is no difference. In the present Ṛk it is said that the eyes of that Viśvakarman are spread everywhere. Here a doubt arises. Has Parameśvara, like ordinary men, eyes, face, arms and legs? Does he, with their help, carry out the works of creation and the like as other men do? To answer these questions one must describe the great nature of Parameśvara himself.

An ordinary man sees with his eyes. Without eyes he cannot see. In the same way he performs work with his arms and movement with his feet. But in the case of the Supreme Self this rule does not apply. He is without parts; he has no need of parts. Since all the things and beings in the world are parts of the Supreme Self and the consciousness of the Supreme Self fills them, and since there is no thing that the Supreme Self does not pervade, there is no thing that the Supreme Self does not see or does not know. Moreover, since all kinds of powers, such as the power of seeing and the power of moving, are parts of the consciousness of the Supreme Self, the Supreme Self does not have to use his eyes to see, as others do, nor to use his arms to work, nor to use his feet to move; that is, this Supreme Self has no need of eyes, face, arms and feet. Without these he can do any work. For he is consciousness itself, and whatever work is to be done, there must be the impulse of consciousness; otherwise it does not happen. Since the Supreme Self is the source of all the consciousness that is manifested in beings in the world, there is nothing that he does not know. The words eye, face, arm and foot mentioned here, the respective

### Printed p. 207

senses are used here to indicate the works that the senses perform. The works that these senses have to carry out the Supreme Self can do without the help of the senses. Therefore, "he has eyes everywhere" means that, since the Supreme Self pervades all places (is all-pervading), he is able to see and know everything: such is the intention. The word चक्षुः (*cakṣuḥ*), eyes, is only for description. The Supreme Self has no need of separate organs called eyes, as we have. Likewise with the arms and the rest. If that is so, what need is there to name these limbs here? The likeness of the senses is stated only in order to explain clearly, so that the mind may grasp it, the unfathomable power of the Supreme Self. This very matter is explained clearly by an example in the second half of this Ṛk.

बाहुभ्यां पतत्रैः सं धमति द्यावाभूमिा (*bāhubhyāṃ patatraiḥ saṃ dhamati dyāvābhūmiā*): the arms of this Parameśvara set the atmosphere or heaven in motion. His feet pervade the earth and set it in motion. This statement is made in order to show that there is a very great distance between the earth and the heaven and atmosphere, and that, even so, Parameśvara by his great power pervades at one and the same time the three worlds, which lie at such distances, and sets them in motion. Besides, how great these heaven and earth are, how immense the distance between them is, and that in spite of this he pervades and sets them in motion at one time by his power: all this indicates the exceeding power and capacity of this Parameśvara. Therefore the intention is that Parameśvara, who has such unlimited power and capacity, creates and maintains the whole world by his extraordinary greatness alone, even without the help of any implements such as original material and instruments.

देव एकः (*deva ekaḥ*): so far it has been said that Parameśvara can create the world by his great power alone, without any material causes, that is, without any instruments. But in this work of creation did this Parameśvara have any helpers? Was there the help of instruments? The words देव एकः (*deva ekaḥ*) are used to state that there was none. This Supreme Self, being alone, without any kind of help or instruments, carried out this whole work of creation by himself alone by his greatness. In this matter:

इदग्ं सर्वमसृजत । यदिदं किंच । तत्सृष्टाव तदेवानु प्राविशत् । तदनु प्रविश्य । सच्च त्यच्चाभवत् । (*idagṃ sarvamasṛjata | yadidaṃ kiṃca | tatsṛṣṭāva tadevānu prāviśat | tadanu praviśya | sacca tyaccābhavat |*) (Trai. U. 8-6)**NOTE**

Upaniṣadic sentences of this kind state how the Supreme Self made the creation of the world. The Supreme Self, who was in an unmanifest form (non-being), created this world and entered it as the inner controller. By doing so, the Supreme Lord, who had been of unmanifest form, became of manifest form

### Printed p. 208

that is, he became both unmanifest and manifest. The one Self-principle was transformed into many kinds of moving and unmoving things. The consciousness that was concentrated in the Supreme Self became manifest in small parts in all beings. The chief intention is that the Supreme Self carried out all these works without anyone's help, by his own greatness alone.

It has been stated above that there is no room for the objection how the creation of the world is possible without adhiṣṭhāna and ārambhaṇa. The praise अणोरणीयान् महतो महीयान् (*aṇoraṇīyān mahato mahīyān*) tells the greatness of Īśvara. This Īśvara is the adhiṣṭhāna, and he is the ārambhaṇa and the material cause; since the whole world consists of his particular states, there is no material cause other than him. By the words "बाहुभ्यां धमति ; पतत्रैः धमति (*bāhubhyāṃ dhamati ; patatraiḥ dhamati*)" the efficient cause has been stated. By विश्वतश्चक्षुः (*viśvataścakṣuḥ*) and the rest the all-pervadingness is stated. Just as pots and the like are transformed from clay into other forms, so Īśvara, who was without a second, takes other forms and manifests in many ways. Agni, Vāyu and Āditya are all transformations of him. This Ṛk is quoted in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad. The same mantra is recited also in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (Tai. Saṃ. 4-6-2-4) and in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka (Nā. U. 10-1-3)**NOTE**. In some places बाहुभ्यां (*bāhubhyāṃ*) is explained as the two arms called dharma and adharma. Śaṅkarācārya has explained धमति (*dhamati*) as संयोजयति (*saṃyojayati*). The purport is that he joins men with arms and birds with wings. There are still other differences of purport of this kind. On the whole the purport is that all the activities of the whole world are impelled by Īśvara. How? Thus:

य एको जालवानीशत ईशनीभिः सर्वाल्लोकानीशत ईशनीभिः । य विवैक उद्भवे संभवे च एतद्विदुरमृतास्ते भवंति ॥ (*ya eko jālavānīśata īśanībhiḥ sarvāllokānīśata īśanībhiḥ | ya vivaika udbhave saṃbhave ca etadviduramṛtāste bhavaṃti ‖*) (Kveṃ. U. 3-1)**NOTE**

The Supreme Person who spreads the net that is the form of his power, who by his majesty is the lord of the whole world, he is eternal. He attains unity with the world that has been created and has attained its state of continuance.

रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव तदस्य रूपं प्रति चक्षणाय । इंद्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते युक्ता ह्यस्य हरयः शता दश ॥ (*rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva tadasya rūpaṃ prati cakṣaṇāya | iṃdro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate yuktā hyasya harayaḥ śatā daśa ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-47-18)

In passages of this kind, as explained before, Īśvara by his power of lordship is of the form of the universe. This is explained still more clearly in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad in this way.

### Printed p. 209

अग्निर्यथैको भुवनं प्रविष्टो रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव । एकस्तथा सर्वभूतांतरात्मा रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बहिश्च ॥ (*agniryathaiko bhuvanaṃ praviṣṭo rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva | ekastathā sarvabhūtāṃtarātmā rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo bahiśca ‖*) (Kaṭh. 2-2-11)**NOTE**

Just as fire, pervading the earth, becomes fire in whatever thing it takes hold of, so this Supreme Self takes on the very form of whatever thing he creates. Likewise,

वायुर्यथैको भुवनं प्रविष्टः रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव । (*vāyuryathaiko bhuvanaṃ praviṣṭaḥ rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva |*) (Ka. 2-2-12)**NOTE**

Just as the wind, moving about in the world, takes on the form of whatever thing it enters, so this Supreme Self too takes on all forms.

विश्वरूपं हरिणं जातवेदसं परायणं ज्योतिरेकं तपंतं । सहस्ररश्मिः शतधा वर्तमानः प्राणः प्रजानामुदयत्येष सूर्यः ॥ (*viśvarūpaṃ hariṇaṃ jātavedasaṃ parāyaṇaṃ jyotirekaṃ tapaṃtaṃ | sahasraraśmiḥ śatadhā vartamānaḥ prāṇaḥ prajānāmudayatyeṣa sūryaḥ ‖*) (Praśna. 1-8)**NOTE**

Āditya rises, he who has all forms, who is of golden form, all-knowing, the final refuge of the whole world, with a thousand rays, existing in thousands of forms, the life of the whole world. This is the Supreme Self.

एषोग्निस्तपत्येष सूर्य एष पर्जन्यो मघवानेष वायुः । एष पृथिवी रयिर्देवः सदसच्चामृतं च यत् ॥ (*eṣognistapatyeṣa sūrya eṣa parjanyo maghavāneṣa vāyuḥ | eṣa pṛthivī rayirdevaḥ sadasaccāmṛtaṃ ca yat ‖*) (Praśna. 25)**NOTE**

In the form of fire he burns. In the form of Āditya he shines. He is Parjanya, who abundantly pours down rain. He is the wind. He is the earth. He is the one of the form of being and the one of the form of non-being. Immortality too is he.

अरा इव रथनाभौ प्राणे सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितं । ऋचो यजूग्ंषि सामानि यज्ञः क्षत्रं ब्रह्म च ॥ (*arā iva rathanābhau prāṇe sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ | ṛco yajūgṃṣi sāmāni yajñaḥ kṣatraṃ brahma ca ‖*) (Praśna. 2-6)

Just as all the spokes of a wheel are joined to the central region that is the nave, so every thing in the world depends on this universal life-breath. The Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, sacrifice, the warrior power and wisdom all rest on it.

### Printed p. 210

इंद्रस्त्वं प्राण तेजसा रुद्रोऽसि परिरक्षिता । त्वमंतरिक्षे चरसि सूर्यस्त्वं ज्योतिषां पतिः ॥ (*iṃdrastvaṃ prāṇa tejasā rudro 'si parirakṣitā | tvamaṃtarikṣe carasi sūryastvaṃ jyotiṣāṃ patiḥ ‖*) (Praśna. 2-9)

O life-breath, who art the support of the whole world and of the form of the Supreme Self, by thy extraordinary power thou art Indra. Because thou art the protector, thou art Rudra. In the atmosphere too thou movest in the form of the sun. Thou art the lord of the whole sphere of lights. By sentences of this kind the Supreme Self's having faces everywhere and eyes everywhere is described and praised. This section will be explained later in the Special Topics of the Puruṣa-sūkta (10-90).**NOTE**

#### Ṛk 4

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> किं स्वि॒द्वनं॒ क उ॒ स वृ॒क्ष आ॑स॒ यतो॒ द्यावा॑पृथि॒वी नि॑ष्कृत॒क्षुः ।  
> मनीषिणो मनसा पृच्छतेदु तद्यदध्यतिष्ठद्भुवनानि धारयन् ॥ ४ ॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> किं । स्मित् । वनं । कः । ऊं इति । सः । वृक्षः । आस । यतः । द्यावापृधिवी इति । नि 5-  
> ततक्षुः ।  
> मनीषिणः । मनसा । पृच्छत । इत् । ऊं इति । तत् । यत् । अधिs अतिष्ठत् । भुवनानि । द्वारयन् ॥ ४ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> पूर्वस्यामृच्युक्तं ब्रह्मैव भूम्यादिकारणमिति । तदेवानया प्रश्नकथनव्याजेनोच्यते । लोके हि प्रौढं प्रासादं निर्मिमाणः कस्मिंश्चित्प्रौढे वने कंचिन्महांतं वृक्षं भित्त्वा तक्षणादिना स्तंबादिकं संपादयति । इह तु परमेश्वरप्रेरिता
> जगत्सृष्टारो यतो यस्माद्वनाद्यं वृक्षमादाय द्यावापृथिवी निष्टतक्षुः तक्षणेन
> द्यावापृथिव्यौ निष्पादितवंतः तद्वनं किं स्वित् किं नाम स्यात् । तथा क उ स वृक्ष
> आस । कस्तादृशो महान्वृकोऽभूत् । हे मनीषिणो मनस ईश्वराः तदुभयं
> मनसा जिज्ञासायुक्तन पृच्छतेदु । पृच्छतैव । किंचेश्वरो भुवनानि धारयन्य-

### Printed p. 211

> त्स्थानमध्यतिष्ठत् तवपि पृच्छत । एतस्य सर्वस्याप्युत्तरं ब्रह्म स वृक्ष आसीदित्यादिकमुत्तरं ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa says that in the previous Ṛk it was stated that Brahman alone is the cause of the earth and the rest, and that this very matter is now stated under the guise of a question. In the world, one who is building a great palace takes a great tree in some great forest, cuts it by hewing and the like, and prepares posts and the like. Here, however, those who create the world, impelled by Parameśvara, have taken a tree from a forest and, by hewing, have fashioned heaven and earth out of it: निष्टतक्षुः (*niṣṭatakṣuḥ*). What was that forest, किं स्वित् (*kiṃ svit*), what could it be called? And what was that tree, what great tree was it? He addresses the wise, the lords of the mind: ask both of these with your mind, with a longing to know. Moreover, ask also on what position Īśvara stood, holding the worlds. The answer to all this is Brahman: "he was that tree", and so on; that is the reply.**NOTE**

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- यतः (*yataḥ*)—from which forest-tree and the like
- द्यावापृथिवी (*dyāvāpṛthivī*)—heaven and earth
- निष्पतक्षुः (*niṣpatakṣuḥ*)—did the world-makers fashion
- वनं (*vanaṃ*)—that forest
- किं स्वित् (*kiṃ svit*)—which is it?
- सः वृक्षः (*saḥ vṛkṣaḥ*)—that tree
- क उ आस (*ka u āsa*)—which is it?
- मनीषिणिः (*manīṣiṇiḥ*)—O wise ones
- मनसा (*manasā*)—in the form of meditation
- पृच्छतेदु (*pṛcchatedu*)—inquire into and understand that matter
- यत् (*yat*)—which truth
- भुवनानि (*bhuvanāni*)—all the worlds
- धारयन् (*dhārayan*)—holding
- अध्यतिष्ठत् (*adhyatiṣṭhat*)—was stationed
- तत् (*tat*)—inquire into and understand that matter also

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

From which forest-tree and the like did the world-makers fashion heaven and earth? Which is that forest? Which is that tree? O wise ones, inquire into that matter in meditation and understand it. Inquire into that being which stood holding all the worlds.

##### English translation
Which was the forest, which the tree, from which they fabricated heaven and earth ? Inquire, sages, in your minds what (place) he was stationed in when holding the worlds.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

What was the tree that Viśvakarman (or the deities beginning with Indra) used for the construction of heaven and earth? From what forest did they bring that tree and use it? This is the question in the present Ṛk. Just as trees and the like are absolutely necessary for the building of a house, so the notion that they are absolutely necessary also for the building of the house called heaven and earth arises naturally. A metaphor of this kind (comparing the construction of heaven and earth to the building of a house, and calling the materials needed for it trees and the like) can be seen in many contexts in the Vedic sentences. They must be there also at the time of house-building. First, cutting down trees and preparing them; measuring the site and setting it right; planting four posts at the four corners with a good support, and constructing two great doors in the front; obtaining cross-beams, roof, rafters and the like: all these stages can be examined in the Saṃhitā sentences, where they are described in the work of creating the universe.

### Printed p. 212

Although the non-duality of Īśvara before creation is stated in many places, beginning with आत्मा वा इदमेक एवाग्र आसीत् । नान्यत् किंचन मिषत् (*ātmā vā idameka evāgra āsīt | nānyat kiṃcana miṣat*), and although Vedic sentences stating that the world of the form of being had no absolute non-existence and that the form of being cannot arise from the form of non-being were quoted above, and it was stated that for the world of the form of being the material causes of the form of being are the origin, yet, even while believing in the existence of material causes of the form of being, the seers in many places expressed their longing to know what the nature of these causal things is, and what the regions are where they are found, and the like.

पाकः पृच्छामि मनसा विजानन्देवानामेना निहिता पदानि । वत्से बष्कयेऽधि सप्त तंतून्वि तत्निरे कवय ओतवा उ ॥ (*pākaḥ pṛcchāmi manasā vijānandevānāmenā nihitā padāni | vatse baṣkaye 'dhi sapta taṃtūnvi tatnire kavaya otavā u ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-5)

In Āditya, who is the abode of the whole universe, the poets have spread seven threads in order to weave the warp and weft that is the form of the world. What are they? Even the deities cannot know the truth of the highest meaning. Therefore I, of small understanding, of unripe intellect, unable to know the secret principles, wish to know these.

किं स्विध्वनं क उ स वृक्ष आस यतो द्यावापृथिवी निष्पतक्षुः । संतस्थाने अजरे इतऊती अहानि पूर्विरुषसो जरंत ॥ (*kiṃ svidhvanaṃ ka u sa vṛkṣa āsa yato dyāvāpṛthivī niṣpatakṣuḥ | saṃtasthāne ajare itaūtī ahāni pūrviruṣaso jaraṃta ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-31-7)

What is the nature of the tree from which the deities fashioned heaven and earth? What is the forest in which that tree is found? For such a creation of the universe the praisers are grateful to the deities and praise them always. And they wish also to know these original principles. Sentences of this kind, full of longing (curiosity to know), are abundant. The act of measuring heaven and earth, the ancient dwelling places, is also described.

इमामू ष्वासुरस्य श्रुतस्य महीं मायां वरुणस्य प्र वोचं । मानेनेव तस्थिवा अंतरिक्षे वि यो ममे पृथिवीं सूर्येण ॥ (*imāmū ṣvāsurasya śrutasya mahīṃ māyāṃ varuṇasya pra vocaṃ | māneneva tasthivā aṃtarikṣe vi yo mame pṛthivīṃ sūryeṇa ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-85-5)

"We praise the exceeding wisdom of that Varuṇa who, standing in the atmosphere, measures out and separates heaven and the earth with the sun, which is like a measuring rod." Sentences of this kind state the act of Varuṇa and the others of fixing measures for the worlds that they create.

### Printed p. 213

In the same way, in passages such as अयं षळुर्वीरमिमात (*ayaṃ ṣaḷurvīramimāta*) (6-47-3), this same indication of measures and act of construction are described. It is also well known that Viṣṇu, by his stride, delimited and divided the worlds.

It is the tradition that work on a house and the like begins from the east. Indra and the others follow that tradition too.

सद्मेव प्राचो वि मिनाय मानैर्वज्रेण खान्यतृणन्नदीनां । वृथासृजत्पथिभिर्दिीर्घयाथैः सोमस्य ता मद इंद्रश्चकार ॥ (*sadmeva prāco vi mināya mānairvajreṇa khānyatṛṇannadīnāṃ | vṛthāsṛjatpathibhirdiīrghayāthaiḥ somasya tā mada iṃdraścakāra ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2. 5-3)**NOTE**

Just as people build sacrificial houses by measuring from the east, so Indra too measured from the eastern quarter and created the earth and the rest. He also made the channels for the flow of the rivers. Thus acts of measuring are described. Like this act of indicating measures, the spreading out and extending of the worlds, making them come within the range of man's vision, and similar works are likewise possible by the favour of Indra, Agni, Varuṇa and others.

The door of the house that is the universe must also face east. Through this great door the rays of the sun must enter.

विदा दिवो विष्यन्नद्रिमुक्थैरायत्या उषसो अर्चिनो गुः । अपावृत व्रजिनीरुत्स्वर्गाद्वि दुरो मानुषीर्देव आवः ॥ (*vidā divo viṣyannadrimukthairāyatyā uṣaso arcino guḥ | apāvṛta vrajinīrutsvargādvi duro mānuṣīrdeva āvaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-45-1)

Indra was impelled by the praises. He wielded the thunderbolt. The rays of Uṣas spread everywhere. The sun rose. The sun opened the great doors, fit for the passage of men.

वि श्रयंतामृतावृधः प्रयै देवेभ्यो महीः । पावकासः पुरुस्पृहो द्वारो देवीरसश्चतः ॥ (*vi śrayaṃtāmṛtāvṛdhaḥ prayai devebhyo mahīḥ | pāvakāsaḥ puruspṛho dvāro devīrasaścataḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-142-6)

There is a praise that the deities of the doors, who cause the sacrifice to grow, who are of great nature, mighty to purify the world, and of separate position, should move far aside for the entrance of the gods and make room for an excellent entrance. Who these door deities are:

द्वारस्तु देव्यो याः प्रोक्ता विश्वेषां तास्तु पत्नयः । (*dvārastu devyo yāḥ proktā viśveṣāṃ tāstu patnayaḥ |*) (Bṛ. De. 3-6)

### Printed p. 214

It is stated that these door deities are the wives of the gods, that they dwell firmly in Agni, and that they are the protectors of the sacrifice, which is the root of the activity of the world.

विराट्समाड्विभ्वीः प्रभ्वीर्बह्वीश्च भूयसीश्च याः । दुरो घृतान्यक्षरन् ॥ (*virāṭsamāḍvibhvīḥ prabhvīrbahvīśca bhūyasīśca yāḥ | duro ghṛtānyakṣaran ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1.188-5)

The first two named in the verse are shining doors. They are the ways by which the gods come to the sacrifice. These doors are as wide as the earth. They are many in number. These doors pour out a stream of ghee.**NOTE** These doors are praised abundantly in the Āprī hymns. In the same way, principles that reflect the beams, the roof and so on of a house are also described. But in some places the skill of the maker of the house that is the universe is praised in this manner:

स इत्स्वपा भुवनेष्वास य इमे द्यावापृथिवी जजान । उर्वी गभीरे रजसी सुमेके अवंशे धीरः शच्या समैरत् ॥ (*sa itsvapā bhuvaneṣvāsa ya ime dyāvāpṛthivī jajāna | urvī gabhīre rajasī sumeke avaṃśe dhīraḥ śacyā samairat ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-56-3)

The works of Prajāpati show surpassing skill. He produced heaven and earth, and set the wide atmosphere (vaṃśa) in place without support. In this context the word vaṃśa may mean a supporting pillar or beam useful for a house.

This same idea is described at length in the Chāndogya in this manner:

असौ वादित्यो देवमधु तस्य द्यौरेव तिरश्चीनवंशोंतरिक्षमपूपो मरीचयः पुत्राः । (*asau vādityo devamadhu tasya dyaureva tiraścīnavaṃśoṃtarikṣamapūpo marīcayaḥ putrāḥ |*) (Chā. U. 3-1-1)

The sun, standing in the atmosphere, is the divine honey. This heaven itself is the cross-beam and the roof; the atmosphere is the honeycomb, and so on. Thus to build and set up the atmosphere and the rest without pillar or roof is also a skill. How is this?

सविता यंत्रैः पृथिवीमरम्मादस्कंभने सविता द्यामद्यंहत् । अश्वमिवाधुक्षद्दु निमंतरिक्षमतूर्ते बद्धं सविता समुद्रं ॥ (*savitā yaṃtraiḥ pṛthivīmarammādaskaṃbhane savitā dyāmadyaṃhat | aśvamivādhukṣaddu nimaṃtarikṣamatūrte baddhaṃ savitā samudraṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-149-1)

Savitṛ has firmly established the earth with binding materials. Without any supporting pillar he has made the atmosphere stand firm. All this is his greatness.

Heaven and earth and the atmosphere, all together, form the house of the universe. The earth is the support of all these. (Earth, भूमि (*bhūmi*), क्षा (*kṣā*), ग्मा (*gmā*)) It is the most extended. Earth, Urvī, Uttāna, Apāra: these

### Printed p. 215

show the extent of the earth and of the heavenly world. Only for the earth is the qualifying word idam ("this") used, to show its difference from the heavenly world and the atmosphere. In passages such as भूम्याश्चतस्रः प्रदितः (*bhūmyāścatasraḥ praditaḥ*) (10-19-8) the four quarters of this earth are stated. Those who dwell in this house of the universe, which includes the three worlds, are the five peoples. They are also called the five settlements. The five peoples are not only the men on the earth; the gods, gandharvas and the rest all belong to this group. For these five peoples, spread through the three worlds, a lamp in the house of the universe is indispensable. The light common to all is supplied by the sun.

महत्तन्नाम गुह्यं पुरुस्सृग्येन भूतं जनयो येन भव्यं । प्रत्नं जातं ज्योतिरदस्य प्रियं प्रियाः समविशंत पंच ॥ (*mahattannāma guhyaṃ purussṛgyena bhūtaṃ janayo yena bhavyaṃ | pratnaṃ jātaṃ jyotiradasya priyaṃ priyāḥ samaviśaṃta paṃca ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10.55-2)

The form of this Indra, who is of the nature of the sun, is great. It is mysterious. It is desired by all. By this greatness he has produced all the past and the future times. It is stated that the five peoples, the gods, gandharvas and others who dwell pervading the three worlds, live by worshipping the radiance of this all-pervading sun. Thus, besides the radiance common to all, since a separate light is necessary for each part of the house of the universe, the one original light has spread in three divisions. After the house of the universe was built, this light of the universe came into being. Its transformed form, Agni:

मूर्धा दिवो नाभिरग्निः पृथिव्या अथाभवदरती रोदस्योः । तं त्वा देवासोऽजनयंत देवं वैश्वानर ज्योतिरिदार्याय ॥ (*mūrdhā divo nābhiragniḥ pṛthivyā athābhavadaratī rodasyoḥ | taṃ tvā devāso 'janayaṃta devaṃ vaiśvānara jyotiridāryāya ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-5)(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-59-2)**NOTE**

He is like the head of the heavenly world, the navel of the earth. The gods produced this Agni for the Āryas (the revered), the gods and men and others.

वि सूर्य्य अमतिं न श्रियं सादोर्वाद्गर्वां माता जानती गात् । धन्वर्णसो नद्यंगिस्वादोअर्णाः स्थूणेव सुमिता दृंहत द्यौः ॥ (*vi sūryya amatiṃ na śriyaṃ sādorvādgarvāṃ mātā jānatī gāt | dhanvarṇaso nadyaṃgisvādoarṇāḥ sthūṇeva sumitā dṛṃhata dyauḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-45-2)

The sun rises. He spreads light. The heavenly world, like the supporting pillar of a house, bears the universe and stands firm. All this is the command of the sun, the light of the universe. The universal work of Agni, relating to the house of the universe, is reflected in the Vanaspati who is described in the Āprī hymns. He is well known as the lord of the house.

### Printed p. 216

The work of building the house of the universe in this manner belongs to the deities Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra and the rest. But Tvaṣṭṛ**NOTE** and the Ṛbhus, who have skill in that same work, are well known to have distinguished skill in this work. The skill in action of the Ṛbhus has been described earlier.

The purpose of the creation of the universe is not only the attainment of well-being by man. The gods, men and others help one another on both sides (परस्परं भावयंतः श्रेयः (*parasparaṃ bhāvayaṃtaḥ śreyaḥ*) Bha. Gī.)**NOTE**. When men nourish the gods by sacrifice, and the gods nourish men by rain and the like, and thus produce harmony in the activity of the universe, then the purpose of the whole creation of the universe is fulfilled. Therefore, just as man has the wish for a house and the like, the gods too have the same wish. The question where the tree for the building of this house came from, from which forest, is the special subject of the present Ṛk.

To this question the answer is found in the Vedic sentences themselves. In the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa this very question is quoted and then its answer is given. The question is only that which is in the sentences of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā; the answer, however, is in the sentences of the Brāhmaṇa.

को अद्धा वेद क इह प्रवोचत् । कुत आ जाता कुत इयं विसृष्टिः । अर्वाग्देवा अस्य विसर्जनाय । अथा को वेद यत आ बभूव । इयं विसृष्टिर्यत आ बभूव । यदि वा दधे यदि वा न । यो आस्त्याध्यक्षः परमे व्योमन् । सो अंग वेद यदि वा न वेद । किग्न् स्विद्वनं क उ स वृक्ष आसीत् । यतो द्यावापृथिवी निष्कृतक्षुः । मनीषिणो मनसा पृच्छतेदु तत् । यदध्यतिष्यद्भवनानि धारयन् । ब्रह्म वनं ब्रह्म स वृक्ष आसीत् । यतो द्यावापृथिवी निष्कृतक्षुः । मनीषिणो मनसा विब्रवीमि वः । ब्रह्माध्यतिष्यद्भवनानि धारयन् ॥ (*ko addhā veda ka iha pravocat | kuta ā jātā kuta iyaṃ visṛṣṭiḥ | arvāgdevā asya visarjanāya | athā ko veda yata ā babhūva | iyaṃ visṛṣṭiryata ā babhūva | yadi vā dadhe yadi vā na | yo āstyādhyakṣaḥ parame vyoman | so aṃga veda yadi vā na veda | kign svidvanaṃ ka u sa vṛkṣa āsīt | yato dyāvāpṛthivī niṣkṛtakṣuḥ | manīṣiṇo manasā pṛcchatedu tat | yadadhyatiṣyadbhavanāni dhārayan | brahma vanaṃ brahma sa vṛkṣa āsīt | yato dyāvāpṛthivī niṣkṛtakṣuḥ | manīṣiṇo manasā vibravīmi vaḥ | brahmādhyatiṣyadbhavanāni dhārayan ‖*) (Tai. Brā. 2-8-9-5, 6, 7)

All the ideas contained in the Ṛks 10-21-1 to 4 above are contained in these Brāhmaṇa sentences. What is the original cause of the creation of the world is the first question. Then what is the tree for this house of the universe, what is the forest, is the second question. Who is the overseer of this house of the universe is the third question. The answer to these three is stated clearly right here.

1) As to what the original cause of the creation of the universe is, there are schools of thought that do not believe in the authority of scripture, or do not give it special preference. There are also schools that say that Brahman is the principal cause of the creation of the universe, but he is only the efficient cause, while the material causes are different.

### Printed p. 217

(For making a pot, the potter is the efficient cause; clay is the material cause.) Or there are schools that say that everything undergoes a natural transformation and that Brahman's agency is not needed at all. For example, the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika school holds that atoms are the original cause. The Sāṃkhyas say that the independent and unconscious primal nature is the material cause. The Mādhyamikas (a group among the Buddhists) say that the world arises from the void. The Lokāyatikas (also a sect among the Buddhists) say that everything is transformed naturally and that the presidency of Brahman is not wanted. But the view of none of these is correct. The Brahman principle that is praised with epithets such as विश्वतत्त्वक्षुः (*viśvatattvakṣuḥ*), विश्वतोमुखः (*viśvatomukhaḥ*)**NOTE** and so on, and as Prajāpati, Viśvakarman, Hiraṇyagarbha and so on, that Brahman principle itself is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the whole creation and activity of the world.

2) Secondly, the construction of the house of the universe. In this context the commentator explains in this manner.

लोके हि गृहं चिकीर्षुः पुमान् वनं गत्वा तत्र किंचिद्वृक्षं छित्वा तदीयैः काष्ठैर्गृहं निर्मिमाते । तद्दृष्टांतेनात्रापि यतः यस्माद्वनजन्यात् द्यावापृथिवी द्युलोकभूलोकौ तक्षणेन निर्मितवंतः । तादृशं वनं किंस्विद्भवेत् । कश्च तादृशः स वृक्ष आसीत् ॥ (*loke hi gṛhaṃ cikīrṣuḥ pumān vanaṃ gatvā tatra kiṃcidvṛkṣaṃ chitvā tadīyaiḥ kāṣṭhairgṛhaṃ nirmimāte | taddṛṣṭāṃtenātrāpi yataḥ yasmādvanajanyāt dyāvāpṛthivī dyulokabhūlokau takṣaṇena nirmitavaṃtaḥ | tādṛśaṃ vanaṃ kiṃsvidbhavet | kaśca tādṛśaḥ sa vṛkṣa āsīt ‖*)

In the world, one who builds a house goes to the forest, cuts down some convenient tree there, and builds the house with its timber. By the same example, here too the question is: from what forest-tree have they built heaven and earth? What is that forest? That is the question. Brahman is that forest. Brahman is that tree. It is all-powerful: this is the answer.

3) The same answer holds for the question यः अस्य अध्यक्षः (*yaḥ asya adhyakṣaḥ*). Since this Brahman itself bears the whole world, it stands in the position of overseer of the whole world. It is the controller of all the activities of the world.

Another point must be noted in the use of a worldly example. To build a house, the whole tree is not used; only the parts needed for the house are used. Moreover, a house is not built entirely of wood; other materials are also necessary for it. But this symbol in the form of a tree, described in the Vedic sentences, includes the whole world. The whole world, moving and unmoving, is contained in this tree, which is of the form of Brahman, and this tree itself has spread out in the form of the universe. The nature of this tree of the universe is described in the Maitrāyaṇī Upaniṣad in this manner.

### Printed p. 218

द्वे नाव ब्रह्मणो रूपे मूर्तं चामूर्तं च । अथ यन्मूर्तं तदसत्यं, यदमूर्तं तत्सत्यं तद्ब्रह्म, तज्योतिः, यज्योतिः स अदित्यः............ प्रणीतारं भारूपं विगतनिद्रं विजरं विमृत्युं त्रि पदं, त्रैक्षरं, पुनः पंचधा ज्ञेयं निहितं गुहायामित्येवं ह्याहोर्द्वमूलं त्रिपाद्ब्रह्म शाखाकाशवाय्गुद्यदकभूम्यादय एकोऽश्वत्थनामैतद्ब्रह्मैतस्यैतत्तेजो यदसावादित्यः ॥ (*dve nāva brahmaṇo rūpe mūrtaṃ cāmūrtaṃ ca | atha yanmūrtaṃ tadasatyaṃ, yadamūrtaṃ tatsatyaṃ tadbrahma, tajyotiḥ, yajyotiḥ sa adityaḥ............ praṇītāraṃ bhārūpaṃ vigatanidraṃ vijaraṃ vimṛtyuṃ tri padaṃ, traikṣaraṃ, punaḥ paṃcadhā jñeyaṃ nihitaṃ guhāyāmityevaṃ hyāhordvamūlaṃ tripādbrahma śākhākāśavāygudyadakabhūmyādaya eko 'śvatthanāmaitadbrahmaitasyaitattejo yadasāvādityaḥ ‖*) (Mai. U. 6-3, 4)**NOTE**

Brahman has two forms, embodied and unembodied. In the practical sense, what is embodied is untrue. What is unembodied is true. That is of the form of radiance. This radiance is the sun. He is of the form of the Udgītha and of the form of Praṇava. He is ageless, deathless, has three feet and three syllables. He is the one who is hidden in the cave that is the heart. The Śrutis praise this Supreme Self in this manner. For this Supreme Brahman with three feet, the root is in the upper part. The sky, wind, fire, water and earth are the branches of this tree that is of the form of Brahman. This Supreme Brahman is well known by the name Aśvattha. He is also called the sun, who is of the form of radiance. This radiance itself is the Praṇava.

Thus the identity of the tree of the universe and the sun, who is of the form of the Supreme Brahman, is stated in many places. In the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā too, praising the greatness of this tree in the form of the sun, it is stated in this manner.

यस्मिन् वृक्षे मध्वदः सुपर्णा निविशंते सुवते चाधि विश्वे । तस्यॆदाहुः पिप्पलं स्वाद्वग्रे तन्नोन्नशद्यः पितरं न वेद ॥ (*yasmin vṛkṣe madhvadaḥ suparṇā niviśaṃte suvate cādhi viśve | tasyèdāhuḥ pippalaṃ svādvagre tannonnaśadyaḥ pitaraṃ na veda ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-22)

In that tree, which is of the form of the Supreme Self, the bird-like senses, easy of movement and enjoying the tasting of knowledge, in their time of sleep turn back from their objects and merge in the Self itself, and afterwards, in the waking time, again come into contact with the fruits that are their objects. The nature of such a Supreme Self, that is, the taste of the fruit of this tree in the form of the Supreme Self, surpasses the taste of all other fruits. And not only does it bear a tasteful fruit, but also:

धर्ता दिवो विभाति तपसस्पृथिव्यामिति । धर्ता ह्येष दिवो विभाति तपसस्पृथिव्यां धर्ता देवो देवानाममर्त्यस्तपोज्णा ॥ (*dhartā divo vibhāti tapasaspṛthivyāmiti | dhartā hyeṣa divo vibhāti tapasaspṛthivyāṃ dhartā devo devānāmamartyastapojṇā ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 14-1-4-7) **GLOSS**

### Printed p. 219

This same sun is the supporter of all the worlds and the giver of fruit to all the worlds. The fruit of this tree in the form of the sun is both nourishing and full of sap. (पिप्पलं स्वादु (*pippalaṃ svādu*)) Who is the cause that this tree supports the worlds and gives excellent fruit? It is:

अहं वृक्षस्य रेरिवा । कीर्तिः पृष्ठं गिरेरिव । ऊर्ध्वपवित्रो वाजिनीवस्वमृतमस्मि । द्रविणग्ं सवर्चसं । सुमेधा अमृतोक्षितः । (*ahaṃ vṛkṣasya rerivā | kīrtiḥ pṛṣṭhaṃ gireriva | ūrdhvapavitro vājinīvasvamṛtamasmi | draviṇagṃ savarcasaṃ | sumedhā amṛtokṣitaḥ |*) (Tai. U. 1.10-1)**NOTE**

I myself am the impeller of this tree. My fame is renowned like the peak of a mountain. The eternal sun is a treasure of radiance, and so on: thus the Supreme Self, of the form of the sun, proclaims. (This is the statement of Triśaṅku, who had realised the Supreme Self.) I am also of the form of the tree. The description of its nature is this:

ऊर्ध्वमूलोऽवाक्‌शाख एषोऽश्वत्थस्सनातनः । तदेव शुक्रं तद्ब्रह्म तदेवामृतमुच्यते ॥ तस्मिन् लोकाः श्रितास्सर्वॆ तदु नात्येति कश्चन । एतद्वै तत् । (*ūrdhvamūlo 'vākśākha eṣo 'śvatthassanātanaḥ | tadeva śukraṃ tadbrahma tadevāmṛtamucyate ‖ tasmin lokāḥ śritāssarvè tadu nātyeti kaścana | etadvai tat |*) (Kaṭha. 32. 6 1)**NOTE**

The root of this ancient Aśvattha tree is above. Its branches spread downwards. It is utterly pure. This itself is the Supreme Brahman. It is immortal. In it alone all the worlds are established. Nothing goes beyond it. This is the truth.

#### Ṛk 5

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> या ते॒ धामा॑नि पर॒माणि॒ याव॒ना या म॑ध्य॒मा वि॑श्वकर्मन्नु॒तेमा ।  
> शिक्षा॒ सखि॑भ्यो ह॒विषि॑ स्वधावः स्व॒यं य॑जस्व त॒न्वं॑ वृधा॒नः ॥

> उत । इमा ।  
> शिक्ष । सखभ्य । हविषि । स्वधावः । स्वयं । यजस्व । तन्वं । वृधानः ॥ ५ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> साकमेधेषु वैश्वकर्मण एककपालस्य या ते धामानीत्येषा याज्या ।
> सूत्रितं च । विश्वकर्मन्हविषा वावृधानो या ते धामानि परमाणि यावमा ।
> आ. २-१८ । इति ॥ पूर्वोक्तस्य पशोर्हविष एष्येव याज्या । सूत्रितं च । या ते
> धामानि परमाणि यावमा य इमे द्यावापृथिवी जनित्री । आ. ३-८ । इति ॥
> अनया भौवनो विश्वकर्मा जगत्कारणं विश्वकर्मदेवं स्तौति । हे विश्वकर्मन् या यानि ते तव परमाणि धामानि शरीराणि संति या यानि च मध्यमानि
> शरीराणि संति उतापि च या यान्यवमावमानि धामानि शरीराणि संति उतापि च
> तानीमानि सर्वाणि शरीराणि सखिभ्योऽस्मभ्यं यष्टुं हविषि मयि हविर्भूते सति
> शक्ष ! देहि । हे स्वधावो हनिर्लक्षणान्नवन् स्वयमेव त्वं तन्नं स्वकीयं
> पूर्वोक्तं त्रिविधं शरीरं वृधानो हविषा वर्धमानः सन् । अनेन धामत्रैविध्योपन्यासेनोत्तमभूतानि देवादिशरीराणि मध्यमभूतानि मनुष्यादिशरीराणि
> निकृष्टभूतानि कृमिकीतादिशरीराणि च परिगृहीतानि । किं बहुना सर्वं जगदुपात्तं
> भवति । उक्तव्यतिरेकेण निरवयवस्य परमेश्वरस्य विग्रहाभावात् तदैक्षत बहुः स्यां
> प्रजायेय । छां. उ. ६-२-३ । इत्यादिश्रुतिभ्यः परमेश्वरस्यॆव देवादिभेदेन
> बहुभावावगमात् ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

This Ṛk is the yājyā verse for the one-potsherd cake of Viśvakarman in the Sākamedha offerings. He cites the sūtra (Ā. 2-18), which has the Ṛk's opening as the yājyā. Of the animal offering mentioned before, the same Ṛk is the yājyā of the oblation, and a second sūtra (Ā. 3-8) is cited for that. By this Ṛk Viśvakarman, the Lord of the worlds, the cause of the world, is praised. O Viśvakarman, whatever supreme, whatever middle and whatever lowest bodies are yours, all these bodies give to us, your friends, to offer sacrifice, when the oblation is made. O possessor of the oblation in the form of food, yourself, increasing your own threefold body already mentioned through the oblation, offer worship. By this statement of the threefold abodes, the bodies of the gods and others are taken as the highest, the bodies of men and others as the middle, and the bodies of worms, insects and the like as the lowest. In short, the whole world is included, since the Supreme Lord, who is without parts, has no form apart from what is stated. This follows from Śruti passages such as तदैक्षत बहु स्यां प्रजायेय (*tadaikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeya*) (Chā. U. 6-2-3), which show that the one Lord himself becomes many through the distinctions of gods and the rest.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- विश्वकर्मन् (*viśvakarman*)—O Viśvakarman
- ते (*te*)—your
- या (*yā*)—which
- परमाणि धामानि (*paramāṇi dhāmāni*)—most excellent bodies there are
- या (*yā*)—which
- मध्यमा (*madhyamā*)—those of middle form
- उत (*uta*)—and
- या (*yā*)—which
- अवमा (*avamā*)—those that are the lowest
- ता इमा (*tā imā*)—all those various bodily forms
- हविषि (*haviṣi*)—at the time of offering the oblation
- सखिभ्यः (*sakhibhyaḥ*)—to us, your friends
- शिक्ष (*śikṣa*)—give
- स्वधावः (*svadhāvaḥ*)—O Viśvakarman, possessor of food
- स्वयं (*svayaṃ*)—you yourself also
- तन्नं (*tannaṃ*)—this body of yours in all its forms
- वृधानः (*vṛdhānaḥ*)—nourishing
- यजस्व (*yajasva*)—worship

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Viśvakarman, possessor of food in the form of the oblation, whatever excellent, middle and lowest varieties of body are yours, all these various bodily forms, at the time of offering the oblation, give to us your friends. O Viśvakarman, possessor of food, do you yourself also, nourishing this body of yours in all its forms, offer worship.

##### English translation
Grant to your friends, Vishwakarman, at the oblation, your best, your worst and your intermediate forms, and to these do you yourself,

### Printed p. 221

possessor of the oblation, becoming augmented in person (by oblations), offer worship.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

The extension of Viśvakarman's body, which is of the form of the universe, is indicated in the present Ṛk. In this extension there are three varieties: supreme, middle and lowest. These may be the heavenly world, the atmosphere and the earth. Or they may be threefold as of the form of gods, the form of men, and the form of worms, insects and the like. That is, the purport is that everything in the universe, all that is sentient and insentient, is a special manifestation of the divine glory of the Lord. This extension in the form of the universe is the fruit of the sacrifice. How this extension takes place is explained in the present Ṛk; what the nature of the sacrifice of the Self is, and how all-pervasiveness results from it, will be stated in the Special Topics of the next Ṛk.

तदैक्षत बहु स्यां प्रजायेय (*tadaikṣata bahu syāṃ prajāyeya*) (Chā. U. 6-2-3)

As soon as the Lord, the one without a second, wished "I must be extended in many forms", he attained manyness. This principle, which was in a subtle form, took on a threefold body, created the three worlds, and expanded in all three worlds. How is that?

हिरण्यमांडं व्यरुजन्नाह तर्हि का चन प्रतिष्ठास तदेनमिदमेव हिरण्मयमांडं यावत्संवत्सरस्य वेलासी तावद्भिभ्रत्पर्यप्लवत । (*hiraṇyamāṃḍaṃ vyarujannāha tarhi kā cana pratiṣṭhāsa tadenamidameva hiraṇmayamāṃḍaṃ yāvatsaṃvatsarasya velāsī tāvadbhibhratparyaplavata |*) (Śa. Brā. 11-1-6-2)

The golden egg floated on the water for a year. After a year Prajāpati appeared. At that time Prajāpati had no resting place. He too, for a year, depended on the egg in the form of the golden womb, and afterwards uttered speech. How is that?

स भूरिति व्याहरत्सेयं पृथिव्यभवद्भुव इति तदिदमंतरिक्षमभवत्स्वरिति सासौ दौरभवत्तस्मादु................ (*sa bhūriti vyāharatseyaṃ pṛthivyabhavadbhuva iti tadidamaṃtarikṣamabhavatsvariti sāsau daurabhavattasmādu................*) (Śa. Brā. 11-1-6-3)

After a year Prajāpati uttered भूः (*bhūḥ*). This became the earthly world (the earth). The word he uttered, भुवः (*bhuvaḥ*), became the atmosphere. And the word he uttered, स्वः (*svaḥ*), became the heavenly world. The Lord is he who pervades these three worlds and is beyond them. These three worlds are three bodies. They became an extension in the form of space. In the other forms too, the pervasion of this threefold extension is possible, and over and above the three, a still further greatness; thus it is praised in the Taittirīya and other texts in this manner.

### Printed p. 222

भूर्भुवस्सुवरिति वा एतास्तिस्रो व्याहृतयः । तासामुहस्मैतां चतुर्थीं । माहाच मस्यः प्रवेदयते । मह इति । तद् ब्रह्म । स आत्मा । अंगान्यन्या देवताः ॥ (*bhūrbhuvassuvariti vā etāstisro vyāhṛtayaḥ | tāsāmuhasmaitāṃ caturthīṃ | māhāca masyaḥ pravedayate | maha iti | tad brahma | sa ātmā | aṃgānyanyā devatāḥ ‖*)

भूरिति ना अयं लोकः । भुव इत्यंतरिक्षं । सुवरित्यसौ लोकः । मह इत्यादित्यः । आदित्येन वाव सर्वॆ लोका महीयंते ॥ (*bhūriti nā ayaṃ lokaḥ | bhuva ityaṃtarikṣaṃ | suvarityasau lokaḥ | maha ityādityaḥ | ādityena vāva sarvè lokā mahīyaṃte ‖*) (Tai. U. 1-5-1, 2)**NOTE**

भूः (*bhūḥ*), भुवः (*bhuvaḥ*), सुवः (*suvaḥ*) are the three vyāhṛtis manifested by Prajāpati. These are within the range of the worlds. The fourth principle, the great, which goes beyond them, was realised by Māhācamasya, who knew its greatness; that is the divine Self. All the other deities are its transformations. This is the Supreme Brahman.

भूः (*bhūḥ*) is this earthly world. भुवः (*bhuvaḥ*) is the atmosphere. सुवः (*suvaḥ*) is the heavenly world. महः (*mahaḥ*) is the sun. Through the sun these three worlds attained greatness. In what other forms, apart from the forms of the worlds भूः (*bhūḥ*) and the rest, the divine body of Prajāpati is extended, is this:

भूरिति वा अग्निः । भुव इति वायुः । सुवरित्यादित्यः । मह इति चंद्रमाः । चंद्रमसा वाव सर्वाणि ज्योतीगंषि महीयंते । (*bhūriti vā agniḥ | bhuva iti vāyuḥ | suvarityādityaḥ | maha iti caṃdramāḥ | caṃdramasā vāva sarvāṇi jyotīgaṃṣi mahīyaṃte |*) (Tai. U. 1-5-2)

भूः (*bhūḥ*) is Agni. भुवः (*bhuvaḥ*) is Vāyu. सुवः (*suvaḥ*) is the sun. महः (*mahaḥ*) is the moon. By the power of the moon all the luminous bodies attain greatness.

भूरिति वा ऋचः । भुव इति सामानि । सुवरिति यजूग्ंषि । मह इति ब्रह्म । ब्रह्मणा वाव सर्वे वेदा महीयंते (*bhūriti vā ṛcaḥ | bhuva iti sāmāni | suvariti yajūgṃṣi | maha iti brahma | brahmaṇā vāva sarve vedā mahīyaṃte*) (Tai. U. 1-5-2)

भूः (*bhūḥ*) is the Ṛgveda. भुवः (*bhuvaḥ*) is the Sāman. सुवः (*suvaḥ*) is the Yajurveda. महः (*mahaḥ*) is Brahman. Through Brahman all the Vedas attain greatness.

भूरिति वै प्राणः । भुव इत्यपानः । सुवरिति व्यानः । मह इत्यन्नं । अन्नेन वाव सर्वे प्राणा महीयंते । (*bhūriti vai prāṇaḥ | bhuva ityapānaḥ | suvariti vyānaḥ | maha ityannaṃ | annena vāva sarve prāṇā mahīyaṃte |*) (Tai. U. 1-5-4)

भूः (*bhūḥ*) is prāṇa. भुवः (*bhuvaḥ*) is apāna. सुवर्ण (*suvarṇa*)**NOTE** is vyāna. महः (*mahaḥ*) is food. Through food all the vital breaths attain greatness. In this way the three vyāhṛtis are praised as the three varieties of body of the Lord, and the fourth as the greatness that is beyond them. What are the three kinds of principles produced from these three worlds? How do these reflect the Lord? It is as follows.

### Printed p. 223

प्रजापतिर्लोकानभ्यतपत्तेषां तप्यमानानां रसान् प्रावृहदग्निं पृथिव्या वायुमंतरिक्षादादित्यं दिवः ॥ (*prajāpatirlokānabhyatapatteṣāṃ tapyamānānāṃ rasān prāvṛhadagniṃ pṛthivyā vāyumaṃtarikṣādādityaṃ divaḥ ‖*) (Chā. U. 4-17-1)

Prajāpati performed meditative austerity directed to the worlds, to obtain their essence. Then he caused Agni from the earth, Vāyu from the atmosphere and the sun from the heavenly world to be manifested outward and shine.

स एतास्ति स्रो देवता अभ्यतपत्तासां तप्यमानानां रसान् प्रावृहदग्नेर्यचो वायोर्यजूग्ंषि सामान्यादित्यात् । (*sa etāsti sro devatā abhyatapattāsāṃ tapyamānānāṃ rasān prāvṛhadagneryaco vāyoryajūgṃṣi sāmānyādityāt |*) (Chā. U. 4-17-2)

He performed austerity directed to these three deities. Then he pressed out the essence of those deities. From Agni came the Ṛks, from Vāyu the Yajus formulas, from the sun the Sāman chants.

स एतां त्रयीं विद्यामभ्यतपत्तस्यास्तप्यमानाया रसान् प्रावृहद्भूरिश्यृग्भो भुवरिति यजुभ्यः स्वरिति सामभ्यः ॥ (*sa etāṃ trayīṃ vidyāmabhyatapattasyāstapyamānāyā rasān prāvṛhadbhūriśyṛgbho bhuvariti yajubhyaḥ svariti sāmabhyaḥ ‖*) (Bhā. U. 4-17-3)**NOTE**

When he performed austerity directed to this threefold knowledge, he made भूः (*bhūḥ*) shine forth by the Ṛk mantras, भुवः (*bhuvaḥ*) by the Yajus mantras, and स्वः (*svaḥ*) by the Sāmans. All the manifestations of new principles described in this way are the extension of the body of Prajāpati. This extension and this pervasion are also the fruit of the sacrifice that is austerity. For that very reason it is stated in the next Ṛk: हविषा तन्नं वावृधानः (*haviṣā tannaṃ vāvṛdhānaḥ*)**NOTE**. How the sacrifice is thus the root cause of the extension of Prajāpati's body will be stated in the Special Topics of the next Ṛk.

Regarding the use: in the single-potsherd offering made to the deity Viśvakarman in the Sākamedha sacrifices, this Ṛk, या ते धामानि (*yā te dhāmāni*), is to be recited as the yājyā mantra; this is explained in the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra by the sūtra विश्वकर्मन्हविषा वावृधानो या ते धामानि परमाणि यावमा (*viśvakarmanhaviṣā vāvṛdhāno yā te dhāmāni paramāṇi yāvamā*) (Ā. 2-18). And in the animal offering in the same sacrifice, when the oblation is offered, this same Ṛk is to be recited as the yājyā mantra; this is explained in the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra by the sūtra या ते धामानि परमाणि यावमा य इमे ध्यावापृथिवी जनित्रि (*yā te dhāmāni paramāṇi yāvamā ya ime dhyāvāpṛthivī janitri*) (Ā. 3-8).
