They answered: "We lived dumb, without the help of speech, living by the breaths of inhalation and exhalation, seeing with the eyes, hearing with the ears, knowing everything with the mind, and begetting offspring with the seed." After they had said this, speech entered the body with dignity.

In the same way, when the eye, the ear and the mind also each left the body and went out for a year, the other senses, without that one sense, carried on their work. The man remained alive. Whichever of them left the body, no kind of decay came to the remaining senses of the body. After that the breath wished to test its own distinction.

अथ ह प्राण उत्क्रिमिष्यन्यथा महासुहयः सैंधवः पद्वीशशंकून् संवृहे- (*atha ha prāṇa utkrimiṣyanyathā mahāsuhayaḥ saiṃdhavaḥ padvīśaśaṃkūn saṃvṛhe-*)

### Printed p. 255

देवं हैवेमान् प्राणान् संववर्ह ते होचुर्मा भगव उत्क्रमीर्न वै रक्ष्यामस्त्वदृते जीवितुमिति तस्यो मे बलिं कुरुतेति तथेति ॥ (*devaṃ haivemān prāṇān saṃvavarha te hocurmā bhagava utkramīrna vai rakṣyāmastvadṛte jīvitumiti tasyo me baliṃ kuruteti tatheti ‖*) (Bṛ. U. 6-1-13)

When the breath wished to test its own distinction and power, it began to leave the body. At once all the other senses became loose. As a fine horse of the Sindhu country, trying to run, shakes and pulls its rope and tears up together all the pegs that serve to bind its feet and starts off, so this breath loosened all the senses that depended on it, so that they would leave the body together with it. Then the senses begged: "O breath, do not leave us. We cannot live without you. You alone are the best of us all." Then the breath said to them: "If I am the best, offer me your service as an oblation." As soon as it asked, they agreed, saying "So be it." The Supreme Brahman is present in this form of breath, which is the lord of the senses and the nourisher of the senses. The same matter, that without it the other senses are of no use, is also stated in the Praśna Upaniṣad. This account is somewhat different from the one given above. How? Thus—

अथ हैनं भार्गवो वैदर्भिः पप्रच्छ । भगवन् कत्येव देवाः प्रजां विधारयंते ? कतर एतत्पकाशयंते । कः पुनरेषां वरिष्ठ इति ॥ (*atha hainaṃ bhārgavo vaidarbhiḥ papraccha | bhagavan katyeva devāḥ prajāṃ vidhārayaṃte ? katara etatpakāśayaṃte | kaḥ punareṣāṃ variṣṭha iti ‖*) (Praśna. 2-1)

"O revered one, which powers sustain this manifest world? Which are the powers that give light to this world? And which of them is the best?" Thus Bhārgava of the country of Vidarbha questioned Sippalāda. **NOTE** In answer Sippalāda spoke in this way.

तस्मै स होवाच आकाशे ह वा एष देवो वायुरग्निरापः पृथिवी वाज्मनश्चक्षुश्योत्रं च । ते प्रकाश्याभिवदंति वयपेतद्बाणमुवप्पभ्य विधानयामः ॥ (*tasmai sa hovāca ākāśe ha vā eṣa devo vāyuragnirāpaḥ pṛthivī vājmanaścakṣuśyotraṃ ca | te prakāśyābhivadaṃti vayapetadbāṇamuvappabhya vidhānayāmaḥ ‖*) (Praśna. 2-2)

Space is this power. Besides, air, fire, water, earth, speech, mind, eye and ear, all these are helpers. All of them give power to the world. Therefore they said: "All of us together keep this body firm; its support is from us." But the breath opposed this declaration and gave this reply.

तान् वरिष्ठः प्राण उवाच । मा मोहमापद्यथ अहमेवैतत्पंचधात्मानं प्रविभज्यैतद्बाणमवष्टभ्य विधारयामीति तेश्रद्धधाना बभूपुः ॥ (*tān variṣṭhaḥ prāṇa uvāca | mā mohamāpadyatha ahamevaitatpaṃcadhātmānaṃ pravibhajyaitadbāṇamavaṣṭabhya vidhārayāmīti teśraddhadhānā babhūpuḥ ‖*) (Praśne. 2-3)

### Printed p. 256

The breath, which is the highest of them all, said to them: "O senses, give up your false pride that you are the supporters of the body and that the good state of the body is from you. I myself, dividing my own form into five parts in your forms, sustain the body." Then none of them believed this word. To make them believe, the breath made this attempt.

सोऽभिमानादूर्ध्वमुत्क्रमत इव । तस्मिन्नुत्क्रामत्यथेतरे सर्व एवोत्क्रामंते । तस्मिंश्च प्रतिष्ठमाने सर्व एव प्रातिष्ठंते । तद्यथा मक्षिता मधुकरराजानमुत्क्रामंतं सर्वा एवोत्क्रामंते । तस्मिंश्च प्रतिष्ठमाने सर्वा एव प्रातिष्ठंत एवं वाङ्मनश्चक्षुःशोत्रं च ते प्रीताः प्राणं स्तुवंति ॥ (*so 'bhimānādūrdhvamutkramata iva | tasminnutkrāmatyathetare sarva evotkrāmaṃte | tasmiṃśca pratiṣṭhamāne sarva eva prātiṣṭhaṃte | tadyathā makṣitā madhukararājānamutkrāmaṃtaṃ sarvā evotkrāmaṃte | tasmiṃśca pratiṣṭhamāne sarvā eva prātiṣṭhaṃta evaṃ vāṅmanaścakṣuḥśotraṃ ca te prītāḥ prāṇaṃ stuvaṃti ‖*) (Praśna. 2-4)

Then the breath, to show its might, rose upward to leave the body. With it the other senses also rose up. When it was established again in the body, the other senses also were established. As, when the king of the bees rises, the other bees settle down, so all of them, understanding the superiority of the breath, praised it for all the comings and goings of the breath, which is like a king. Explaining this same matter in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, the greatness of the breath is stated in this way.

अथातो व्रतमीमांसा प्रजापतिर्ह कर्माणि सस्यजे तानि सृष्टान्यन्नोन्येनास्पर्धंत वदिष्टाम्येवाहमिति वाग्दध्रॆ द्रक्ष्याम्यहमिति चक्षुः श्रोष्याम्यहमिति श्रोश्रमेवमन्यानि कर्माणि यथा कर्म तानि मृत्युः श्रमो भूत्वा उपयेमे तान्याप्नोत्तान्याप्ता मृत्युरनारुंध तस्माच्छाम्यत्येव वाक् श्राम्यति चक्षुः श्राम्यति श्रोत्रमथेममेव नाप्पोद्योऽयं मध्यमः प्राणस्तानि ज्ञातुं दधिरे । (*athāto vratamīmāṃsā prajāpatirha karmāṇi sasyaje tāni sṛṣṭānyannonyenāspardhaṃta vadiṣṭāmyevāhamiti vāgdadhrè drakṣyāmyahamiti cakṣuḥ śroṣyāmyahamiti śrośramevamanyāni karmāṇi yathā karma tāni mṛtyuḥ śramo bhūtvā upayeme tānyāpnottānyāptā mṛtyuranāruṃdha tasmācchāmyatyeva vāk śrāmyati cakṣuḥ śrāmyati śrotramathemameva nāppodyo 'yaṃ madhyamaḥ prāṇastāni jñātuṃ dadhire |*) अयं वै नः श्रेष्ठो यः संचरंश्चासंचरंश्च न व्यथतेऽथो न रिष्यति हंतास्यैव सर्वे रूपमसामेति त एतस्यॆव सर्वे रूपमभवंस्तस्मादेत एतेनाख्यायंते प्राणा इति तेन ह वाव तत्कुलमाचक्षते यस्मिन् कुले भवति य एवं वेद य उ हैवं विदा स्पर्धतेऽनुशुष्यत्यनुशुष्य हैवांततो म्रियत इत्यध्यात्मं ॥ (*ayaṃ vai naḥ śreṣṭho yaḥ saṃcaraṃścāsaṃcaraṃśca na vyathate 'tho na riṣyati haṃtāsyaiva sarve rūpamasāmeti ta etasyèva sarve rūpamabhavaṃstasmādeta etenākhyāyaṃte prāṇā iti tena ha vāva tatkulamācakṣate yasmin kule bhavati ya evaṃ veda ya u haivaṃ vidā spardhate 'nuśuṣyatyanuśuṣya haivāṃtato mriyata ityadhyātmaṃ ‖*) (Bṛ. U. 1-5-21)

Prajāpati created the senses, which accomplish actions. As soon as they were created, rivalry arose among them. The eye said: "I am the one who sees"; speech said: "I am the one who speaks"; the ear said: "I am the one who hears." In the same way the other senses also, each

### Printed p. 257

displaying its own prowess, showed pride. Then death, the cause of weariness, caught them in its grip and took away their independence. Then the eye and the other senses all lost their vigour and were unable to carry on their actions. Death could not seize only the breath that stands in the middle and make it dependent. Then all the senses together, understanding their own weakness and the power of the breath, said: "This breath is more excellent than all of us. It is not subject to the harm of death," and considered all of them to be transformations of that breath. Since the breath is the chief of them all, the whole group of senses came to be called by the name of breath.

एषोग्निस्तपत्येष सूर्य एष पर्जन्यो मघवानेष वायुः । एष पृथिवी रयिर्देवः सदसच्चामृतं च यत् ॥ (*eṣognistapatyeṣa sūrya eṣa parjanyo maghavāneṣa vāyuḥ | eṣa pṛthivī rayirdevaḥ sadasaccāmṛtaṃ ca yat ‖*)

This breath is Agni and burns in the form of fire. It is the sun. It is the god Parjanya, the giver of wealth. It is the earth. It is the earthly wealth. All the principles, both what is and what is not, are this itself. It is eternal.

आरा इव रथनाभौ प्राणे सर्वं प्रतिष्ठितं । यचो यजूग्ंषि सामानि यज्ञः क्षत्रं ब्रह्म च ॥ (*ārā iva rathanābhau prāṇe sarvaṃ pratiṣṭhitaṃ | yaco yajūgṃṣi sāmāni yajñaḥ kṣatraṃ brahma ca ‖*) (Praśna. 2-6)

As all the spokes of a wheel are joined in the hub of the wheel, all the principles of the universe are established in this breath. The Ṛk, the Yajus, the Sāman, the sacrifice, the warrior power, and all the speech and all the powers called Brahman rest on this breath and are established here.

इंद्रस्त्वं प्राण तेजसा रुद्रोऽसि परिरक्षिता । त्वमंतरिक्षे चरसि सूर्यस्त्वं ज्योतिषां पतिः ॥ (*iṃdrastvaṃ prāṇa tejasā rudro 'si parirakṣitā | tvamaṃtarikṣe carasi sūryastvaṃ jyotiṣāṃ patiḥ ‖*) (Gra. 2-9) **NOTE**

O Prajāpati, who are of the nature of breath, you alone are the lord of the whole world (the creator), you alone are Rudra, and radiant you alone are the protector. You alone move in the sky in the form of the sun. You alone are the universal light, the original form of all lights.

Thus the principle that is described as the producer and the nourisher of the whole body, which consists of the group of senses, is described in the Upaniṣads and elsewhere as the all-pervading principle of light. That is what Sāyaṇa has stated in explaining the second purport of the epithet चक्षुषः पिता (*cakṣuṣaḥ pitā*).

चक्षुः ख्यापकं तेजः । तस्य उत्पादयिता। (*cakṣuḥ khyāpakaṃ tejaḥ | tasya utpādayitā|*) It is the light that is the means of knowledge and gives illumination.

### Printed p. 258

is indicated by the word चक्षुस् (*cakṣus*). The supreme principle in the form of Viśvakarman, who is the producer of this light, is the second purport. This purport too is in keeping with the context.

चक्षुः—ख्यातेर्वा चष्टेर्वा । (*cakṣuḥ—khyātervā caṣṭervā |*) The author of the Nirukta has explained the derivation of this word: it is formed either from the root ख्या (*khyā*) meaning knowledge, or from the root meaning sight (Ni. 4-3).

सूर्यो यथा सर्वलोकस्य चक्षुः । (*sūryo yathā sarvalokasya cakṣuḥ |*) (Kara. 5.11.) **NOTE**

Since it is described in the Upaniṣads and elsewhere that the sun is the eye of all the worlds, the same meaning is also appropriate in the verse under discussion. This eye of the world, being itself full of light, is the producer and nourisher of the other lights as well.

हिरण्मये परे कोशे विरजं ब्रह्म निष्कलं । तच्चुभ्रं ज्योतिषां ज्योतिस्तद्यदात्मविदो विदुः ॥ (*hiraṇmaye pare kośe virajaṃ brahma niṣkalaṃ | taccubhraṃ jyotiṣāṃ jyotistadyadātmavido viduḥ ‖*) (Muṇḍaka. 2-2-9)

In the highest golden sheath abides Brahman, stainless, perfect and pure. The meaning of Sāyaṇa is that the very Supreme Light, which is described as the light of all lights, the original light of all luminaries, is described here as चक्षुषः पिता (*cakṣuṣaḥ pitā*). The greatness of this light is this—

न तत्र सूरो भाति न चंद्रतारकं नेमा विद्युतो भांति कुतोऽयमग्निः । तमेव धांतमनुभाति सर्वं तस्य भासा सर्वमिदं विभाति ॥ (*na tatra sūro bhāti na caṃdratārakaṃ nemā vidyuto bhāṃti kuto 'yamagniḥ | tameva dhāṃtamanubhāti sarvaṃ tasya bhāsā sarvamidaṃ vibhāti ‖*) (Muṇḍaka. 2-2-10)

When this Supreme Light is pervading the whole universe in the form of the Supreme Brahman, that is, when Brahman is in the unmanifest state in the form of light, neither the sun nor the moon nor the stars nor lightnings nor earthly fire can shine; for the sun and the others are not yet created at that time. All the other lights shine by the radiance of that divine light. That great light which is described in the Ṛk-saṃhitā thus—

शरणिर्विश्वदर्शतो ज्योतिष्कृतदसि सूर्य । विश्वमाभासि रोचनं ॥ (*śaraṇirviśvadarśato jyotiṣkṛtadasi sūrya | viśvamābhāsi rocanaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1.50-4)

"O Sūrya, you are the maker of all light; by you everything is made to shine"; the same is described here also.

### Printed p. 259

Because the whole universe is thus subject to the control of this Viśvakarman, he is described as मनसा हि धीरः (*manasā hi dhīraḥ*). न हि मत्समोऽस्ति कश्चिदिति बुद्धा, दृष्टो विश्वकर्मा (*na hi matsamo 'sti kaściditi buddhā, dṛṣṭo viśvakarmā*): there is none equal to me; all the others are subject to me; thus the boldness of Viśvakarman, who displays this steadfastness, is also described. The Upaniṣads also describe this same point in this way.

भीषास्माद्वातः पवते। भीषोदेति सूर्यः । भीषास्मादग्निश्चेंद्रश्च । मृत्युर्धावति पंचम इति ॥ (*bhīṣāsmādvātaḥ pavate| bhīṣodeti sūryaḥ | bhīṣāsmādagniśceṃdraśca | mṛtyurdhāvati paṃcama iti ‖*) (Kṛ. U. 2.8.) **NOTE**

Out of fear of this Supreme Principle the wind blows. The sun too rises, subject to its control. Agni and Indra and all these perform their respective duties out of fear of the rule of this Supreme Principle. Therefore the point that he is the lord of all and, himself subject to no one's lordship, enjoys his imperial dignity, is indicated by मनसा हि धीरः (*manasā hi dhīraḥ*).

यदेदंता आददृहंत पूर्वे (*yadedaṃtā ādadṛhaṃta pūrve*)—by the power of this Viśvakarman all the boundary regions of heaven and earth were firmly established. Since heaven and earth are like the limbs of Viśvakarman, the question arises: what are these boundary regions, and what is their relation to Viśvakarman? In answer, the description of these boundary regions is given at length in the Upaniṣads. Because Brahman contains these boundaries, he is described as having four parts. They are, first—

ब्रह्मणश्च ते पादं ब्रवाणीति ब्रवीतु मे भगवानिति तस्मै होवाच प्राचे दिक्कला प्रतीची दिक्कला दक्षिणा दिक्कलोदीची दिक्कलैष वै सोम्य चतुष्कलः पादो ब्रह्मणः प्रकाशवान्नाम ॥ (*brahmaṇaśca te pādaṃ bravāṇīti bravītu me bhagavāniti tasmai hovāca prāce dikkalā pratīcī dikkalā dakṣiṇā dikkalodīcī dikkalaiṣa vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādo brahmaṇaḥ prakāśavānnāma ‖*) (Chā. U. 4.25-2)

Brahman has four parts; he has four feet. The east is one foot; the south is the second foot; the west is the third; the north is the fourth. Thus these four are the four feet of Brahman. They are most brilliant. These very ones are described in the verse under discussion as अंता अददृहंत (*aṃtā adadṛhaṃta*). Besides this, the parts of Brahman taught by Agni to Satyakāma are of another kind.

ब्रह्मणः सोम्य ते पादं ब्रवाणीति ब्रवीतु मे भगवानिति तस्मै होवाच पृथिवी कलांतरिक्षं कला द्यौः कला समुद्रः कलैष वै सोम्य चतुष्कलः पादो ब्रह्मणोऽनंतवान्नाम ॥ (*brahmaṇaḥ somya te pādaṃ bravāṇīti bravītu me bhagavāniti tasmai hovāca pṛthivī kalāṃtarikṣaṃ kalā dyauḥ kalā samudraḥ kalaiṣa vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādo brahmaṇo 'naṃtavānnāma ‖*) (Bhā. U. 4-6-2) **NOTE**

For Brahman the earth is one foot, the atmosphere the second, the heavenly world the third, and the ocean the

### Printed p. 260

fourth. O Satyakāma, all these have received the name Anantavat. Besides this, the swan also taught Satyakāma the nature of the feet of Brahman in another way.

तस्मै होवाचाग्निः कला सूर्यः कला चंद्रः कला विद्युत्कलैष वै सोम्य चतुष्कलः पादो ब्रह्मणो ज्योतिष्मान्नाम ॥ (*tasmai hovācāgniḥ kalā sūryaḥ kalā caṃdraḥ kalā vidyutkalaiṣa vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādo brahmaṇo jyotiṣmānnāma ‖*) (Bhā. U. 4-7-2)

Fire, sun, moon and lightning, these four are the four kinds of feet. They have the name Jyotiṣmat. He who knows their nature becomes possessed of light. Thus, since all the quarters and regions are parts of Brahman, all of them are well known as the feet of Brahman. Besides what has been said above, the water-bird named Madgu describes these feet of Brahman to Satyakāma in yet another way.

ब्रह्मणः सोम्य ते पादं ब्रवाणीति ब्रवीतु मे भगवानिति तस्मै होवाच प्राणः कला चक्षुः कला श्रोत्रं कला मनः कलैष वै सोम्य चतुष्कलः पादो ब्रह्मण आयतनवान्नाम ॥ (*brahmaṇaḥ somya te pādaṃ bravāṇīti bravītu me bhagavāniti tasmai hovāca prāṇaḥ kalā cakṣuḥ kalā śrotraṃ kalā manaḥ kalaiṣa vai somya catuṣkalaḥ pādo brahmaṇa āyatanavānnāma ‖*) (Chā. U. 4-8-2)

O Satyakāma, eye, ear, mind and breath, all these are the four feet of Brahman. These are of the nature of supports. Because he possesses them, Brahman has the name आयतनवान् (*āyatanavān*).

Thus, even if the word चक्षुस् (*cakṣus*) is taken to mean the senses, it is understood that Brahman is the producer of the senses and the nourisher of the body, which consists of the group of senses. Even if it is taken to mean light, this meaning too is appropriate, because he possesses the four boundaries in the form of light. The chief purport of the verse is that by the resolve of Viśvakarman, the father of these eyes, all the quarters and boundaries obtained stability, and that he is the complete upholder and nourisher of them all.

#### Ṛk 2

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> वि॒श्वक॑र्मा॒ विम॑ना॒ आद्विहा॑या धा॒ता वि॑धा॒ता प॑र॒मोत  ॒
> संदृक् ।  
> तेषा॑मि॒ष्टानि॒ समि॒षा म॑दंति॒ यत्रा॑ सप्तऋ॒षीन्व॒र एक॑मा॒हुः॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> विश्वकर्मा । विमनाः । आत् । विहायाः । धाता । विधाता । परमा । उत ।  
> संदृक् ।  
> शे षां । इष्टानि । सं । इषा । मदंति । यत्र । सप्तऋषीन् । परः । एकं । अहुः ॥

### Printed p. 261

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> वैश्वकर्मणस्य पशोर्हविष विषानुवाक्या । विश्वकर्मा विमना आद्विहायाः
> किं स्विदासीदधिष्ठानं । आ. ३-८ इति सूत्रितं ॥
> अयं मंत्रोऽधियज्ञाध्यात्मयोर्भेदेन द्विधा व्याख्यॆयः । तत्र प्रथमं
> दैवतमधिकृत्योच्यते । विश्वकर्मा बहुविधप्रकारवृष्टि प्रदानादिकर्मणां कर्तादित्यः
> स च विमना विभूतमनाः । आदित्यनर्थकः सर्वत इत्यर्थे ना । विहाया विविधमाप्ता । महानित्यर्थः । धाता वृष्टादिकर्ता च विधाता जगतः कर्ता च परमा
> परमः संदृक् संद्रष्टा च भूतानां । तेषां सप्तर्षिणां । ज्योतिषां रश्मीनामित्यर्थः । चरमपादे वक्षमाणत्वात् । इष्टानि स्थानानि शरीराणि वेषोदकेन
> सं मदंति संमोदंते यत्रयस्मिन्नादित्ये तं देवं सप्तर्षीन्। सप्तर्षिभ्य इत्यर्थः।
> तेभ्यः परः परस्तादेकमेवादित्यमाहुर्मंत्रविदः ॥ अध्यात्मपक्ष उच्यते! विश्वकर्मायः परमात्मा प्राणप्रकाशाभ्यामुपेतः सन् बहुकर्मा भवति स च विमना विभूतमना विहाया वस्तुतो महान् विशेषेण सुकृतदुष्कृतफलस्याप्ता धाता विधाता
> च परमोत संदृक् परमश्च संद्रष्टेंद्रियाणां । तेषां सप्तर्षिणां द्रष्टणामिंद्रियाणामिष्टानि स्वरूपाणीषान्नेन सह सं मदंति संमोदंते यत्र यस्मिन्नात्मनि तमात्मानं सप्तर्षिन्नप्तसंख्याकेभ्यः सर्पणस्वभावेभ्यो वा परः परस्ता
> द्वर्तमानमिंद्रियाद्यतीतमेकं परमात्मानमाहुस्तत्त्वविदः ॥ अत्र विश्वकर्मा
> विभूतमना व्याप्त्यादि निरुक्तमनुसंधेयं । १०-२६ ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The verse is the anuvākyā (invitatory) for the offering of the victim of the Vaiśvakarmaṇa animal sacrifice; this use is stated in the sūtra beginning with the first words of this verse (Ā. 3-8). The mantra is to be explained in two ways, according to the sacrifice and the Self; first it is explained with reference to the deity. Viśvakarman is the sun, who performs the many kinds of acts such as the giving of rain. He is of wide mind, great, the maker of rain and the rest, the maker of the world, supreme, and the beholder of all beings. Of those, of the seven seers, that is, of the lights, the rays, since this is to be stated in the last quarter of the verse, the desired places, the bodies, rejoice with water, in which sun; the knowers of the mantra call that one sun higher than the seven seers. **NOTE**

Then the Self-side is stated. Viśvakarman is the Supreme Self, who, endowed with breath and light, becomes of many works; he is of wide mind, in truth great, the special obtainer of the fruit of good and evil deeds, the supporter and arranger, supreme, and the beholder of the senses. Of those seven seers, the seeing senses, the desired forms rejoice together with food, in which Self; the knowers of the truth call him the one Supreme Self, who is beyond the seven seers, whether the seven are the number seven or those of a creeping nature, and beyond the senses and the rest. Here the explanation of Viśvakarman as of wide mind, as pervading and so on, is to be taken from the Nirukta (10-26). **NOTE**

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- विश्वकर्मा (*viśvakarmā*)—the god Viśvakarman
- विमनाः (*vimanāḥ*)—he of special insight, who has a mind
- विहायाः (*vihāyāḥ*)—the great-souled
- धाता (*dhātā*)—the maker of rain and the rest
- विधाता (*vidhātā*)—the maker of the whole world
- परमा (*paramā*)—the supreme
- संदृक् (*saṃdṛk*)—he who sees everything minutely
- यत्र (*yatra*)—in which Viśvakarman
- तेषां (*teṣāṃ*)—of all lights
- इष्टानि (*iṣṭāni*)—forms and resolves
- इषा (*iṣā*)—together with water
- सं मदंति (*saṃ madaṃti*)—are satisfied together; that Viśvakarman
- सप्तर्षीन् परः (*saptarṣīn paraḥ*)—higher than the seven seers
- एकं (*ekaṃ*)—the one, the incomparable Āditya
- आहुः (*āhuḥ*)—those who know say

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

Viśvakarman is of special insight and mind, great-souled, the maker of rain and the rest, the maker of the whole world, supreme, and one who sees everything minutely. Those who know say that this Viśvakarman, in whom the forms and resolves of all lights, joined with water, are satisfied together, is the Āditya who is higher than the seven seers and incomparable.

### Printed p. 262

##### English translation
Vishwakarman, of comprehensive mind and manifold greatness, is all-pervading, the creator, the arranger and the supreme supervisor ; him in whom the desires of their (senses) are satisfied with food, they call (him) supreme beyond the seven Rishis.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In the animal offering made to the deity named Viśvakarman, while the oblation is being offered, this Ṛk विश्वकर्मा विमना (*viśvakarmā vimanā*) is to be recited as the anuvākyā mantra; this is stated by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana-śrauta-sūtra, विश्वकर्मा विमना अद्विहायाः किं स्विदासीदधिष्ठानं (*viśvakarmā vimanā advihāyāḥ kiṃ svidāsīdadhiṣṭhānaṃ*) (Ā. 3.8).

In explaining who Viśvakarman is and what the nature of this deity is, Yāska has given the explanation of this Ṛk in both the adhidaivata and the adhyātma views—

विश्वकर्मा विभूतमना व्याप्ता धाता च विधाता च परमश्च संद्रष्टा भूतानां तेषामिष्टानि वा, कांतानि वा क्रांतानि वा, गतानि वा, मतानि वा, नतानि वाद्भिः सह संमोदंते यत्रैतानि सप्तऋषीणानि ज्योतींषि तेभ्यः पर आदित्यस्तान्येतस्मिन्नेकं भवंतीत्यधिदैवतं ॥ (*viśvakarmā vibhūtamanā vyāptā dhātā ca vidhātā ca paramaśca saṃdraṣṭā bhūtānāṃ teṣāmiṣṭāni vā, kāṃtāni vā krāṃtāni vā, gatāni vā, matāni vā, natāni vādbhiḥ saha saṃmodaṃte yatraitāni saptaṛṣīṇāni jyotīṃṣi tebhyaḥ para ādityastānyetasminnekaṃ bhavaṃtītyadhidaivataṃ ‖*) (Ni. 10-26) (3. 10-26) **NOTE**

Here for the word विमनाः (*vimanāḥ*) the meaning विभूतमनाः (*vibhūtamanāḥ*) is given. That is—विभूतप्रज्ञानः, सर्वत्राप्रतिहतमस्य प्रज्ञानं । (*vibhūtaprajñānaḥ, sarvatrāpratihatamasya prajñānaṃ |*) For the word Viśvakarman the meaning Āditya is given. Therefore the insight of Viśvakarman, or Āditya, who is set forth in this Ṛk, is unobstructed everywhere. There is no obstruction at all to the insight (knowledge) of that Viśvakarman (Āditya) in any place or in any matter. His insight spreads pervading all. Has this Viśvakarman only such knowledge? Has he no other power? The answer is धाता च विधाता च (*dhātā ca vidhātā ca*): he is not merely the one who pervades the whole world in every way, but he is the creator of all classes of beings. He it is who brings all creatures into being, and he beholds (is the witness of all) these creatures that he has produced, engaged according to their own deeds in higher and lower actions; that is, he is the controller of their deeds and an excellent guide. And having given to these creatures that he has made the desired fruits they long for, he gratifies them with the waters that are the means to them. Here for the word इष्टानि (*iṣṭāni*) various meanings are given: desired wishes, objects dear to them, things that they desire; wishes that reach, or that are longed for, or that are the means to their goal.

### Printed p. 263

And for the sentence सं इषा मदंति (*saṃ iṣā madaṃti*)—इषा उदकेन सह मोदंते (*iṣā udakena saha modaṃte*): the materials of comfort needed by all creatures, that is, food, clothing and other objects of enjoyment, all have rain as their means. It is well known in worldly experience that if rain falls in due season, all wealth is obtained through the growth of plants. Therefore it is beyond dispute that Āditya gratifies all creatures by the giving of rain. For the sentence यत्रा सप्तऋषीन् पर एकमाहुः (*yatrā saptaṛṣīn para ekamāhuḥ*) the explanation is यत्र्यतानि सप्तऋषीणानि ज्योतींषि तेभ्यः पर आदित्यस्तान्वेतस्मिन्नेकं भवंतीत्यधिदैवतं (*yatryatāni saptaṛṣīṇāni jyotīṃṣi tebhyaḥ para ādityastānvetasminnekaṃ bhavaṃtītyadhidaivataṃ*) **NOTE**. The seven kinds of lights or particular rays; that Āditya, beyond them, in whom or in whose orb they shine gathered into one, is the cause of the rain, which is the means to the happiness and joy of all creatures. He is the enjoyer of sacrifice, gift and austerity. All the limbs of that Āditya, from the nails to the beard and hair, are golden. Such an Āditya they call परः (*paraḥ*), that is, the supreme deity (the Supreme Self), higher than everything. This is the explanation of the adhidaivata view. The explanation of the second, the adhyātma view, has been given in this way—

विश्वकर्मा विभूतमना व्याप्ता धाता च विधाता च परमश्च संदर्शयितेंद्रियाणामेषामिष्टानि वा, कांतानि वा, क्रांतानि वा, गतानि वा, मतानि वा, नतानि वान्नेन सह संमोदंते यत्रेमानि सप्तऋषीणानींद्रियाण्येभ्यः पर आत्मा तान्येतस्मिन्नेकं भवंतीत्यात्मगतिमाचष्टे ॥ (*viśvakarmā vibhūtamanā vyāptā dhātā ca vidhātā ca paramaśca saṃdarśayiteṃdriyāṇāmeṣāmiṣṭāni vā, kāṃtāni vā, krāṃtāni vā, gatāni vā, matāni vā, natāni vānnena saha saṃmodaṃte yatremāni saptaṛṣīṇānīṃdriyāṇyebhyaḥ para ātmā tānyetasminnekaṃ bhavaṃtītyātmagatimācaṣṭe ‖*) (Ni. 10-26)

Here the meaning relating to the Supreme Self or the Self is explained. Here Viśvakarman means the Supreme Self who has the power to create everything. He has also the name Kṣetrajña, that is, he is the inner Self in the bodies of all creatures and impels their actions and their intellect. Without his impulse not even the movement of the wind can take place. This Self is not only possessed of power; he is also possessed of knowledge. Therefore he is said to be विमनाः (*vimanāḥ*)—विभूतमनाः (*vibhūtamanāḥ*), of all knowledge, possessed of special powers of knowledge in every direction. Because he has these qualities, they call him महान् (*mahān*), of a great nature. This Self, endowed with the quality of great nature, creates all creatures, and appoints the creatures that he has created to their respective fitting actions. And this Self is also the guide of the senses in the enjoyment of their objects, or the watcher who looks without attachment at the activities that creatures perform. For those senses (the eye and the other senses in the body)

### Printed p. 264

he provides the food and other things that are dear to them, or that those senses desire, long for and wish to have, and so makes those senses also remain happy. Who is that Self who performs such acts? He is the one in whom the seven kinds of senses (these senses are called lights) are gathered, that is, joined into one, but who is distinct from the senses, that is, who is beyond them; he is the Self. This Self is higher than all things, he is ever satisfied, and he has no need of food and other nourishment. But the senses and the rest of the body, taking food and the like that give strength, are satisfied together with the Self who dwells within the body. For this Self there is no sorrow, delusion, old age or death. Those who know the truth of the Self call this very Self the Supreme Brahman. Because there is nothing higher than he (or no thing different from him), this Self has received the name Supreme Self or Supreme Brahman. The Śruti sentence तस्माद्वान्यन्न परः किंचनास (*tasmādvānyanna paraḥ kiṃcanāsa*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-19-2) supports this. **NOTE** This is the explanation of the adhyātma view, which explains the course of the Self.

The author of the Nirukta, and Sāyaṇa who followed him, have given two kinds of purport for this Ṛk: one the adhidaivata view, the other the adhyātma view. According to the first, it is the description of Āditya, who is of wide mind, great, the maker and the arranger. According to the second purport, it is the description of the Supreme Self with these same epithets. In the place where it says that the seven seers rejoice, having obtained their desires, if it refers to Āditya, the seven rays are meant. The purport is that Āditya is higher than these seven seers and, having them, is beyond them. If it refers to the Supreme Self, the senses are meant; the purport is that he is the Supreme Self, distinct from the senses and the rest. In stating these two purports, the special meaning of the epithets such as विमनाः (*vimanāḥ*) must be examined.

In giving the meaning referring to Āditya, Durgācārya has explained these epithets in this way.

विमनाः- विभूतमनाः ; विभूतप्रज्ञानः : सर्वत्र अप्रतिहतं अस्य प्रज्ञानं । (*vimanāḥ- vibhūtamanāḥ ; vibhūtaprajñānaḥ : sarvatra apratihataṃ asya prajñānaṃ |*) The insight of this Āditya is all-pervading; it is unobstructed and unimpeded.

विहायाः— अप्पसौ आत्मना विहायाः । आत्मनापि सर्वप्रकारं महान् (*vihāyāḥ— appasau ātmanā vihāyāḥ | ātmanāpi sarvaprakāraṃ mahān*) **NOTE** He possesses his own personal power or greatness.

धाता (*dhātā*)—he who brings all beings into existence.

विधाता (*vidhātā*)—he who produces, in accordance with each place and time, the other things useful for the life of beings.

### Printed p. 265

परमोत संदृक् (*paramota saṃdṛk*)—he who examines and watches the dealings of all beings, and so on. All these great qualities of Āditya have been explained and stated earlier. The explanation of the seven seers as seven rays has to be set out in detail in the present context. In such contexts the word "seven" has a still wider meaning. For example, the course (ayana), season, month, fortnight, day, night and muhūrta can be the seven limbs of Āditya. Likewise—

सप्तविधमभिसंपद्यत एकशतधा वासावादित्यो विहितः सप्तसु देवलोकेषु प्रतिष्ठितः सप्त वै देवलोकाश्च तस्रो दिशस्त्रय इमे लोका एते वै सप्त देवलोकास्तेष्टेव प्रतिष्ठितः ॥ (*saptavidhamabhisaṃpadyata ekaśatadhā vāsāvādityo vihitaḥ saptasu devalokeṣu pratiṣṭhitaḥ sapta vai devalokāśca tasro diśastraya ime lokā ete vai sapta devalokāsteṣṭeva pratiṣṭhitaḥ ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 10-2-4-4)

The rays of Āditya are of a hundred kinds. If his divine form is added, the number becomes a hundred and one. All these can be included in a group of seven kinds. How? Āditya is established in this universe, which has seven divisions. The four quarters and the three worlds, earth, atmosphere and heaven, together make seven divisions. In the midst of this sevenfold universe Āditya shines. One meaning can be that the seven rays also resort to him and enjoy the joy of their gathering of sap. Or—

सप्तविधमभिसंपद्यत एकशतधा वा असावादित्यो विहिशः सप्तस्वशुषु सप्तसु स्तोमेषु सप्तसु पृष्ठेषु सप्तसु च्छंदस्सु सप्तसु प्राणेषु सप्तसु दिक्षु प्रतिष्ठितः ॥ (*saptavidhamabhisaṃpadyata ekaśatadhā vā asāvādityo vihiśaḥ saptasvaśuṣu saptasu stomeṣu saptasu pṛṣṭheṣu saptasu cchaṃdassu saptasu prāṇeṣu saptasu dikṣu pratiṣṭhitaḥ ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 10-2-4-5)

In this universe of seven kinds Āditya is established in seven ways. These are the seven seasons (if the intercalary month is counted as a season, there are seven seasons). The seven stomas, the seven pṛṣṭhas, the seven metres, the seven breaths and the seven quarters all rest on Āditya and stand surrounding him. Moreover—

सप्तविधमभिसंपद्यत एकशतधा वा असावादित्यो विहितः सप्ताक्षरे ब्रह्मन् प्रतिष्ठितः सप्ताक्षरं वै ब्रह्मर्गित्येकमक्षरं यजुरिति द्वे सामेति द्वैथ यदतोऽन्यद्ब्रह्मैव तद्व्यक्षरं वै ब्रह्म तदेत्सर्वसप्ताक्षरं ब्रह्म तदेत्सर्वसप्ताक्षरं ब्रह्म तस्मिन्नेष प्रतिष्ठितः ॥ (*saptavidhamabhisaṃpadyata ekaśatadhā vā asāvādityo vihitaḥ saptākṣare brahman pratiṣṭhitaḥ saptākṣaraṃ vai brahmargityekamakṣaraṃ yajuriti dve sāmeti dvaitha yadato 'nyadbrahmaiva tadvyakṣaraṃ vai brahma tadetsarvasaptākṣaraṃ brahma tadetsarvasaptākṣaraṃ brahma tasminneṣa pratiṣṭhitaḥ ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 10-2-4-6) **NOTE**

Āditya, who has a hundred and one forms, is established in Brahman, who has seven syllables. Brahman is itself of the nature of seven syllables. One is of the form of the Ṛk, two are of the form of the Yajus, two of the Sāman, and the one that is of the nature of Brahman itself

### Printed p. 266

is two. Thus Brahman, whose nature is seven syllables in all, is the universe. In this Brahman who pervades the universe, Āditya is established; thus the seven kinds are described. The seven rays, in seven ways, squeeze out the essence of the world and join Āditya.

This is the purport of the sentence इष्टानि समिषा मदंति (*iṣṭāni samiṣā madaṃti*). The word इष (*iṣa*) has been explained as water. The rays of Āditya, issuing from his excellent place, spread in many directions and distribute water to the whole world. Again they gather the same water and are satisfied. The meaning is that Āditya is established in the midst of these rays full of water. The same matter is described in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa in this way. If the sap is what is agreeable to each ray, then it need not be taken here as mere water; the meaning is that the rays, having gathered the water that is sap, are satisfied. How? Thus—

तस्य ये प्रांचो रश्मयस्ता एवास्य प्राज्यो मधुनाड्यः । यच एव मधुकृत ऋग्वेद एव पुष्पं ता अमृता आपस्ता वा एता ऋचः । एतमृग्वेदमभ्यतपंस्तस्याभितप्तस्य यशस्सेज इंद्रियं वीर्यमन्नाद्यं रसोऽजायत । तद्व्यक्षरत्तदादित्यमभितोऽश्रयत् ॥ (*tasya ye prāṃco raśmayastā evāsya prājyo madhunāḍyaḥ | yaca eva madhukṛta ṛgveda eva puṣpaṃ tā amṛtā āpastā vā etā ṛcaḥ | etamṛgvedamabhyatapaṃstasyābhitaptasya yaśasseja iṃdriyaṃ vīryamannādyaṃ raso 'jāyata | tadvyakṣarattadādityamabhito 'śrayat ‖*) (Cha. U. 3-1) **NOTE**

The rays of Āditya that spread to the east are the honey-channels of the eastern quarter. The Ṛks are the bees. The Ṛgveda is the flower. The offerings of ghee and milk made in the sacrifice are the drops of nectar. After the Ṛk mantras ripened, fame, brilliance, sense-power, virility and strength, and sap arose from the sacrifices and other rites. Afterwards all these fruits in the form of sap and the rest spread toward Āditya and joined him. The rays of Āditya enjoy the delight of this tasting of sap. The description of the various spreadings of the rays of Āditya, of the various kinds of gathering of sap and of the enjoyment of delight has been given earlier in the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā, Part 12, pp. 333-334.

This tasting of sap is what the verse under discussion states by तेषामिष्टानि समिषा मदंति (*teṣāmiṣṭāni samiṣā madaṃti*). These saps are what the rays of Āditya like, approve, desire and hold dear. Moreover, in explaining the epithet पुरीषी (*purīṣī*) of Āditya in the part (12) mentioned above, the relation between the rays of Āditya and water has also been stated.

That the rays of Āditya obtain this tasting of sap is the purport in the adhidaivata sense. This is the meaning referring to Āditya.

The purport stated in the adhyātma view refers to the Supreme Self. विमनाः विभूतमनाः सर्वप्रज्ञानः सर्वतोमुखाभिः विशेषविज्ञानशक्तिभिः । (*vimanāḥ vibhūtamanāḥ sarvaprajñānaḥ sarvatomukhābhiḥ viśeṣavijñānaśaktibhiḥ |*) He who can know everything and is endowed with an all-sided

### Printed p. 267

special power of knowledge. The meaning is that he is described by epithets such as प्रज्ञेत्येनमुपासीत (*prajñetyenamupāsīta*) (Bṛ. U. 4-3-2) and प्रज्ञानघनः (*prajñānaghanaḥ*). Moreover, this Supreme Self is described as—

स ना एष महानात्मा, अन्यादो वसुदानः ॥ (*sa nā eṣa mahānātmā, anyādo vasudānaḥ ‖*) (Bṛ. U. 4-4-24)

This Supreme Self is the one who himself eats all food and the giver of food to the world. It is because he has these two powers that he is a great being,

महान् भवति प्रजया पशुभिर्ब्रह्मवर्चसेन । महान् कीर्त्या ॥ (*mahān bhavati prajayā paśubhirbrahmavarcasena | mahān kīrtyā ‖*) (Tai. U. 3-6-1)

he is possessed of food, an eater of food; because he has cattle and offspring he is a great being. Because he is endowed with brilliance and with the splendour of Brahman he is a great being. He is a great being also through fame. The Supreme Self who is praised thus in the Upaniṣads and elsewhere is praised in the present verse by the epithet विहायाः (*vihāyāḥ*).

धाता (*dhātā*) and विधाता (*vidhātā*) show the power of creation and the variety of creation.

A special meaning is stated only for तेषामिष्टानि समिषा मदंति; (*teṣāmiṣṭāni samiṣā madaṃti;*) यत्रा सप्तर्षीन् पर एकमाहुः (*yatrā saptarṣīn para ekamāhuḥ*). The seven seers are the seven senses. These senses, united with their dear food (their objects), enjoy delight. The meaning is an experience in the form of knowledge of the Supreme Self. The Supreme Self is the object of these senses. And this Supreme Self is distinct from that whole group of senses. In this connection the explanation of Durgācārya is as follows.

न यतः परतरमस्ति तस्मिन् परतरे विश्वकर्मणि यदन्नं शक्तिमात्रं यदुपविष्टंभात् परमात्मा नित्यतृप्तः तेनान्नेन परमात्मनि तद्विज्ञानोपासनात् तेन सहभूता मोदंते । यथा च अनुपक्षीणस्तधाशक्ति निततृप्तं सर्वभावपरं तत्परं ब्रह्म यदात्मविदः प्रतिपद्यंते— (*na yataḥ parataramasti tasmin paratare viśvakarmaṇi yadannaṃ śaktimātraṃ yadupaviṣṭaṃbhāt paramātmā nityatṛptaḥ tenānnena paramātmani tadvijñānopāsanāt tena sahabhūtā modaṃte | yathā ca anupakṣīṇastadhāśakti nitatṛptaṃ sarvabhāvaparaṃ tatparaṃ brahma yadātmavidaḥ pratipadyaṃte—*) (Si. Vai. 10-26) **NOTE**

In that Viśvakarman, who is the highest and than whom there is nothing higher, the food, which is mere power, and by whose support the Supreme Self is ever satisfied; with that food in the Supreme Self, through the knowledge and worship of him, the beings rejoice together with him. In that Supreme Self, than whom there is no other or higher principle, the senses are satisfied by that same excellent food with which he is satisfied, that is, by making him their object and worshipping him. It is said that the Supreme Self, who has imperishable wealth, who possesses food, who is ever satisfied and without any other beyond him, is the subject of the description here. Durgācārya has set forth the mantra quoted below as describing this same Supreme Principle in the Ṛk-saṃhitā also.

### Printed p. 268

न मृत्युरासीदमृतं न तर्हि न रात्रा अह्न आसीत्प्रकेतः । आनीदवातं स्वधया तदेकं तस्माद्दान्यन्न परः किं चनास ॥ (*na mṛtyurāsīdamṛtaṃ na tarhi na rātrā ahna āsītpraketaḥ | ānīdavātaṃ svadhayā tadekaṃ tasmāddānyanna paraḥ kiṃ canāsa ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-129-2) **NOTE**

It is stated that the very subject set forth here is the Supreme Principle that the Ṛk mantras praise, namely that which is beyond death, not subject to the restriction of day and night, established by its own greatness, and beyond which there is no other principle. In the present context it must be examined how the seers can have the meaning of senses; what is meant by their obtaining their desire and being satisfied; and what is the purport of the Supreme Self being distinct from them. It is also a matter to be understood how the Supreme Self can be the object of those very senses that are well known as obstructions to the vision of the Supreme Self. The account of the seven seers, who reflect the seven senses, is stated clearly in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka. First one should examine that and afterwards the exact meaning of it can be understood.

यो ह वै शिशुं साधानं सप्रत्याधानं सस्थूणं सदामं वेद सप्त ह द्विषतो भ्रातृव्यानवरुणद्धि । अयं नाव शिशुर्योऽयं मध्यमः प्राणस्तस्येदमेवाधानमिदं प्रत्याधानं प्राणः स्थूणान्नं धाम ॥ (*yo ha vai śiśuṃ sādhānaṃ sapratyādhānaṃ sasthūṇaṃ sadāmaṃ veda sapta ha dviṣato bhrātṛvyānavaruṇaddhi | ayaṃ nāva śiśuryo 'yaṃ madhyamaḥ prāṇastasyedamevādhānamidaṃ pratyādhānaṃ prāṇaḥ sthūṇānnaṃ dhāma ‖*) (Bṛ. U. 2-2-1)

Here the life of man is likened to a child nourished from the highest limb (the head). This child has an excellent dwelling, a good covering, a post (pillar) fit to lean on, and a good rope. He who knows this truth keeps his seven enemies far away.

The breath established in the middle of the body is this child. The body is its house. The head is the covering. The breath is the supporting pillar. Food is the binding rope. Here it is said that the breath, or the man, has seven enemies. Who are these seven enemies? They are—

परांचि खानि व्यतृणत्स्वयंभूस्तस्मात्पराज् पश्यति नांतरात्मन् । कश्चिद्धीरः प्रत्यगात्मानमैक्षदावृत्तचक्षुरमृतत्वमिच्छन् ॥ (*parāṃci khāni vyatṛṇatsvayaṃbhūstasmātparāj paśyati nāṃtarātman | kaściddhīraḥ pratyagātmānamaikṣadāvṛttacakṣuramṛtatvamicchan ‖*) (Kara. 4-1) **NOTE**

Man must go beyond the senses, free himself from their grip, and know the Supreme Principle that is distinct from them. The Supreme Principle is not to be obtained with the help of the senses. The senses are obstructions to this knowledge

### Printed p. 269

and therefore the wise man does not take the senses as helps to the realisation of the Self; thus the obstructive nature of the senses is indicated. It is a matter to be understood whether the senses that are obstructive are the very ones called here the seven bhrātṛvyas, that is, seven enemies. In this context the explanation of Śrī Śaṅkarācārya is as follows—

सप्त ये शीर्षण्याः प्राणा विषयोपलब्धिद्वाराणि तत्प्रभवा विषयरागाः सहजत्वात् भ्रातृव्याः । ते ह्यस्य स्वात्मस्थां दृष्टिं विषयविषयां कुर्वंति । तेन ते द्वेष्टारो भ्रातृव्याः । प्रत्यगात्मेक्षणप्रतिषेधकरत्वात् ॥ (*sapta ye śīrṣaṇyāḥ prāṇā viṣayopalabdhidvārāṇi tatprabhavā viṣayarāgāḥ sahajatvāt bhrātṛvyāḥ | te hyasya svātmasthāṃ dṛṣṭiṃ viṣayaviṣayāṃ kurvaṃti | tena te dveṣṭāro bhrātṛvyāḥ | pratyagātmekṣaṇapratiṣedhakaratvāt ‖*) (Bṛ. U. Śaṃ. Bhā. 2-2-1) **NOTE**

The senses, the eye and the others, become the causes of the arising of passion and obstructions to the realisation of the Supreme Self. They make the vision of man impure; they give no room to divine vision. Therefore they are to be understood as hostile; thus the nature of the seven senses is described. Therefore what is spoken of in the present context is not those gross senses. What are they? **NOTE**

तमेताः सप्ताक्षितय उपतिष्ठंते तद्या इमा अक्षन्‌लोहिन्यो राजयस्ताभिरेनं रुद्रोऽन्वायत्तोऽथ या अक्षन्नापस्ताभिः पर्जन्यो या कनीनका तयादित्यो यत्कृष्टं तेनाग्निर्यच्चुक्लं तेनेंद्रोऽधरय्यनं वर्तन्या पृथिव्यन्वायत्ता दौरुत्तरया नास्यान्नं क्षीयते य एवं वेद ॥ (*tametāḥ saptākṣitaya upatiṣṭhaṃte tadyā imā akṣanlohinyo rājayastābhirenaṃ rudro 'nvāyatto 'tha yā akṣannāpastābhiḥ parjanyo yā kanīnakā tayādityo yatkṛṣṭaṃ tenāgniryaccuklaṃ teneṃdro 'dharayyanaṃ vartanyā pṛthivyanvāyattā dauruttarayā nāsyānnaṃ kṣīyate ya evaṃ veda ‖*) (Bṛ. U. 2-2-2)

The seven subtle instruments that supply food to the subtle body serve this Puruṣa (the breath). The red lines in the eye show the relation between this Puruṣa, who is of the nature of breath, and Rudra. The water principle in the same eye shows the relation of the Puruṣa to Parjanya. Its pupil shows the relation of the Puruṣa to Āditya. **NOTE** In the same way the black region of the eye shows the relation to Agni, the white region the unity with Indra, the lower eyelid the relation to the earth, and the upper eyelid the relation to the atmosphere. Since all these are imperishable subtle principles, he who knows them obtains imperishable food. This passage is described in this way by a mantra of the seers.

तदष्टे श्लोको भवति । अर्वाग्बिलश्चमस ऊर्ध्वबुध्नस्तस्मिन्यशो निहितं विश्वरूपं । तस्यासत ऋषयः सप्त तीरे वागष्टमी ब्रह्मणा संविदाना । इति । (*tadaṣṭe śloko bhavati | arvāgbilaścamasa ūrdhvabudhnastasminyaśo nihitaṃ viśvarūpaṃ | tasyāsata ṛṣayaḥ sapta tīre vāgaṣṭamī brahmaṇā saṃvidānā | iti |*)

### Printed p. 270

There is a bowl (camasa) with its head-part turned downward and its bottom turned upward (the head). In this the fame of the all-formed is also placed. Around its rim the seven seers are established. The eighth, the principle of speech, is united with the mantra in the form of Brahman. The purport of this mantra, with this meaning, is explained in the Upaniṣad also, in this way.

आर्वाग्बिलश्चमस ऊर्ध्वबुध्न इतीदं शच्चिर एष आर्वाग्बिलश्चमस ऊर्ध्वबुध्नस्तस्मिन् यशो निहितं विश्वरूपमिति प्राणा वै यशो विश्वरूपं प्राणानेतदाह तस्यासत ऋषयः सप्ततीर इति प्राणा ना ऋषयः प्राणानेतदाह वागष्टमी ब्रह्मणा संविदानेति वागृष्टमी ब्रह्मणा संवित्ते ॥ (*ārvāgbilaścamasa ūrdhvabudhna itīdaṃ śaccira eṣa ārvāgbilaścamasa ūrdhvabudhnastasmin yaśo nihitaṃ viśvarūpamiti prāṇā vai yaśo viśvarūpaṃ prāṇānetadāha tasyāsata ṛṣayaḥ saptatīra iti prāṇā nā ṛṣayaḥ prāṇānetadāha vāgaṣṭamī brahmaṇā saṃvidāneti vāgṛṣṭamī brahmaṇā saṃvitte ‖*) (Bṛ. U. 2-2-3)

The camasa bowl with its head turned downward and its bottom turned upward is the head of man. This description is given because the fame of the all-formed is established in the breaths, and because this breath is established in the head. The seven breaths are called the seven seers. The eighth, speech, is united with Brahman in the form of mantra. Who are these seven breaths called seers, or who are these seven seers of the nature of breath? They are—

इमावेव गोतमभरद्वाजावयमेव गोतमोऽयं भरद्वाज इमावेव विश्वामित्रजमदग्नी आयमेव विश्वामित्रोऽयं जमदग्निरिमावेव वसिष्ठकश्यपावयमेव वसिष्टोऽयं कश्यपो वागेवात्रिर्वाचा ह्यन्नमद्यतेऽक्तिर्ह वै नामैतद्यदत्रिरिति सर्वस्यात्ता भवति सर्वमस्यान्नं भवतिय एवं वेद । (*imāveva gotamabharadvājāvayameva gotamo 'yaṃ bharadvāja imāveva viśvāmitrajamadagnī āyameva viśvāmitro 'yaṃ jamadagnirimāveva vasiṣṭhakaśyapāvayameva vasiṣṭo 'yaṃ kaśyapo vāgevātrirvācā hyannamadyate 'ktirha vai nāmaitadyadatririti sarvasyāttā bhavati sarvamasyānnaṃ bhavatiya evaṃ veda |*) (Bṛ. U. 9-2-4) **NOTE**

Of these two ears one is Gotama and the other Bharadvāja; of these two eyes one is Viśvāmitra and the other Jamadagni; of these two nostrils (parts of the nose) one is Vasiṣṭha and the other Kaśyapa; because it eats food, the tongue (speech) is the seer Atri. He who knows these truths becomes an enjoyer of the wealth of food and ... **NOTE**

In sum, that the principle of breath is chief and that the other senses have taken shelter in it was stated in the special topics of the preceding Ṛk. And resorting to this very breath they experience their enjoyments. That the Lord of the world is himself of this form of breath was stated earlier. The purport is that, having obtained the shelter of this breath, all the senses obtain their respective objects and also the experience of pleasure that results from them. Moreover,

### Printed p. 271

तास्यस्मिन्नेकं भवंतीत्यात्मगतिमाचष्टे । (*tāsyasminnekaṃ bhavaṃtītyātmagatimācaṣṭe |*) (Ni. 80-96) **NOTE**

All these senses become one in the Self, who is of the nature of breath. This declares the course of the Self; this is the purport of the author of the Nirukta.

What is the purport of saying that all the seers, who are of the form of senses, become one in the Self, who is of the form of breath? How is this Self, in the form of the senses, the nourisher of the body that is endowed with the senses? These and similar points are stated in the Itareya-āraṇyaka in this way.

एष इमं लोकमभ्यार्चत्पुरुषरूपेण य एष तपति प्राणो वाव तदभ्यार्चत्प्राणो ह्येष य एष तपति । तं शतं वर्षाण्यभ्यार्चत्तस्माच्छतं वर्षाणि पुरुषायुषो भवंति तं यच्छतं वर्षाण्यभ्यार्चत् तस्माच्छर्चिनः इत्याचक्षते । (*eṣa imaṃ lokamabhyārcatpuruṣarūpeṇa ya eṣa tapati prāṇo vāva tadabhyārcatprāṇo hyeṣa ya eṣa tapati | taṃ śataṃ varṣāṇyabhyārcattasmācchataṃ varṣāṇi puruṣāyuṣo bhavaṃti taṃ yacchataṃ varṣāṇyabhyārcat tasmāccharcinaḥ ityācakṣate |*) (Ja. Ā. 9-2.1) **NOTE**

The shining Universal Self entered the world in the form of a Puruṣa. He is of the nature of breath. As breath he shines here also. Because he shines for a hundred years, a hundred years of life are fixed for man. That is why the name Śatarcin (the one of a hundred rays) is well known for the breath.

य इदं संतं मध्यतो दधे यदिद्दं किंच स यदिदं सर्वं मध्यतो दधॆः यदिदं किंच तस्मान्माध्यमास्तस्मान्माध्यमा इत्याचक्षत एतमेव संतं । प्राणो वै गृत्सः अपानो मदः..................तस्माद्गृत्समद इत्याचक्षतेश ॥ (*ya idaṃ saṃtaṃ madhyato dadhe yadiddaṃ kiṃca sa yadidaṃ sarvaṃ madhyato dadhèḥ yadidaṃ kiṃca tasmānmādhyamāstasmānmādhyamā ityācakṣata etameva saṃtaṃ | prāṇo vai gṛtsaḥ apāno madaḥ..................tasmādgṛtsamada ityācakṣateśa ‖*) (Ai. Ā. 2.2-1)

This Self, who is of the nature of breath, was established in the middle of the man's body. That is why he is called Madhyama. As breath he swallows everything. As apāna he is the cause of delight (mada). Therefore those who know the truth also call him Gṛtsamada, who is in the form of prāṇa and apāna.

तस्येदं विश्वं मित्रमासीद्यदिदं किंच.... ....तस्माद्विश्वामित्र इत्याचक्षते ॥ (*tasyedaṃ viśvaṃ mitramāsīdyadidaṃ kiṃca.... ....tasmādviśvāmitra ityācakṣate ‖*)

Everything in the world is friendly to this breath. That is why the name Viśvāmitra is well known for him.

तं देवा अब्रुवन्नयं वै नः सर्वेषां वा इति तं यद्देवा........तस्माद्वामदेव इत्याचक्षते ॥ (*taṃ devā abruvannayaṃ vai naḥ sarveṣāṃ vā iti taṃ yaddevā........tasmādvāmadeva ityācakṣate ‖*)

### Printed p. 272

The gods wished that he should be the one who brings dear things to all of us. Since he became dear (vāma) to all of them, he is well known as Vāmadeva.

य इदं सर्पं पाप्यनोऽत्रायत यदिदं किंच......... तस्मादत्रय इत्याचक्षत एतमेव संतं ॥ (*ya idaṃ sarpaṃ pāpyano 'trāyata yadidaṃ kiṃca......... tasmādatraya ityācakṣata etameva saṃtaṃ ‖*)

Because this Self, who is of the nature of breath, protected (trāṇa) everything from evil, he has the name Atri. The prāṇas, apānas and the rest are well known as Atrayaḥ.

एष उ एव बिभ्रद्वाजः प्रजा वै वाजः ता एष बिभर्ति यद्बिभर्ति तस्माद्भरद्वाजः । (*eṣa u eva bibhradvājaḥ prajā vai vājaḥ tā eṣa bibharti yadbibharti tasmādbharadvājaḥ |*)

Offspring (progeny) are called vāja (food). Since this Self, who is of the nature of breath, bears and nourishes these vājas, he is Bharadvāja.

तं देवा अब्रुवन्नयं वै नः सर्वेषां वसिष्ठ इति........तस्माद्वसिष्ठ इत्याचक्षत एतमेव संतं । (*taṃ devā abruvannayaṃ vai naḥ sarveṣāṃ vasiṣṭha iti........tasmādvasiṣṭha ityācakṣata etameva saṃtaṃ |*)

The gods wished that he should be the best among us all and endowed with exceeding wealth. Since he is the most excellent (vasiṣṭha) among them all, he became well known as Vasiṣṭha. Thus the meaning of the word ṛṣi is explained. The purport is that the Self, who is of the nature of breath, is the lord of all these senses, and that the senses, nourished by this lord and serving him, experience happiness.

The purport of the sentence तेषां इष्टानि समिषा मदंति (*teṣāṃ iṣṭāni samiṣā madaṃti*) is explained at length in the Chāndogya and other Upaniṣads. The performance of the sacrifice by the seers, who are of the form of senses, and the satisfaction of Prajāpati, who is of the form of breath, by that sacrifice, will all be stated in the special topics of the 4th Ṛk of this same sūkta.

> यः । देवानां । नामधाः । एकः । एव । तं । संप्रश्नं । भुवना । यंति । अन्या ॥
