> यातुधानस्य । रक्षसः । बलं । वि । रुज । वीर्यं ॥ २५ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> हे अग्ने हरसा त्वदीयेन तेजसा । तथा च यास्कः । हरो हरतेज्र्योतिर्णर
> उच्यते नि. ४-१९ । इति ॥ यातुधानस्य राक्षसस्य हरो हरणशीलं बलं प्रति शृणीहि ।
> नाशयेत्यर्थः । तथा रक्षसो राक्षसस्य वीर्यं च वि रुज । भंजय ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

O Agni, with your own radiance (haras); and so Yāska says: हरो हरतेज्र्योतिर्णर उच्यते (*haro haratejryotirṇara ucyate*) (Ni. 4-19) **GLOSS** **NOTE**. Break the harmful, seizing strength of the Yātudhāna Rākṣasa; the meaning is, destroy it. Likewise shatter the vigour of the Rākṣasa; make it break.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- अग्ने (*agne*)—O Agni
- हरसा (*harasā*)—with your burning radiance
- यातुधानस्य (*yātudhānasya*)—of the Asura
- हरः (*haraḥ*)—harmful
- बलं (*balaṃ*)—the strength
- प्रति शृणीहि (*prati śṛṇīhi*)—destroy
- रक्षसः (*rakṣasaḥ*)—of the Rākṣasa
- वीर्यं (*vīryaṃ*)—the strength
- वि रुज (*vi ruja*)—destroy

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Agni, destroy with your burning radiance the harmful strength of the Asura. Destroy the strength of the Rākṣasa.

### Printed p. 522

##### English translation
Destroy, Agni, with your flame, the impetuous might of the Yatudhana ; break the strength of the Rakshasa.

## Sūkta 88 (Maṇḍala 10)

**NOTE**

In this sūkta Sūrya-Vaiśvānara Agni is praised. An explanation of Sūrya and of Vaiśvānara Agni is therefore necessary. We shall first explain the subject of Sūrya in detail, and then examine Sūrya-Vaiśvānara Agni as Yāska has explained him.

सुष्टु अर्यः स्वामिा । यद्वा सर्वांतर्यामितया सुष्टु प्रेरकः। यद्वा शोभनवीर्यः । (*suṣṭu aryaḥ svāmiā | yadvā sarvāṃtaryāmitayā suṣṭu prerakaḥ| yadvā śobhanavīryaḥ |*) **GLOSS** Yāska says सूर्यः सर्तेर्वा, सुवतेर्वा, स्वीर्यतेर्वा (*sūryaḥ sartervā, suvatervā, svīryatervā*) (Ni. 12 14). From the root सृ (*sṛ*), which means going, the word sūrya is formed; on this view it means one who moves about. When it is formed from the root पूञ (*pūña*), which means to bring forth, it means one who creates. When the formation of the word sūrya is stated from the root ईश (*īśa*), which means going or trembling, with the prefix सु (*su*), it is said वायुना ह्ययं सुष्टु ईर्यते प्रेय्यते (*vāyunā hyayaṃ suṣṭu īryate preyyate*), that he is greatly impelled by the wind. Having thus explained the meaning in three ways, Yāska quotes the Ṛk that teaches the identity of the well-known Sūrya with Jātavedas Agni: उदु त्यं जातवेदसं देवं वहन्ति केतवः । दृशे विश्वाय सूर्यं ॥ (*udu tyaṃ jātavedasaṃ devaṃ vahanti ketavaḥ | dṛśe viśvāya sūryaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-50-1) **GLOSS** And he quotes the Ṛk that teaches that this Sūrya is the self of all: चित्रं देवानामुदगादनीकं चक्षुर्मित्रस्य वरुणस्याग्नेः । आप्रा द्यावापृथिवी अंतरिक्षं सूर्य आत्मा जगतस्तस्थुषश्च ॥ (*citraṃ devānāmudagādanīkaṃ cakṣurmitrasya varuṇasyāgneḥ | āprā dyāvāpṛthivī aṃtarikṣaṃ sūrya ātmā jagatastasthuṣaśca ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-185-1) **GLOSS** **NOTE** Here, having established that the well-known Agni has the qualities that are found in Sūrya, he gives the meaning that Agni is lord of everything, the inner controller of all, therefore the impeller of all, and one of excellent vigour.

सर्वस्य प्रेरक आदित्यः (*sarvasya preraka ādityaḥ*) means Sūrya, who impels the whole world, that is, all the beings in the world. If we did not receive the heat that goes out from Sūrya through his rays,

### Printed p. 523

we could not live. As is said in Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-115-1, सूर्य आत्मा जगतः (*sūrya ātmā jagataḥ*), Sūrya is himself the self of the whole world. Without the radiance of Sūrya not even a blade of grass on the earth could move. For the whole of the animal kingdom and for human beings the radiance of Sūrya (his heat) is absolutely necessary. Because heat (fire) is one of the five elements, the radiance of Sūrya is as necessary as air, water and food. There is a difference between the radiance that arises from fire and the like and the radiance of Sūrya. The radiance of Sūrya has the power to remove poison and to produce health. For that very reason the sharp rays of the midday sun destroy poison, as is said here in the words पुरु विश्वानि विषाणि जूर्वन्.हिंसन् (*puru viśvāni viṣāṇi jūrvan.hiṃsan*) Formerly the seer Praskaṇva (prayed): हृद्रोगं मम सूर्य हरिमाणं च नाशय (*hṛdrogaṃ mama sūrya harimāṇaṃ ca nāśaya*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-50-11). The prayer "O Sūrya, destroy the disease that pervades my heart and the yellow colour (leprosy) produced on my skin by the disease of leprosy" is an example of Sūrya's power to remove disease.

In the Ṛgveda and in the Yajurveda it is said in many places that Mitra is the lord of the day and Varuṇa the lord of the night. Many Vedic passages can be given as examples, such as मैत्रं वा अहः । वारिणी रात्रिः (*maitraṃ vā ahaḥ | vāriṇī rātriḥ*) But what is the relation of Sūrya to Mitra and Varuṇa? It is said that this Sūrya, who is seen by our eyes, is like the eyes of Mitra and Varuṇa: चक्षुर्मित्रस्य वरुणस्माग्नेः (*cakṣurmitrasya varuṇasmāgneḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1.115-1), चक्षुर्मित्रस्य वरुणस्य (*cakṣurmitrasya varuṇasya*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-63-1), नमो मित्रस्य वरुणस्य चक्षसे (*namo mitrasya varuṇasya cakṣase*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10.37-1). In these and many other Ṛks Sūrya is known as the eye of Mitra and Varuṇa.

Sūrya is the son of the world of heaven: दिवस्पुत्राय सूर्याय शंसत (*divasputrāya sūryāya śaṃsata*) (10.37-1). In some places Sūrya is also regarded as the son of Aditi: सूर्यमादितेयं (*sūryamāditeyaṃ*) (10 88-1). Sūrya sits on a chariot. One horse or many horses draw his chariot. Ordinarily seven horses bear his chariot: सप्ताश्वा हरितः सूर्यस्य (*saptāśvā haritaḥ sūryasya*) (1-115-3, 4). Sūrya is the self of the whole world; that is, as the inner self in the bodies of living beings he regulates their movements. Sūrya is the cause also of the movement of inanimate things: सूर्या आत्मा जगतस्तस्थुषश्च (*sūryā ātmā jagatastasthuṣaśca*) (1.115-1). Impelled by the power of Sūrya, people become able to do their several works: नूसं जनाः सूर्येण प्रसूता अयन्नर्थांसि कृणवन्नपांसि (*nūsaṃ janāḥ sūryeṇa prasūtā ayannarthāṃsi kṛṇavannapāṃsi*)

### Printed p. 524

He sees everything, even what is very far away; he sees all the good and bad deeds that men do (1-50-2, 7; 7-61-1; 7-63-1, 4, etc.).

Explaining the meaning of the word Sūrya, Yāska says:

सूर्यः सर्वेर्, सुवर्तेर्वा स्वीयतेर्वा ॥ (*sūryaḥ sarver, suvartervā svīyatervā ‖*) (Ni. 12-14)

That is, the word Sūrya may be formed from the root सृ (*sṛ*), "to move", or from the root पूज् (*pūj*) "to produce" **NOTE**, or from सु+ईरयति (*su+īrayati*), which means "to impel". In the morning Sūrya rises in the east, moves in the sky without a break, and towards evening reaches the west and sets. His movement is therefore unbroken. All living beings in the world, and plants and the like, come into being by the power of Sūrya. The air, heated by Sūrya's rays, becomes by its movements the cause of manifold changes in the world. By the heat of Sūrya's rays the water of the seas and other reservoirs turns to vapour, pours down as rain from the clouds in the sky, and becomes the cause of the growth of plants and the like. From plants, animals and men are produced: अद्भ, ओषधयः । ओषधीभ्योऽन्नं । अन्नात्पुरुषः ॥ (*adbha, oṣadhayaḥ | oṣadhībhyo 'nnaṃ | annātpuruṣaḥ ‖*) (Tai. U. 2.1-1). The movements of inanimate things too arise from the heat of Sūrya. How? As is said in सूर्य आत्मा जगतस्तस्थु षश्च (*sūrya ātmā jagatastasthu ṣaśca*), Sūrya, a mass of radiance, though he stands in the middle of his orb, pervades everything with his heat, and so, as the inner controller of all, impels each thing to act in accordance with its time. Therefore he is the cause of the production of the whole group of effects among moving things (living beings and the like) and stationary things (inanimate objects). As soon as Sūrya has risen, he rouses the living beings who during the night lay as if dead, without knowledge or power to do any work, and makes them engage in their several tasks; this power belongs to Sūrya alone.

योऽसौ तपन्नुदेति । स सर्वेषां भूतानां प्राणानादायोदेति।......... (*yo 'sau tapannudeti | sa sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ prāṇānādāyodeti|.........*)

आसौ योऽस्तमेति । स सर्वेषां भूतानां प्राणानादायास्तमेति । ..... (*āsau yo 'stameti | sa sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ prāṇānādāyāstameti | .....*)

असौ य अपूर्यति । स सर्वेषां भूतानां प्राणैरापूर्यति । (*asau ya apūryati | sa sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ prāṇairāpūryati |*)

(Tai. Ā. 1-14-1)

As these Vedic sentences say, when Sūrya sets he takes away with him the vital powers of all living beings, that is, their powers of movement and the like and their activity of knowing. Therefore at night living beings, unable to do any work, fall asleep.

### Printed p. 525

Again in the morning, when Sūrya rises, he brings back with him the vital powers of all those beings, that is, the powers to perform works and the activity of knowing, and rises. Then he fills those beings with the power that is his own energy: so it is said. Because Sūrya gives knowledge and the power of action to the whole world, and by his rising and setting makes it conscious or unconscious, his greatness is described here: he is the self and the life-self of all things, moving and unmoving.

Moreover, according to the science of today (Scientific view) too, Sūrya is the cause of the movements of all things in this world. From Sūrya we obtain every kind of energy. Sūrya, or the rays of Sūrya, are the cause of the movements that go on among living beings, of the movement of the air in the sky, the formation of clouds, the falling of rain and the like, and of all kinds of activity on the earth, such as the ceaseless growth of plants and the flowing movement of rivers. Without the light of Sūrya deep darkness would cover this world, and not even the movement of a blade of grass would take place. Therefore it is proper to give as the meaning of the sentence सूर्य आत्मा जगतस्तस्थु षश्च (*sūrya ātmā jagatastasthu ṣaśca*): The sun is the source of all the energies, for as this world (earth) is concerned **NOTE**.

In the Purāṇas and elsewhere Sūrya is called by words such as Āditya, Pūṣan, Mitra and Savitṛ. But in the Vedas, and especially in the Ṛgveda, the distinctive character of Sūrya is one thing, that of Āditya another, and that of deities such as Pūṣan, Mitra and Savitṛ yet another. Although the qualities of Sūrya are found in the twelve Ādityas beginning with Mitra, yet in sacrifices and the like, where Sūrya is praised, Āditya is not praised. All these are regarded as different deities. Not only that: in the Vedas, when one deity has a particular quality of his own, the deity together with that quality is regarded as a different one. For example, when Indra is called मरुत्वानिंद्रः (*marutvāniṃdraḥ*) or महानिंद्रः (*mahāniṃdraḥ*), Indra is one, Marutvān Indra (Indra together with the Marut deities) is another, and Mahān Indra (Indra of great form) is another, and they are worshipped each according to the occasion. In the same way such distinctions as अग्निः (*agniḥ*) and अग्निःपावकः (*agniḥpāvakaḥ*) are found among other deities too.

**A brief introduction to Vaiśvānara Agni**

वैश्वानरः ! इति त्रीणि पदानि । वैश्वानरः कस्माद्विश्वान्नरान्नयति! विश्व एनं नरा नयंतीति वा । अपि वा विश्वानर एव स्यात् प्रत्युतः सर्वाणि भूतानि तस्य वैश्वानरः ॥ (*vaiśvānaraḥ ! iti trīṇi padāni | vaiśvānaraḥ kasmādviśvānnarānnayati! viśva enaṃ narā nayaṃtīti vā | api vā viśvānara eva syāt pratyutaḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni tasya vaiśvānaraḥ ‖*) (Ni. 7-2-)

### Printed p. 526

Now we shall explain the word Vaiśvānara. This word Vaiśvānara denotes a deity containing the meaning of the three words विश्वान् नरान् नयति (*viśvān narān nayati*). If it is asked why Vaiśvānara has this name: this deity विश्वान् नरान् नयति (*viśvān narān nayati*), leads all people along the good path; that is, he is the guide of all people on the good path. Therefore this deity is called Vaiśvānara. Or विश्वं एनं नरा नयंतीति वा (*viśvaṃ enaṃ narā nayaṃtīti vā*): or all men carry this deity to the northern altar in the sacrifices they perform; that is, when the rite called agnipraṇayana is performed in sacrifices, they take the fire, kindled by friction, from the place where it was produced, in the prescribed manner to the neighbourhood of the northern altar and establish it there; or all people carry fire to their own houses and establish it in places such as the kitchen for cooking. Therefore this Agni is called Vaiśvānara. Or else विश्वानर (*viśvānara*) himself is Vaiśvānara. This विश्वानर (*viśvānara*), pervading the bodies of all living beings in the form of the digestive fire, digests the food and other things the living beings eat. Therefore the विश्वानर (*viśvānara*) who is in the bodies of all beings is the fire Vaiśvānara.

वैश्वानरस्य सुमतौ स्याम राजा हिकं भुवनानामभि श्रीः । इतो जातो विश्वमिदं विचष्टे वैश्वानरो यतते सूर्येण ॥ (*vaiśvānarasya sumatau syāma rājā hikaṃ bhuvanānāmabhi śrīḥ | ito jāto viśvamidaṃ vicaṣṭe vaiśvānaro yatate sūryeṇa ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-98-1)

This Ṛk praises the fire Vaiśvānara. May we become worthy of the gracious favour of the fire Vaiśvānara. For this Vaiśvānara is a king, and a king is the support of all the worlds. Born in this world, he surveys the whole universe. Together with Sūrya he pervades everything: this is the chief meaning of the Ṛk.

**Who is Vaiśvānara Agni? Is he a deity of the middle region?**

इतो जातः सर्वमिदमभिविपश्यति वैश्वानरः संयतते सूर्येण राजा यः सर्वेषां भूतानामभिश्रयणीयस्तस्य वयं वैश्वानरस्य कल्याणां मत् स्यामेति । तत्को वैश्वानरः । मध्यम इत्याचार्याः ॥ (*ito jātaḥ sarvamidamabhivipaśyati vaiśvānaraḥ saṃyatate sūryeṇa rājā yaḥ sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāmabhiśrayaṇīyastasya vayaṃ vaiśvānarasya kalyāṇāṃ mat syāmeti | tatko vaiśvānaraḥ | madhyama ityācāryāḥ ‖*) (Ni. 7-22)

This is the explanation of the Ṛk. This fire Vaiśvānara, born in this very world, is able to see the whole universe. Together with Sūrya he pervades the whole universe. May we become worthy of the best mind, that is, the favour, of such a Vaiśvānara. He is the king and the support of all created living beings. But who is this Vaiśvānara? What is his nature? Some teachers say that this Vaiśvānara is a deity who dwells in the middle region (the sky),

### Printed p. 527

because it is their view that this Vaiśvānara is the cause of rain. Therefore the Ṛk that describes the part played by this Vaiśvānara in the work of rain is quoted here.

प्र नू महित्वं वृषभस्य वोचं यं पूरवो वृत्रहणं सचंते । वैश्वानरो दस्युमग्निर्जघन्वा अधूनोत्काष्ठा अव शंबरं भेत् ॥ (*pra nū mahitvaṃ vṛṣabhasya vocaṃ yaṃ pūravo vṛtrahaṇaṃ sacaṃte | vaiśvānaro dasyumagnirjaghanvā adhūnotkāṣṭhā ava śaṃbaraṃ bhet ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-59-6)

I shall describe in a special way the greatness of this fire Vaiśvānara, the giver of desired things. Many people serve with devotion this fire Vaiśvānara, the slayer of Vṛtra. This fire Vaiśvānara slew Vṛtra, the dasyu. He split Śambara (the cloud) and killed it, and made the waters stored in the clouds fall on the earth as rain: this is the chief meaning of the Ṛk.

The explanation of this Ṛk is:

प्रब्रवीमि तन्महित्वं महाभाग्यं वृषभस्य वर्षितुरपां यं पूरवः पूरयितव्या मनुष्या वृत्रहणं मेघहनं सचंते सेवंते वर्षकामाः । दस्युर्दस्यते क्षयार्थादुपदस्यंत्यस्मिन्नसा उपदासयति कर्माणि तमग्निर्वृश्वानरो घ्नन्नवाधूनोदपः काष्ठा अभिनच्छंबरं मेघं ॥ (*prabravīmi tanmahitvaṃ mahābhāgyaṃ vṛṣabhasya varṣiturapāṃ yaṃ pūravaḥ pūrayitavyā manuṣyā vṛtrahaṇaṃ meghahanaṃ sacaṃte sevaṃte varṣakāmāḥ | dasyurdasyate kṣayārthādupadasyaṃtyasminnasā upadāsayati karmāṇi tamagnirvṛśvānaro ghnannavādhūnodapaḥ kāṣṭhā abhinacchaṃbaraṃ meghaṃ ‖*) (Ni. 7-23)

So it stands. I shall describe in a special way the great greatness (the surpassing power) of this fire Vaiśvānara, who pours down rain. People who desire what they wish, and who desire rain, serve with reverence, with praises and the like, this Vaiśvānara, who destroys the demon Vṛtra (the cloud). The word dasyu is formed from the root दस् (*das*), "to destroy", and means an evil one who prevents the water from falling on the earth and destroys it. The fire Vaiśvānara struck such a dasyu, Śambara (the cloud; the word Śambara is read among the names of the cloud), scattered the waters that had gathered in the cloud, and made them fall on the earth as rain: this is the chief meaning.

**The view of the earlier ritualists: Vaiśvānara is Āditya**

(Objections and answers on this subject)

अथासावादित्य इति पूर्वे याज्ञिकाः । एषां लोकानां रोहेण सवनाना रोह आम्मातो रोहात् प्रत्यवरोहश्चिकीर्षितस्तामनुकृतिं होताग्नि- (*athāsāvāditya iti pūrve yājñikāḥ | eṣāṃ lokānāṃ roheṇa savanānā roha āmmāto rohāt pratyavarohaścikīrṣitastāmanukṛtiṃ hotāgni-*)

### Printed p. 528

मारुते शस्त्रे वैश्वानरीयेण सूक्तेन प्रतिपद्यते सोऽपि न स्तोत्रियमाद्रियेताग्नेयो हि भवति । तत अगच्छति मध्यस्थाना देवता रुद्रं च मरुतश्च ततोऽग्निमिहस्थानमत्रवै स्तोत्रियं शंसति ॥ (*mārute śastre vaiśvānarīyeṇa sūktena pratipadyate so 'pi na stotriyamādriyetāgneyo hi bhavati | tata agacchati madhyasthānā devatā rudraṃ ca marutaśca tato 'gnimihasthānamatravai stotriyaṃ śaṃsati ‖*) (Ni. 7-23)

Some ancient teachers, skilled in the performance of sacrifices, say that this Āditya who is seen by our eyes is Vaiśvānara. They give this reason: in sacrificial rites such as the morning pressing there is an order of ascent and descent, that is, of going up and coming down. The same is so in the worlds: the earth (the lower region), the sky (the middle region) and heaven (the region of heaven); and likewise among the pressings there are three, the morning pressing, the midday pressing and the third pressing. In sacrifices and the like the Hotṛ at the morning pressing invokes and praises the deities of the earth, at the midday pressing the deities of the middle region, and at the third pressing the deities of the region of heaven. This is the order of ascent. After the ascent comes the order of descent: first the deities of the region of heaven, then the deities of the middle region, then the deities of the earth are praised in order. This is the order of descent. In the order of descent he first praises the fire Vaiśvānara with the sūkta वैश्वानराय पृथुपाजसे (*vaiśvānarāya pṛthupājase*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-3-1); then the deities of the middle region, Rudra and the Maruts, with the sūkta आते पितर्मरुतां (*āte pitarmarutāṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-23-1); then the fire Agni, the deity of the earth, with the sūkta यज्ञायज्ञावो अग्नये (*yajñāyajñāvo agnaye*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-48-1). Since in the order of descent the praise of the fire Vaiśvānara comes first, and since this Āditya is a deity of the region of heaven, this fire Vaiśvānara is Āditya: this is the line of their argument.

अथापि वैश्वानरीयो द्वादशकपालो भवत्येतस्य हि द्वादशविधं कर्म । (*athāpi vaiśvānarīyo dvādaśakapālo bhavatyetasya hi dvādaśavidhaṃ karma |*)

Moreover, to the fire Vaiśvānara an oblation on twelve potsherds is always offered. Just as for Āditya an offering on twelve potsherds is prescribed in आदित्यं द्वादशकपालं (*ādityaṃ dvādaśakapālaṃ*), an offering in twelve divisions, pointing to the twelve months, is prescribed for Āditya, so it is prescribed for the fire Vaiśvānara also. Therefore this fire Vaiśvānara is Āditya.

अथापि ब्राह्मणं भवत्यसौ वा आदित्योऽग्निर्वैश्वानरः ॥ (*athāpi brāhmaṇaṃ bhavatyasau vā ādityo 'gnirvaiśvānaraḥ ‖*)

Moreover, there is also a Brāhmaṇa sentence: this Āditya is the fire Vaiśvānara.

आथापि निवित् सौर्यवैश्वानरी भवत्या यो द्यां भात्या पृथिवीमित्येष हि द्यावापृथिव्यावाभासयति । (*āthāpi nivit sauryavaiśvānarī bhavatyā yo dyāṃ bhātyā pṛthivīmityeṣa hi dyāvāpṛthivyāvābhāsayati |*)

### Printed p. 529

A nivid mantra is a particular mantra that praises one deity and, in the midst of the śastra mantras, praises the distinctive quality of that deity. It is a separate mantra inserted and recited in the middle of the śastra mantras. Here, when the nivid mantras addressed to Āditya are recited, the mantra addressed to Sūrya and Vaiśvānara is recited; that is, that nivid mantra praises Sūrya and the fire Vaiśvānara (it sings the qualities of those deities). That mantra begins आ यो द्यां भात्र्या पृथिवीं (*ā yo dyāṃ bhātryā pṛthivīṃ*) **NOTE** and means "who illumines heaven and earth with his own light". It is Āditya who illumines heaven and earth with his own light; therefore the fire Vaiśvānara taught by this mantra is Āditya.

अथापि छांदोमिकं सूक्तं सौर्यवैश्वानरं भवति दिव पृष्टो आरोचत इत्येष हि दिवि पृष्टो आरोचतेति ॥ (*athāpi chāṃdomikaṃ sūktaṃ sauryavaiśvānaraṃ bhavati diva pṛṣṭo ārocata ityeṣa hi divi pṛṣṭo ārocateti ‖*)

And the chandomika sūkta दिवि पृष्ठो अरोचित (*divi pṛṣṭho arocita*) (Vā. Saṃ. 33-92) has Sūrya and Vaiśvānara as its deity. It says that he shines on the back (the lower part) of heaven. One who shines in heaven is Āditya. Since Vaiśvānara is praised by this very sūkta, this fire Vaiśvānara is Āditya.

अथापि हविष्वांतीयं सूक्तं सौर्यवैश्वानरं भवति । (*athāpi haviṣvāṃtīyaṃ sūktaṃ sauryavaiśvānaraṃ bhavati |*)

And the sūkta हविष्वांतमजरं (*haviṣvāṃtamajaraṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-88), the haviṣvāntīya sūkta (the sūkta recited at the time of drinking the oblation), has Sūrya and the fire Vaiśvānara as its deity; that is, this sūkta is addressed to Sūrya and the fire Vaiśvānara. In the Ṛk of this sūkta

विश्वस्मा अग्निं भुवनाय देवा वैश्वानरं केतुमह्नामकृण्वन् । (*viśvasmā agniṃ bhuvanāya devā vaiśvānaraṃ ketumahnāmakṛṇvan |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-88-2)

it is said that the gods appointed this fire Vaiśvānara to make days (daytimes), in order to produce light for the whole world. Because it is Sūrya who makes days, and because this fire Vaiśvānara too has the power to make days, this fire Vaiśvānara and Āditya are one person; that is, this fire Vaiśvānara is Āditya. All this is the view of the earlier teachers, the ritualists.

**The view of Śākapūṇi: Vaiśvānara is the terrestrial fire (not Āditya)**

(Objections and answers on this subject)

अयमेवाग्निर्वैश्वानर इति शाकपूणिः । विश्वासरावेते उत्तरे ज्योतिषी वैश्वानरोऽयं यत्ताभ्यां जायते । कथं न्वयामॆताभ्यां जायत इति (*ayamevāgnirvaiśvānara iti śākapūṇiḥ | viśvāsarāvete uttare jyotiṣī vaiśvānaro 'yaṃ yattābhyāṃ jāyate | kathaṃ nvayāmètābhyāṃ jāyata iti*)

### Printed p. 530

यत्र वैद्युतः शरणमभिहंति यावदनपात्तो भवति मध्यमधर्नैव तावद्भवत्युदकेंधनः शरीरोपशमन उपादीयमान एवायं संपद्यत उदकोपशमनः शरीरदीप्तिः ॥ (*yatra vaidyutaḥ śaraṇamabhihaṃti yāvadanapātto bhavati madhyamadharnaiva tāvadbhavatyudakeṃdhanaḥ śarīropaśamana upādīyamāna evāyaṃ saṃpadyata udakopaśamanaḥ śarīradīptiḥ ‖*)

This is the view of the teacher named Śākapūṇi: that this terrestrial fire is the fire Vaiśvānara. For the terrestrial fire is produced from two lights (the viśvānara fires), the light of Āditya, which is in the region of heaven, and the light of lightning, which is in the middle region. Therefore the fire produced from the two viśvānara fires is called Vaiśvānara; that is, the terrestrial fire is the fire Vaiśvānara. How the terrestrial fire is produced from the two lights called the light of Āditya and the light of lightning, this he explains.

The light of Āditya, which undergoes no change in place or in nature, is called the first quality. That is, this light of Āditya, remaining where it is, draws up by its rays the waters of the seas and other reservoirs and changes those waters into clouds. This is the work of the first light. Next, the fire of lightning is called the second. The nature of this fire of lightning is the middle quality, that is, it is different. This fire of lightning is by nature one that moves in the midst of the waters (the clouds), and one that strikes and destroys what gives people shelter, such as trees and houses. That is, since this fire of lightning is able to move in the waters, it cannot be quenched by water (as ordinary fire is quenched); and ordinary fire, kindled by things such as trees and wood, begins to blaze, but when the fire of lightning touches trees and the like it is stilled right there; that is, its power ends there. It does not grow by trees and the like, and this fire of lightning cannot be held by the hands and the like. This is the nature of the fire of lightning. But the nature of the terrestrial fire (the ordinary fire) is quite the opposite of this. The terrestrial fire can be increased by wood and the like, can be quenched by water, and can be held by the hands and the like. These are the natural qualities of the terrestrial fire.

An explanation is necessary on the point that the terrestrial fire is produced from the two lights, the light of the region of heaven and the light of the middle region. Āditya, the light of the region of heaven, draws up by his rays the waters of the seas and other reservoirs and changes them into clouds; that the terrestrial fire is produced and burns when the fire of lightning, which appears in those clouds, touches trees and the like, is known to all the world. Therefore it is explained here that the terrestrial fire is produced from both lights, the light of the region of heaven and the light of the middle region. Hence the terrestrial fire, produced from the two lights which are the two viśvānara fires, is called Vaiśvānara.

अथादित्यादुदीजेप्रथमगमावृप्त आदिन्ये कंसं ना मणिं वा परिमृज्य (*athādityādudījeprathamagamāvṛpta ādinye kaṃsaṃ nā maṇiṃ vā parimṛjya*) **NOTE**

### Printed p. 531

प्रतिस्वरे यत्र शुष्कगोमयमसस्पर्शयन् धारयति यत् प्रदीप्यते सोऽयमेव संपद्यते ॥ (*pratisvare yatra śuṣkagomayamasasparśayan dhārayati yat pradīpyate so 'yameva saṃpadyate ‖*)

Another example is given on the point that the terrestrial fire is produced from Āditya. When the sun in the sky has turned towards the north, that is, at midday, when he is very hot, if a brightly shining plate of copper or a mirror is held facing the sun, and its rays are made to converge (to gather together) and fall on dried cow-dung powder placed on the ground, fire at once catches. That is, this too is an example showing that the terrestrial fire is produced from Āditya.

अथाप्याह—वैश्वानरो यतते सूर्येण-न च पुनरात्मनात्मा संयततेऽन्येन्वैवान्यः संयतत इति इमानादधात्यमुतोऽमुष्य रश्मयः प्रादुर्भवंतीतोऽस्यार्चिषस्तयोर्भासोः संसंगं दृष्टैवमवक्ष्यत् ॥ (*athāpyāha—vaiśvānaro yatate sūryeṇa-na ca punarātmanātmā saṃyatate 'nyenvaivānyaḥ saṃyatata iti imānādadhātyamuto 'muṣya raśmayaḥ prādurbhavaṃtīto 'syārciṣastayorbhāsoḥ saṃsaṃgaṃ dṛṣṭaivamavakṣyat ‖*)

In the example given, in the sentence वैश्वानरो यतते सूर्येण (*vaiśvānaro yatate sūryeṇa*), the seer of the mantra has said that the fire Vaiśvānara, joined with Sūrya, spreads, that is, pervades everything. Since the place of Sūrya does not change, it is impossible that Sūrya should go forward from his place together with the fire Vaiśvānara and pervade. A thing can be in one place at one time; it cannot be there and also go forward. Only if another thing joins it can it pervade another place. Therefore here Sūrya is one and the fire Vaiśvānara is another, and the two together are able to pervade everything. Here (on the earth itself) they kindle the terrestrial fire. The way of Āditya is that he sets out from the world of heaven by his rays and meets the terrestrial fire on the earth. That is, the light of Sūrya and the light of the fire join and become one, and that light spreads everywhere by the rays. It is with this thought in mind that the seer of the mantra spoke the sentence वैश्वानरो यतते सूर्येण (*vaiśvānaro yatate sūryeṇa*).

अथ यान्येतान्यौत्तमिकानि सूक्तानि भागानि वा सावित्राणि वा सौर्याणि वा पौष्णानि वा वैष्णवानि वा वैश्वदेव्यानि वा तेषु वैश्वानरीयाः प्रवादा अभविष्यन्वादित्यकर्मणा चैनमस्तोष्यन्नित्तुदेषीत्यस्तमेषीति विपर्यॆषीति ॥ आग्नेयेष्टेव हि सूक्तेषु वैश्वानरीयाः प्रवादा भवंति । अग्निकर्माणा चैनं स्तोतीति वहसीति पचसीति दहसीति ॥ (*atha yānyetānyauttamikāni sūktāni bhāgāni vā sāvitrāṇi vā sauryāṇi vā pauṣṇāni vā vaiṣṇavāni vā vaiśvadevyāni vā teṣu vaiśvānarīyāḥ pravādā abhaviṣyanvādityakarmaṇā cainamastoṣyannittudeṣītyastameṣīti viparyèṣīti ‖ āgneyeṣṭeva hi sūkteṣu vaiśvānarīyāḥ pravādā bhavaṃti | agnikarmāṇā cainaṃ stotīti vahasīti pacasīti dahasīti ‖*)

If Vaiśvānara were Āditya, then in the sūktas or the Ṛks connected with Āditya or Savitṛ, or in the sūktas in which Sūrya, Pūṣan, Viṣṇu and the Viśvedevas are the subject,

### Printed p. 532

the qualities and distinctive features of Āditya would have had to be attributed to the fire Vaiśvānara; that is, (as is said of Sūrya) he would have had to be praised by sentences conveying such meanings as "you rise, you set, you move in the sky". But it is not so. Only in sūktas connected with Agni are the sentences that describe the qualities of Agni, such as carrying the oblation, cooking and burning, said in such a way that they apply to Vaiśvānara also. That is, the qualities of Agni are applied to the fire Vaiśvānara in the description. Therefore the fire Vaiśvānara is the terrestrial fire and not Āditya.

यथो एतद्वर्षकर्मणा ह्येनं स्तोतीत्यस्मिन्प्येतदुपपद्यते । समानमेतदुदकमुच्चैत्यव चाहभिः । भूमिं पर्जन्या जिन्वंति दिवं जिस्वंतग्नयः ॥ इति सा निगदव्याख्याता ॥ (*yatho etadvarṣakarmaṇā hyenaṃ stotītyasminpyetadupapadyate | samānametadudakamuccaityava cāhabhiḥ | bhūmiṃ parjanyā jinvaṃti divaṃ jisvaṃtagnayaḥ ‖ iti sā nigadavyākhyātā ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-5) (Ni. 7-23)

There are mantras that praise this fire Vaiśvānara as the impeller of the work of rain. Therefore, since Āditya is the impeller of the work of creation **NOTE**, the fire Vaiśvānara too would have the qualities of Āditya. Could it therefore not be said that the fire Vaiśvānara is Āditya? No, it is not so. Just as days come again and again after the night has passed, so the waters go again and again from the earth upward (to the sky) and from the sky to the earth. Therefore the waters and the days have a common quality. Hence the deity Parjanya satisfies the earth with the water of the rain, and the fires satisfy heaven. How does fire satisfy heaven? The oblations and the like that the sacrificers offer in the fire in a sacrifice take a subtle form, that is, the form of smoke, which is fit for the gods, and give satisfaction to the gods. The gods, pleased, give satisfaction to the dwellers on the earth by rain. Moreover, according to the sentence अग्नौ प्रास्ताहुतिः समृगादित्यमुपतिष्ठते (*agnau prāstāhutiḥ samṛgādityamupatiṣṭhate*), the oblation offered in the fire pleases Āditya in heaven. Since this is so, the fire satisfied heaven or Āditya, and rain became the means by which earth and heaven help each other in turn, from the earth to heaven and from heaven to the earth. For these reasons Agni, or the fire Vaiśvānara, has been praised as the cause of the work of rain; it is not made clear by this that Vaiśvānara is Āditya. Since the meaning of this Ṛk is plain, no further explanation is needed.

कृष्णं नियानं हरयः सुपर्णा अपो वसाना दिवमुत्पतंति । त आववृत्रन्तदनागृतस्यादिघातेन पृथिवी व्युद्यते ॥ (*kṛṣṇaṃ niyānaṃ harayaḥ suparṇā apo vasānā divamutpataṃti | ta āvavṛtrantadanāgṛtasyādighātena pṛthivī vyudyate ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-164-47)

### Printed p. 533

कृष्णं निरयणं रात्रिरादित्यस्य हरयः सुपर्णा हरणा आदित्यरश्मयस्ते यदा. मुतोर्वांचः पर्यावर्तंते सहस्थानादुदकस्यादित्यादथ धृतेनोदकेन पृथिवी व्युद्यते धृतमित्यदकनाम जिघर्तॆः सिंचतिकर्मणः ॥ (*kṛṣṇaṃ nirayaṇaṃ rātrirādityasya harayaḥ suparṇā haraṇā ādityaraśmayaste yadā. mutorvāṃcaḥ paryāvartaṃte sahasthānādudakasyādityādatha dhṛtenodakena pṛthivī vyudyate dhṛtamityadakanāma jighartèḥ siṃcatikarmaṇaḥ ‖*)

The rays, which carry the water and have an excellent movement, cause the dark cloud (or the night), which has a fixed course, to be covered with water; that is, joined with the water they spread upward towards the world of heaven. Then they return from Āditya, the place of the water. Immediately the earth is drenched (soaked) with water. The word निरयण (*nirayaṇa*) can here be said to mean the path of movement; the ordinary meaning of this word is the path of going out. Āditya has two paths of movement, one of dark colour and the other of white colour. The path of movement of dark colour may be taken to mean either the night or the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). Or the southern movement itself may be called Āditya's night movement. Durgācārya has written the following explanation of the above sentence of the Nirukta:

नियानं निरयणं निर्गतिः (निर्याति) निर्गच्छंत्येतदिति नियानं वर्त्म पंथाः । तच्च पुनरेतत् । रात्रिः आदित्यस्य । द्वे ह्यस्यायने शुक्लं चोत्तरं कृष्णं च दक्षिणं । सा हि दैवीरात्रिरभिष्येता । ततो ब्रवीति रात्रिरादित्यस्य ज्योतिषः । स विष भगवानादित्यो यदा जगदनुग्रहाय गर्भमुदकमात्मन्याधित्सुरुत्त रायणं प्रतिपद्यते तदैते हरयः रसहरणाः सुपर्णास्तस्य रश्मयः सर्वस्मादस्माल्लोकादपोवसानाः आत्मन्याच्छादयंतः आददानाः दिवं द्योत. नवंतमेतमादित्यं प्रत्युत्पतंति । (*niyānaṃ nirayaṇaṃ nirgatiḥ (niryāti) nirgacchaṃtyetaditi niyānaṃ vartma paṃthāḥ | tacca punaretat | rātriḥ ādityasya | dve hyasyāyane śuklaṃ cottaraṃ kṛṣṇaṃ ca dakṣiṇaṃ | sā hi daivīrātrirabhiṣyetā | tato bravīti rātrirādityasya jyotiṣaḥ | sa viṣa bhagavānādityo yadā jagadanugrahāya garbhamudakamātmanyādhitsurutta rāyaṇaṃ pratipadyate tadaite harayaḥ rasaharaṇāḥ suparṇāstasya raśmayaḥ sarvasmādasmāllokādapovasānāḥ ātmanyācchādayaṃtaḥ ādadānāḥ divaṃ dyota. navaṃtametamādityaṃ pratyutpataṃti |*) (Nirukta-vyākhyā 7-24)

The course of Āditya is of two kinds: one belongs to the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) and the other to the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). One is called white and the other dark. Here the word night is a synonym for the dark course: कृष्णं नियानं नियमनु रात्रिः । देवानां हि रात्रिर्दक्षिषायनं तत्पति तस्मिन्वर्षाकाले इत्यर्थः । (*kṛṣṇaṃ niyānaṃ niyamanu rātriḥ | devānāṃ hi rātrirdakṣiṣāyanaṃ tatpati tasminvarṣākāle ityarthaḥ |*) **NOTE**. The night time of the gods is called the dakṣiṇāyana. When Āditya follows the course of the uttarāyaṇa, all his rays spread through the world, gather water from all regions, and rejoin Āditya just at this night time. This is the rainy season. In this season rain pours down abundantly. धृत (*dhṛta*) is a name for water. The word धृत (*dhṛta*) is formed from the root जिघर्ति (*jigharti*), "to sprinkle".

अथापि ब्राह्मणं भवत्यग्निर्वा इतोः वृष्टिं समीरयति धामच्छदिति खलु भूत्वा वर्षति मरुतः सृष्टां वृष्टिं नयिंति । (*athāpi brāhmaṇaṃ bhavatyagnirvā itoḥ vṛṣṭiṃ samīrayati dhāmacchaditi khalu bhūtvā varṣati marutaḥ sṛṣṭāṃ vṛṣṭiṃ nayiṃti |*)

### Printed p. 534

यदा खलु वासावादित्योऽग्निं रश्मिभिः पर्यावर्ततेऽथ वर्षतीति । यथो एतद्रोहात् प्रत्यवरोहश्चिकीर्षित इत्याम्नायवचनादेतद्भवति । यथो एतद्वैश्वानरियो द्वादशकपालो भवतीत्यनिर्वचनं कपालानि भवंत्यस्ति हि सौर्य एककपालः पंचकपालश्च । यथो एतद्ब्राह्मणं भवतीति—बहुभक्तिवादीनि हि ब्राह्मणानि भवंति-पृथिवी वैश्वानरः संवत्सरो वैश्वानरो ब्राह्मणो वैश्वानर इति ॥ (*yadā khalu vāsāvādityo 'gniṃ raśmibhiḥ paryāvartate 'tha varṣatīti | yatho etadrohāt pratyavarohaścikīrṣita ityāmnāyavacanādetadbhavati | yatho etadvaiśvānariyo dvādaśakapālo bhavatītyanirvacanaṃ kapālāni bhavaṃtyasti hi saurya ekakapālaḥ paṃcakapālaśca | yatho etadbrāhmaṇaṃ bhavatīti—bahubhaktivādīni hi brāhmaṇāni bhavaṃti-pṛthivī vaiśvānaraḥ saṃvatsaro vaiśvānaro brāhmaṇo vaiśvānara iti ‖*)

Many Brāhmaṇa sentences too support this meaning. For example there is the Brāhmaṇa sentence "Agni sends down rain from this world": अग्नेवै धूमो जायते, धूमादभ्रं, अभ्रात् वृष्टिरिति ह विज्ञायते (*agnevai dhūmo jāyate, dhūmādabhraṃ, abhrāt vṛṣṭiriti ha vijñāyate*). From fire smoke is produced, from smoke the cloud, and from the cloud rain; this is to be understood: such is the meaning. Or, when this Āditya makes the fire turn back with his rays, rain comes. Or, by the order of ascent and descent, that is, that the oblation offered in the fire becomes in subtle form smoke, reaches the gods in heaven, they are satisfied, and from this the work of rain arises: for saying this there is no support other than a Brāhmaṇa sentence. That an oblation on twelve potsherds is prescribed for the fire Vaiśvānara, and an oblation on one potsherd or on five potsherds for Sūrya, is not related to this matter. It relates only to the acts that are parts of the sacrifice. Then, in some other Brāhmaṇa sentences, in sentences such as पृथिवी वैश्वानरः (*pṛthivī vaiśvānaraḥ*), it is said that the earth is Vaiśvānara, the year is Vaiśvānara, the Brāhmaṇa is Vaiśvānara; this is right. In this context it is not that the deities such as the earth are the fire Vaiśvānara; it is to be understood that these are sentences of praise spoken in order to describe the qualities of Vaiśvānara, as one who has the qualities of deities such as the earth.

यथो एतन्निवित्सौर्यवैश्वानरी भवतीत्यस्यैव सा भवति—यो विड्भ्यो मानुषीभ्यो दीदेत्—इत्येष हि विड्भ्यो मानुषीभ्यो दीप्यते। यथो एतच्छांदोमिकं सूक्तं सौर्यवैश्वानरं भवतीत्यस्यैवैतद्भवति जमदग्निभिराहुत इति । जमदग्नयः प्रजमिताग्नयो वा प्रज्वलिताग्नयो वा तैरभिहुतो भवति ॥ (*yatho etannivitsauryavaiśvānarī bhavatītyasyaiva sā bhavati—yo viḍbhyo mānuṣībhyo dīdet—ityeṣa hi viḍbhyo mānuṣībhyo dīpyate| yatho etacchāṃdomikaṃ sūktaṃ sauryavaiśvānaraṃ bhavatītyasyaivaitadbhavati jamadagnibhirāhuta iti | jamadagnayaḥ prajamitāgnayo vā prajvalitāgnayo vā tairabhihuto bhavati ‖*) (Ni. 7-24)

There is a nivid sūkta that praises Sūrya and Vaiśvānara. This sūkta is recited in the Āgnimāruta-śastra.

अग्निर्वैश्वानरः सोमस्य मत्सत् । विश्वेषां देवानां समित् । अजप्रं दैव्यं ज्योतिः । यो विड्भो मानुषीभ्यो दीदेत् । द्युषु पूर्वासु दिद्यु- (*agnirvaiśvānaraḥ somasya matsat | viśveṣāṃ devānāṃ samit | ajapraṃ daivyaṃ jyotiḥ | yo viḍbho mānuṣībhyo dīdet | dyuṣu pūrvāsu didyu-*)

### Printed p. 535

तानः । अजर उषसामनीकॆः । आ यो द्यां भात्या पृथिवीं । और्वमंतरिक्षं । ज्योतिषा यज्ञाय शर्म संयत् । अग्निर्वैश्वानर इह श्रवदिह सोमस्य मत्सत् । प्रेमां देवो देवहूतिमुवतु देव्या धिया । प्रेदं ब्रह्म प्रेदं क्षत्रं । प्रेमं सुन्वंतं यजमानमवतु । चित्रश्मित्राभिरूतिभिः ॥ (*tānaḥ | ajara uṣasāmanīkèḥ | ā yo dyāṃ bhātyā pṛthivīṃ | aurvamaṃtarikṣaṃ | jyotiṣā yajñāya śarma saṃyat | agnirvaiśvānara iha śravadiha somasya matsat | premāṃ devo devahūtimuvatu devyā dhiyā | predaṃ brahma predaṃ kṣatraṃ | premaṃ sunvaṃtaṃ yajamānamavatu | citraśmitrābhirūtibhiḥ ‖*) **GLOSS**

This very sūkta is recited in the Āgnimāruta-śastra with reference to the fire Vaiśvānara. In the middle of this mantra there is the sentence यो विड्वो मानुषीभ्यो दीदेत् (*yo viḍvo mānuṣībhyo dīdet*). Of this it might be said: this god who shines for the benefit of human beings, his subjects, is Sūrya; therefore Sūrya himself is addressed here by the word Vaiśvānara; hence there is no difference between Sūrya and the fire Vaiśvānara. But it is not so. This mantra is recited with reference to Agni. The meaning that on the sacrificial altar it is the terrestrial fire itself that shines for the benefit of the subjects, such as the sacrificers who perform the sacrifice, also applies to this mantra. Therefore it must be said that the fire Vaiśvānara is not Sūrya but the terrestrial fire. Moreover, in the chandomika sacrifice called daśarātra the Sauryavaiśvānara sūkta beginning जमदग्निराहुतः (*jamadagnirāhutaḥ*) is recited. This sūkta too does not relate to Sūrya; it applies to Agni. For the word जमदग्नि (*jamadagni*) means a fire that is well kindled and burns blazing. In sacrifices and the like, when an offering is made in the fire, it is the custom to make the fire blaze with samidh, ghee and other materials and to perform the offering and the like in that fire which burns well. Therefore the idea is that this indicates the terrestrial fire and not Āditya (or Sūrya).

यथो एतद्धविष्णांतीयं सूक्तं सौर्यवैश्वानरं भवतीत्यस्यैव तद्भवति । (*yatho etaddhaviṣṇāṃtīyaṃ sūktaṃ sauryavaiśvānaraṃ bhavatītyasyaiva tadbhavati |*)

हविष्वांतमजरं स्वर्विदि दिविस्पृश्याहुतं जुष्टमग्नौ । तस्य भर्मणे भुवनाय देवा धर्मणे कं स्वधया पप्रथंत ॥ (*haviṣvāṃtamajaraṃ svarvidi divispṛśyāhutaṃ juṣṭamagnau | tasya bharmaṇe bhuvanāya devā dharmaṇe kaṃ svadhayā paprathaṃta ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-89-1) **NOTE**

हविर्यत्पानीयमजरं सूर्यविदि दिविस्पृश्यभिहुतं जुष्टमग्नौ तस्य भरणाय च भावनाय च धारणाय च चैतेभ्यः सर्वेभ्यः कर्मभ्य इममग्निमन्नेनापप्रथंतेति. (*haviryatpānīyamajaraṃ sūryavidi divispṛśyabhihutaṃ juṣṭamagnau tasya bharaṇāya ca bhāvanāya ca dhāraṇāya ca caitebhyaḥ sarvebhyaḥ karmabhya imamagnimannenāpaprathaṃteti.*) (Ni. 7-25)

Further, the sūkta हविष्वांतमजरं (*haviṣvāṃtamajaraṃ*) has Sūrya and the fire Vaiśvānara as its deity. If it is said that the Vaiśvānara praised in this sūkta is Āditya, that is not right. The fire Vaiśvānara spoken of there is the terrestrial fire. This becomes clear if its meaning is examined: this oblation, free from decay

### Printed p. 536

that is, free from destruction, and pleasing, is offered, before it is drunk, in this fire, which touches heaven with its own light and knows Sūrya well. The gods, for the bearing, holding and nourishing of that oblation, join food to it and make it increase: this is the chief meaning of this Ṛk. In this sūkta or Ṛk the oblation that is mentioned is offered in the fire before it is drunk. This oblation is free from destruction and pleasing to the mind (to drink). It is offered in the sacrificial fire, which touches the sky (heaven) with its flames, that is, which is well kindled, and which is conscious of Sūrya. In order to make this oblation possessed of the powers of holding, nourishing, bearing, sustaining and the like, the gods join food with it and make it increase. Since the offering of the oblation is mentioned here, the offering relates to Agni, that is, to the terrestrial fire, and not to Sūrya. The offering is made in the fire, not in Sūrya. Therefore it must be said that the deity Vaiśvānara taught in this sūkta is not Āditya or Sūrya but the terrestrial fire.

He further says: अध्यासाह (*adhyāsāha*) **NOTE**

अपामुपस्थे महिषा अगृभ्यत विशो राजानमुप तस्थुर्ऋग्नियं । आ दूतो अग्निरभरद्विवस्वतो वैश्वानरं मातरिश्वा परावतः ॥ (*apāmupasthe mahiṣā agṛbhyata viśo rājānamupa tasthurṛgniyaṃ | ā dūto agnirabharadvivasvato vaiśvānaraṃ mātariśvā parāvataḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6.8-4)

अपामुपस्थ उपस्थाने महंत्यरिक्षलोक आसीना महांत इति वागृह्णत माध्यमिका देवगणा विश इव राजानमुपतस्थु र्ऋग्मियमृग्यंतमिति वार्चनीयमिति वा पूजनीयमिति वाहरद्यं दूतो देवानां विवस्वत आदित्याद्विवस्वाद्विवासनवान् प्रेरितवतः परागताद्वापि वास्याग्नेर्वैश्वानरस मातरिश्वानमाहर्तारमाह॥ मातरिश्वा वायुर्मातर्यंतरिक्षे श्वसिति मातर्याश्वनितीति वा ॥ (*apāmupastha upasthāne mahaṃtyarikṣaloka āsīnā mahāṃta iti vāgṛhṇata mādhyamikā devagaṇā viśa iva rājānamupatasthu rṛgmiyamṛgyaṃtamiti vārcanīyamiti vā pūjanīyamiti vāharadyaṃ dūto devānāṃ vivasvata ādityādvivasvādvivāsanavān preritavataḥ parāgatādvāpi vāsyāgnervaiśvānarasa mātariśvānamāhartāramāha‖ mātariśvā vāyurmātaryaṃtarikṣe śvasiti mātaryāśvanitīti vā ‖*) (Ni. 7-26)

And on this subject he has given the example of another Ṛk. Near the lap of the waters, that is, in the wide world of the sky, the great and glorious gods of the middle region (dwelling in the sky) welcomed this fire. As subjects welcome their king with extreme respect, so the gods welcomed and honoured this fire, who is the subject of the mantra, worthy of worship, worthy of honour. Mātariśvan (the wind), who dwells in the sky, first

### Printed p. 537

impelled by the gods, brought the fire Vaiśvānara from Āditya, who is in a very distant region. The fire Vaiśvānara first appeared in the sky to Mātariśvan himself. That Mātariśvan brought the fire Vaiśvānara from the neighbourhood of Āditya, who is in a very distant region. Mātariśvan means the wind. This wind has the name मातरिश्वा (*mātariśvā*) either because it dwells in the sky or because it moves swiftly in the sky. What is to be noticed here is this: it is said that the gods of the sky brought the fire from the region where the sun is. No one is able to bring the sun from one region to another. Only the fire can be brought. Therefore it must be understood that here by Vaiśvānara the terrestrial fire is spoken of. Moreover, in many mantras the qualities of Sūrya (Āditya) are spoken of the fire Vaiśvānara: in the mantra विश्वस्मा अग्निं भुवनाय देवा वैश्वानरं केतुमह्नामकृण्वन् (*viśvasmā agniṃ bhuvanāya devā vaiśvānaraṃ ketumahnāmakṛṇvan*), the twelfth Ṛk of the haviṣvānta sūkta **NOTE**, it is said that the gods made the fire Vaiśvānara the maker of the ahas (days, daytimes). The quality of being the maker of days belongs to Sūrya, yet here this quality is spoken of this fire Vaiśvānara. For since in mantras such as अग्निः सर्वा देवताः (*agniḥ sarvā devatāḥ*) (Ai. Brā. 2-1-2) and इंद्रं मित्रं वरुणमग्निमाहुः (*iṃdraṃ mitraṃ varuṇamagnimāhuḥ*) (1-164-46) this fire is said to be the self of all the gods, it is usual to attribute to the fire the qualities of Sūrya and other deities. Therefore the fire Vaiśvānara is the terrestrial fire and not Āditya.

अथैनमेताभ्यां सर्वाणि स्थानान्यभ्यापादं स्तौति । (*athainametābhyāṃ sarvāṇi sthānānyabhyāpādaṃ stauti |*)

मूर्धा भुवो भवति नक्तमग्निस्ततः सूर्यो जायते प्रातरुद्यन् । मायामू तु यज्ञियानामेतामपो यत्तूर्णिश्चरति प्रजानन् ॥ (*mūrdhā bhuvo bhavati naktamagnistataḥ sūryo jāyate prātarudyan | māyāmū tu yajñiyānāmetāmapo yattūrṇiścarati prajānan ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 108-6) **NOTE**

मूर्धा मूर्तमस्मिन्दीयते मूर्धा यः सर्वेषां भूतानां भवति नक्तमग्निस्ततः सूर्यो जायते प्रातरुद्यन् स एव प्रज्ञां श्वेतां मन्यंते यज्ञियानां देवानां यज्ञसंपादिनामपो यत्कर्म चरति प्रजानन् सर्वाणि स्थानान्यनु संचरते त्वरमाणः ॥ (*mūrdhā mūrtamasmindīyate mūrdhā yaḥ sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ bhavati naktamagnistataḥ sūryo jāyate prātarudyan sa eva prajñāṃ śvetāṃ manyaṃte yajñiyānāṃ devānāṃ yajñasaṃpādināmapo yatkarma carati prajānan sarvāṇi sthānānyanu saṃcarate tvaramāṇaḥ ‖*) (Ni. 7-27)

The terrestrial fire is praised in many contexts as if it possessed the distinctive qualities of other particular deities such as Sūrya. On this subject the author of the Nirukta has given two Ṛks as examples: for the whole animal kingdom fire is absolutely necessary in order to live. Without fire (the heat in the body, which is called the fire Vaiśvānara) it is not possible to live. Such a fire (the fire in the form of Sūrya), at night, for the world containing all living beings

### Printed p. 538

shines as the lord. In the morning that same fire rises in the form of Sūrya. The gods are able to know the extraordinary power and capacity of such a fire, that is, that by day in the form of Sūrya and by night in the form of fire it performs its duty. Here it is said that the fire is the lord of the night. To express the meaning "lord", the word मूर्धा (*mūrdhā*) is used in this Ṛk. How the meaning "lord" came to this word is this: among the several limbs of the body the head (mūrdhā or śiras) is the chief. There is the saying सर्वस्य गात्रस्य शिरः प्रधानं (*sarvasya gātrasya śiraḥ pradhānaṃ*). Therefore the use of the word मूर्धा (*mūrdhā*) here indicates the meaning "lord". This fire is the lord of all living beings at night; that is, the idea is that in the night, when there is no heat of Sūrya, the fire provides heat and light to living beings and performs the duty of Sūrya. In the morning this same fire rises as Sūrya and protects living beings. Seers and others who perform sacrifices are able to know such powers and capacities of the gods. The idea is that the fire has the power to move swiftly in all regions in order to do this duty. In this Ṛk it is said that the fire performs the duty of Sūrya. It is to be understood that this is a praise of the extraordinary quality of the fire, and that this Ṛk does not indicate that the fire is Āditya, or that the fire has the powers and capacities of other deities.

तस्योत्तरा भूयसे निर्वचनाय । (*tasyottarā bhūyase nirvacanāya |*)

स्तोमेन हि दिवि देवासो अग्निमजीजनङ्क्तिभी रोदसिप्रां । तमू अकृण्वन्त्रेधा भुवे कं स ओषधीः पचति विश्वरूपाः ॥ (*stomena hi divi devāso agnimajījanaṅktibhī rodasiprāṃ | tamū akṛṇvantredhā bhuve kaṃ sa oṣadhīḥ pacati viśvarūpāḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-88-10)

स्तोमेन हि यं दिवि देवा अग्निमजनयञ्क्तिभिः कर्मभिर्दार्वाण्यथिव्योः पूरणं तमकुर्वंस्त्रेधाभावाय पृथिव्यामंतरिक्षे दिवीति शाकपूणिः यदस्य दिवि तृतीयं तदसावादित्य इति हि ब्राह्मणं तदंगीकृत्य स्तौति. (*stomena hi yaṃ divi devā agnimajanayañktibhiḥ karmabhirdārvāṇyathivyoḥ pūraṇaṃ tamakurvaṃstredhābhāvāya pṛthivyāmaṃtarikṣe divīti śākapūṇiḥ yadasya divi tṛtīyaṃ tadasāvāditya iti hi brāhmaṇaṃ tadaṃgīkṛtya stauti.*) (Ni. 7-28)

The gods produced Agni in heaven by praise. That Agni, by his powers and capacities, filled heaven and earth and shone. Then those gods made that Agni threefold in form. That Agni ripens all plants (herbs); that is, he makes them grow and increase.

The Agni whom the gods, having produced him in heaven by stoma (praise)

### Printed p. 539

and established there, that Agni by his powers and capacities pervaded heaven and earth. That is, the teacher named Śākapūṇi says that the gods produced Agni so that he might be in the three places, earth, sky and heaven. On this point there is also the Brāhmaṇa sentence यदस्य दिवि तृतीयं तदसावादित्यः (*yadasya divi tṛtīyaṃ tadasāvādityaḥ*): the third form of Agni which shines in heaven is this very Āditya who is seen by our eyes. Accepting this very view, the seer praises Agni in the next Ṛk.

अथैनमेतयादित्यीकृत्य स्तौति । (*athainametayādityīkṛtya stauti |*)

यदेदेनमदधुर्यज्जियासो दिवि देवाः सूर्यमादितेयमदितेयं । यदा चरिष्णू मिथुनावभूतामादित प्रापश्यन् भुवनानि विश्वा ॥ (*yadedenamadadhuryajjiyāso divi devāḥ sūryamāditeyamaditeyaṃ | yadā cariṣṇū mithunāvabhūtāmādita prāpaśyan bhuvanāni viśvā ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-88-11)

यदैनमदधुर्यज्ञियाः सर्वे दिवि देवाः सूर्यमादितेयमदितेः पुत्रं यदा चरिष्यू मिथुनौ प्रादुरभूतां सर्वदा सहचारिणावुषाश्चादित्यश्च । मिथुनौ कस्मान्मिनोतिः श्रयतिकर्मा, थु इति नामकरणस्थकारो वा नयतिः परो, वनिर्वा, समाश्रितावन्योन्यं नयतो, वनुतो वा, मनुष्यमिथुनावप्यैतस्मादेव, मेधंतावन्योन्यं वनुत इति वा. (*yadainamadadhuryajñiyāḥ sarve divi devāḥ sūryamāditeyamaditeḥ putraṃ yadā cariṣyū mithunau prādurabhūtāṃ sarvadā sahacāriṇāvuṣāścādityaśca | mithunau kasmānminotiḥ śrayatikarmā, thu iti nāmakaraṇasthakāro vā nayatiḥ paro, vanirvā, samāśritāvanyonyaṃ nayato, vanuto vā, manuṣyamithunāvapyaitasmādeva, medhaṃtāvanyonyaṃ vanuta iti vā.*) (Ni. 72-9) **NOTE**

Accepting the view that this very Agni is Āditya, the seer praises with this Ṛk. When the gods worthy of sacrifice established in heaven Sūrya, the son of Aditi, and when these twin deities (Uṣas and Āditya) were created and began to move together, then they saw all the living beings of the world.

When the gods worthy of sacrifice, that is, the gods who are praised in sacrifices and the like, established in heaven Āditya (Sūrya), the son of Aditi, and when the two who are twinned, that is, who are always together (the two, Uṣas and Āditya), were created, from that time these two deities, Uṣas and Āditya, moving always together, became able to see the whole animal kingdom in the world.

Here the etymology of the word mithuna is stated. The word mithuna is formed from the root मिनोति (*minoti*) with the sense of resorting (the meaning "to resort"). Namely, the root mi in the word mithuna has the meaning "to resort". थु (*thu*), or the letter tha, is the affix. The last letter na, formed from the root नयति (*nayati*) (the root nayati is the latter part), indicates the meaning of leading another

### Printed p. 540

that is, of carrying. That is, the word mithuna means that one resorts to the other mutually and they are together. समाश्रिता अन्नोन्यं प्रति आत्मानं नयतः कालं वा समाश्रिता भवतः परस्परं (*samāśritā annonyaṃ prati ātmānaṃ nayataḥ kālaṃ vā samāśritā bhavataḥ parasparaṃ*) **NOTE**: that is, the word मिथुनौ (*mithunau*) indicates the meaning that two resort to each other mutually, or, in the matter of time, that after one time another time comes (night, day and so on). In the case of human beings too the word mithuna has the meaning of two persons who resort to each other or who pass their time together in mutual company.

अथैनमेतयाग्नीकृत्य स्तौति । (*athainametayāgnīkṛtya stauti |*)

यत्रा वदेते अवरः परश्च यज्ञन्योः कतरो नौ वि वेद । आ शेकुरित्सधमादं सखायो नक्षंत यज्ञं क इदं वि वोचत् ॥ (*yatrā vadete avaraḥ paraśca yajñanyoḥ kataro nau vi veda | ā śekuritsadhamādaṃ sakhāyo nakṣaṃta yajñaṃ ka idaṃ vi vocat ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-88-17)

यत्र विवदेते देव्यौ होतारावयं चाग्निरसौ च मध्यमः कतरो नौ यज्ञे भूयो वेदेत्याशक्कुवंति सत्सहमदनं समानख्याना ऋत्विजस्तेषां यज्ञं समश्नुवानानां को न इदं विवक्ष्यतीति ॥ (*yatra vivadete devyau hotārāvayaṃ cāgnirasau ca madhyamaḥ kataro nau yajñe bhūyo vedetyāśakkuvaṃti satsahamadanaṃ samānakhyānā ṛtvijasteṣāṃ yajñaṃ samaśnuvānānāṃ ko na idaṃ vivakṣyatīti ‖*) (3. 7-30) **NOTE**

The seer has praised with this Ṛk, accepting this fire Vaiśvānara as the terrestrial fire. Of the lower and the upper fires, who know the matter of the sacrifice, which knows more? Who is able to decide this matter? The priests and others who bear equal shares in the sacrifice are able to decide it.

दैव्या होतारौ (*daivyā hotārau*) means the Hotṛs who are of the nature of gods, the fire named Hotṛ who invokes the gods in the sacrifice. Since the word होतारौ (*hotārau*) here is in the dual, the two deities are the terrestrial fire (the sacrificial fire) established on the earth and the wind or lightning fire in the middle region. Since both of these are only forms of fire, they are addressed by the dual word होतारौ (*hotārau*). अवरः परश्च (*avaraḥ paraśca*) means the lower and the upper. By "lower" is to be understood the terrestrial fire in the place of the earth, and by परः (*paraḥ*) the fire (lightning) in the middle region. Which of these two has more knowledge? Among the priests who bear equal shares, that is, the chief parts, in rites such as sacrifices and who know the matter of the sacrifice well, which priest is able to decide this matter?

तस्योत्तरा भूयसे निर्वचनाय । (*tasyottarā bhūyase nirvacanāya |*)

यावन्मात्रमुषसो न प्रतीकं सुपूर्णोऽवसते मातरिश्वः । (*yāvanmātramuṣaso na pratīkaṃ supūrṇo 'vasate mātariśvaḥ |*)

### Printed p. 541

तावद्धधात्युप यज्ञमायान्ब्राह्मणो होतुरवरो निषीदन् ॥ (*tāvaddhadhātyupa yajñamāyānbrāhmaṇo hoturavaro niṣīdan ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-88-19)

यावन्मात्रमुषसः प्रत्यक्तं भवति प्रतिदर्शनमिति वास्तु समानस्य संप्रत्यर्थे प्रयोग इहेव निधेहीति यथा सुपर्ण्यः सुपतना एता रात्रयो वसते मातरिश्वन् ज्योतिर्वर्णस्य तावदुपदधाति याज्ञमागच्छन् ब्राह्मणो होतास्याग्नेर्होतुरवरो निषीदन् ॥ (*yāvanmātramuṣasaḥ pratyaktaṃ bhavati pratidarśanamiti vāstu samānasya saṃpratyarthe prayoga iheva nidhehīti yathā suparṇyaḥ supatanā etā rātrayo vasate mātariśvan jyotirvarṇasya tāvadupadadhāti yājñamāgacchan brāhmaṇo hotāsyāgnerhoturavaro niṣīdan ‖*) (Ni. 7-31)

On this subject another Ṛk has been given as an example. In the preceding Ṛk Agni and Vāyu were praised. In this Ṛk Agni alone is praised. Mātariśvan (the wind), addressing a man, asked: can the Brāhmaṇa, the human Hotṛ taking part in the sacrifice, hold the knowledge (the understanding in the performance of the sacrifice) **NOTE** that Agni, the Hotṛ of the gods, has, that is, can he know it? To this that man gave the following reply.

O Mātariśvan, as long as (for how long) the birds of excellent wings hold the dawn, so long the Brāhmaṇa, the human Hotṛ, seated near on the sacrificial altar, in a place lower than Agni, holds it (that is, by the favour of Agni he knows a little).

The word न (*na*) in this Ṛk does not have the sense of comparison. It has the sense of "now" (samprati). It is to be understood as in the sentence इहैव निधेहि (*ihaiva nidhehi*), where, although the word iha means "here", the sentence means "place it right now". Therefore the sentence यावन्मात्रमुषसो न प्रतीकं (*yāvanmātramuṣaso na pratīkaṃ*) means: for as long, that is, for how long (only a short time), as the dawn-time at the end of the night extends, so long only. The sentence सुपर्ण्यः सुपतना एता रात्रयो वसते मातरिश्वन (*suparṇyaḥ supatanā etā rātrayo vasate mātariśvana*) means: O Mātariśvan, birds of excellent wings, flying, hold the dawn-time. That is, here birds means nights. The word सुपर्ण्य (*suparṇya*), which indicates this, means manifold wings; it indicates the manifold (excellent) colours of the dawn-time. Therefore सुपर्ण्यः (*suparṇyaḥ*) means that when at the end of the night the dawn rises, that dawn has manifold or charming colours: this is the idea. The measure of this dawn-time is very small. Since the sun rises very quickly after the dawn-time, the idea is that the dawn-time is very small in measure, only for a very short time. The human Hotṛ is lower than the Agni who is the Hotṛ of the gods. Therefore the Brāhmaṇa, the human Hotṛ, seated on the sacrificial altar in a place lower than the Agni there established, for a very short time only, by the favour of Agni, who is of special wisdom,

### Printed p. 542

performs the work of the Hotṛ: this is the chief meaning. By this the smallness of man and the greatness of Agni are made evident. Since it is said in this Ṛk that the Brāhmaṇa, the human Hotṛ, seated on the sacrificial altar, performs the work of the Hotṛ while praising Agni, the Hotṛ of the gods, it is clearly shown that here by the fire Vaiśvānara the terrestrial fire is praised, and not Āditya.

होतृजपस्त्वनग्निर्वैश्वानरियो भवति देव सवितरेतं त्वा वृणतेऽग्निं होत्राय सह पित्रा वैश्वानरेणेतीममेवाग्निं सवितारमाह सर्वस्य प्रसवितारं मध्यमं वोत्तमं ना पितरं ॥ यस्तु सूक्तं भजते यस्यै हविर्निरुप्यतेऽयमेव सोऽग्निर्वैश्वानरः । निपातमेवैते उत्तरे ज्योतिषी एतेन नामधेयेन भजेते भजेते ॥ (*hotṛjapastvanagnirvaiśvānariyo bhavati deva savitaretaṃ tvā vṛṇate 'gniṃ hotrāya saha pitrā vaiśvānareṇetīmamevāgniṃ savitāramāha sarvasya prasavitāraṃ madhyamaṃ vottamaṃ nā pitaraṃ ‖ yastu sūktaṃ bhajate yasyai havirnirupyate 'yameva so 'gnirvaiśvānaraḥ | nipātamevaite uttare jyotiṣī etena nāmadheyena bhajete bhajete ‖*) (Ni. 7-31)

The muttered mantras and the like that the Hotṛ recites in a sacrifice praise Vaiśvānara by addressing him, not Agni. The mantra mutter is देवसवितरेतु त्वा वृणतेऽग्निं होत्राय सह पित्रा वैश्वानरेण (*devasavitaretu tvā vṛṇate 'gniṃ hotrāya saha pitrā vaiśvānareṇa*). The sentence "O shining god Savitṛ, the Hotṛ has chosen you, that is, Agni, together with your father Vaiśvānara, for the recitation of praise" needs explanation. Here the seer has called Agni Savitṛ. Here Savitṛ (the word Savitṛ) means the producer of all things (or of living beings). It is in this sense that the word is used here. He has addressed as father the wind, who is of the middle region, or Āditya, who is of the upper (heaven) region.

The Vaiśvānara for whom the oblation is offered, the god praised in the sūkta (the deity to whom the oblation is offered), is this terrestrial fire.

As is said in the sentences सूर्यो वैश्वानरः । अग्निर्वैश्वानरः । (*sūryo vaiśvānaraḥ | agnirvaiśvānaraḥ |*) and the like, the light in the middle region in the form of lightning and the light in the region of heaven in the form of Āditya, these two lights, are referred to by one and the same name, Vaiśvānara; that is, the chief meaning is that the terrestrial fire, which is referred to by the word Vaiśvānara, shines in three forms: in heaven in the form of Āditya, in the sky in the form of lightning, and on the earth in the form of the terrestrial fire.

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> हविष्वांतमित्येकोनविंशत्यृचं सूक्तं चतुर्थं त्रैष्टुभं ! मूर्धन्वानृषिः।
> स जांगिरसो वामदेव्यो ना । सूर्यो वैश्वानरगुणकोऽग्निश्च समुदितो

### Printed p. 543

> देवता । तथा चानुक्रांतं । हविरेकोनांगिरसो मूर्धन्वान्वामदेवो वा
> सौर्यवैश्वानरीयमिति ॥ व्यूढस्य दशरात्रस्य पंचमेऽहन्याग्निमारुत एतद्वैश्वानरीयनिविद्धानं । सूत्रितं च । हविष्कांतमग्निर्होता गृहपतिः स राजा ।
> आ. ८-८ । इति ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sāyaṇa says that the sūkta beginning हविष्वांतं (*haviṣvāṃtaṃ*) has nineteen Ṛks and is the fourth sūkta; it is in the Triṣṭubh metre; the seer is Mūrdhanvān, an Āṅgirasa or a Vāmadeva **NOTE**; the deity is Sūrya and the Agni who has the quality of Vaiśvānara, together. He cites the Anukramaṇī to the same effect. On the fifth day of the vyūḍha daśarātra, at the Āgnimāruta śastra, this is the nivid-dhāna sūkta addressed to Vaiśvānara, and it is prescribed by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra (Ā. 8-8).

##### Anuvāda

This sūkta हविष्वांतं (*haviṣvāṃtaṃ*) is the fourth sūkta in the seventh Anuvāka. It has nineteen Ṛks. The seer of this sūkta is one called Mūrdhanvān. This seer belongs to the Aṅgirasa gotra or the Vāmadeva gotra. The deity of this sūkta is Sūrya and the Agni endowed with the qualities of Vaiśvānara, together. The metre is Triṣṭubh. In the Anukramaṇī it is said हविरेकोनांगिरसो मूर्धन्वान्नामदेव्यो ना सौर्यवैश्वानरीयं (*havirekonāṃgiraso mūrdhanvānnāmadevyo nā sauryavaiśvānarīyaṃ*). On the fifth day of the sacrifice called vyūḍha daśarātra, at the time of reciting the Āgnimāruta śastra mantras, this sūkta is to be recited as the nivid-dhāna sūkta addressed to Vaiśvānara; this is explained by the sūtra of the Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra हविष्वांतमग्निर्होता गृहपतिः स राजा (*haviṣvāṃtamagnirhotā gṛhapatiḥ sa rājā*) (Ā. 8-8).

**NOTE**

Maṇḍala 10; Anuvāka 7; Sūkta 88. Aṣṭaka 8; Adhyāya 4; Vargas 10, 11, 12, 13. Number of Ṛks in the sūkta: 19. Seer: मूर्धन्वानांगिरसो वामदेव्यो वा (*mūrdhanvānāṃgiraso vāmadevyo vā*). Deity: सूर्यवैश्वानरा (*sūryavaiśvānarā*). Metre: त्रिष्टुप् (*triṣṭup*).

#### Ṛk 1

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> ह॒विष्वांत॑म॒जरं॑ स्व॒र्विदि॑ दिवि॒स्पृश्याहु॑तं॒ जुष्ट॑म॒ग्नौ ।  
> तस्य॒ भर्म॑णे॒ भुव॑नाय दे॒वा धर्म॑णे॒ कं स्व॒धया॑ पप्रथंत॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> हविः । पांतं । अजरं । स्वःविदि । दिविस्पृशि । आहुतं । जुष्टं । अग्नौ ।  
> शस्य । भर्मणे । भुवनाय । देवाः । धर्मणे । कं । स्वधया । पप्रथंत ॥ १ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> पांतं पानीयं सोमात्मकमजरं जरारहितं जुष्टं देवानां प्रियं
> यद्धविः स्वर्विदि सूर्यस्य वेदितरि दिविस्पृशिदिवि स्पष्टर्याग्नावाहुतमभिहुतं तस्य

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The oblation (havis) that is fit for drinking (pāntam), of the nature of Soma, ageless, that is, free from old age, and dear to the gods, is offered in the fire, which knows Sūrya (svarvid) and touches heaven (divispṛś); and the gods, for the bearing of that oblation

### Printed p. 544

> सोमात्मकस्य हविषो भर्मणे भरणाय भुवनाय भावनाय च धर्मणे
> धारणाय च कं सर्वस्य सुखकरमिममग्निं देवाः स्वधयान्नेन पप्रथंत । प्रथयंति । तथा च यास्कः । हविर्यत्पानीयमजरं सूर्यविदि दिविस्पृश्यभिहुतं
> जुष्टमग्नौ तस्य भरणाय च भावनाय च धारणाय चैतेभ्यः सर्वेभ्यः कर्मभो
> देवा इममग्निमन्नेनापप्रथंत । नि. ७-२५ । इति ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The gods, for the bearing (भर्मणे (*bharmaṇe*) means "for bearing"), for the becoming (भुवनाय (*bhuvanāya*) means "for becoming") and for the holding (धर्मणे (*dharmaṇe*) means "for holding") of the Soma-form oblation, have extended (पप्रथंत (*paprathaṃta*) means "they extend") with svadhā, that is, with food, this Agni, who is कं (*kaṃ*), the giver of happiness to all. Accordingly Yāska (Ni. 7-25) says: the oblation which is drinkable, ageless, dear, offered in the fire that knows Sūrya and touches heaven; for the bearing, the becoming and the holding of it, for all these works, the gods have extended this Agni with food.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- पांतं (*pāṃtaṃ*)—fit for drinking
- अजरं (*ajaraṃ*)—free from decay
- जुष्टं (*juṣṭaṃ*)—fit for the enjoyment of the gods
- हविः (*haviḥ*)—which Soma-form oblation
- स्वर्विदि (*svarvidi*)—who knows the heavenly world
- दिविस्पृशि (*divispṛśi*)—who touches the world of heaven
- अग्नौ (*agnau*)—in Agni
- आहुतं (*āhutaṃ*)—has been offered
- तस्य (*tasya*)—of that Soma-form oblation
- भर्मणे (*bharmaṇe*)—for the bearing
- भुवनाय (*bhuvanāya*)—for the existence
- धर्मणे (*dharmaṇe*)—for the support
- कं (*kaṃ*)—Agni, the giver of happiness
- देवाः (*devāḥ*)—the gods
- स्वधया (*svadhayā*)—with food
- पप्रथंत (*paprathaṃta*)—have satisfied

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The Soma-form oblation which is fit for drinking, free from decay and fit for the enjoyment of the gods has been offered in Agni, who knows the heavenly world and touches the world of heaven. For the bearing, the existence and the support of that Soma-form oblation, the gods have satisfied Agni, the giver of happiness, with food.

##### English translation
The Soma oblation, undecaying and agreeable to the gods, which is offered to Agni, who is cognizant of heaven, who touches the sky—for its nourishment, existence and support, the gods supply (Agni) the giver of happiness with food.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

For the explanation of the etymology that Yāska has written for this Ṛk, see what is written in the introduction to this sūkta (pages 535-536).

#### Ṛk 2

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> गी॒र्णं भुव॑नं॒ तम॒साप॑गूळ्हमा॒विः स्व॑रभवज्जा॒ते अ॒ग्नौ ।  
> तस्य॑ दे॒वाः पृ॑थि॒वी द्यौरु॒तापोऽर॑णय॒न्नोष॑धीः स॒ख्ये अ॑स्य ॥

### Printed p. 545

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> गीर्णं । भुवनं । तमसा । अप्यगूळ्हं । आविः । स्वः । अभवत् । जाते । अग्नौ ।  
> तस्य । देवाः । पृथिवी । द्यौः । उत । अपः । अरणयन् । ओषधीः । सख्ये । अस्य ॥ २ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> गीर्णं पूर्वं निगीर्णं तमसांधकारेणापगूढमाच्छादितं स्वः सर्वं
> भुवनमग्नौ यस्मिन्वैश्वानरे जात उत्पन्ने सत्याविरभवत् आविर्भवति तस्यास्य वैश्वानरस्याग्नेः सख्ये सखिकर्मणि देवा इंद्रादयः पृथिवी भूमिश्च द्यौश्चापोऽंतरिक्तं
> चोदकानि वौषधीरोषध्यश्चारणयत् । अरमंत । प्रीतिं कृतवंत इत्यर्थः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The whole world (स्वः (*svaḥ*)), formerly swallowed up (गीर्णं (*gīrṇaṃ*)) and hidden (अपगूढं (*apagūḍhaṃ*)) by darkness, became manifest when Agni, that is Vaiśvānara, was born. In the friendship, that is the fellowship, of this Agni, the gods, Indra and the others, and earth, and heaven, and the atmosphere (अपः (*apaḥ*)) and the waters (चोदकानि (*codakāni*)) **NOTE**, and the plants rejoiced (अरणयन् (*araṇayan*) means "they took delight"), that is, they showed affection.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- गीर्णं (*gīrṇaṃ*)—that which was at first absorbed
- तमसा (*tamasā*)—by darkness
- अपगूढं (*apagūḍhaṃ*)—enveloped
- स्वः भुवनं (*svaḥ bhuvanaṃ*)—the whole world
- अग्नौ (*agnau*)—Vaiśvānara Agni
- जाते (*jāte*)—when he was born
- आविरभवत् (*āvirabhavat*)—became manifest
- तस्य अस्य (*tasya asya*)—of this Vaiśvānara Agni
- सख्ये (*sakhye*)—to obtain the friendship
- देवाः (*devāḥ*)—all the gods
- पृथिवी (*pṛthivī*)—the earth
- द्यौः (*dyauḥ*)—the world of heaven
- अपः (*apaḥ*)—the atmosphere
- ओषधीर् (*oṣadhīr*)—the plants
- अरणयन् (*araṇayan*)—obtained delight

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The whole world, which at first was absorbed and invisible and enveloped by darkness, became manifest when Vaiśvānara Agni was born. To obtain the friendship of this Vaiśvānara Agni all the gods, the earth, the world of heaven, the atmosphere and the plants obtained delight.

##### English translation
The whole world swallowed up, hidden in darkness, was made manifest when Agni was born: the gods, heaven and earth, the waters and the plants rejoiced in his friendship.

> यः । भानुना । पृथिवीं । द्यां । उत । इमां । आततान । रोदसी इति । अंतरिक्षं॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> यज्ञियेभिर्यज्ञार्हैर्देवेभिर्देवैरिंद्रादिभिर्नु क्षिप्रमिषितोऽहमजरं
> जरारहितं बृहंतं महांतमग्निं तं वैश्वानराग्निं स्तोषाणि । स्तोषामि । यो
> वैश्वानराग्निर्भानुना तेजसा पृथिवीं भूमिमुतापि चेमां द्यां दिवं चाततान
> आतनोति । तदेव दर्शयति । रोदसी द्यावापृथिव्यौ चाततान आतनोति । विस्तारयतीत्यर्थः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Sent (इषितः (*iṣitaḥ*)) quickly (नु (*nu*) means "quickly") by the gods, Indra and the others, who are worthy of sacrifice, I praise (स्तोषाणि (*stoṣāṇi*) means "I praise") that Vaiśvānara Agni, the ageless, that is free from old age, and great. That Vaiśvānara Agni with his radiance (भानुना (*bhānunā*) means "with brilliance") extends the earth and this heaven. He shows the same: he extends also the two worlds, heaven and earth.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- यः (*yaḥ*)—which Agni
- भानुना (*bhānunā*)—by his own brilliance
- पृथिवीं (*pṛthivīṃ*)—the earth
- उत (*uta*)—and
- इमां द्यां (*imāṃ dyāṃ*)—this world of heaven
- रोदसी (*rodasī*)—heaven and earth
- अंतरिक्षं (*aṃtarikṣaṃ*)—the atmosphere
- आततान (*ātatāna*)—caused to spread
- अजरं (*ajaraṃ*)—free from decay
- बृहंतं (*bṛhaṃtaṃ*)—exceedingly great
- अग्निं (*agniṃ*)—Vaiśvānara Agni
- यज्जियेभिः (*yajjiyebhiḥ*)—who are worthy of worship
- देवेभिः (*devebhiḥ*)—by the gods
- नु (*nu*)—quickly
- इषितः (*iṣitaḥ*)—impelled
- स्तोषाणि (*stoṣāṇi*)—I praise

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

That free-from-decay, exceedingly great Vaiśvānara Agni who by his own brilliance has caused the earth, heaven and earth, and the atmosphere to spread—him, impelled by the gods who are worthy of worship, I praise.

##### English translation
Sent by adorable gods I praise the undecaying and mighty Agni, who by his radiance has spread forth the earth and this heven, the two worlds and the firmament.

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> यः । होता । आसीत् । प्रथमः । देवजुष्टः । यं । संआंजन् । आजेन ।  
> वृणानाः ।  
> सः । पतत्रि । इत्वरं । स्थाः । जगत् । यत् । श्वात्रं । अग्निः । अकृणोत् । जातवेदाः ॥ ४ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> यो वैश्वानरोऽग्निर्देवजुष्टो दॆवैः सेवितः प्रथमो मुख्यो होतासीत् अभूत् यं च वैश्वानराग्निं यजमाना वृणाना आज्येन समांजन् समंजति
> जातवेदा जातप्रज्ञो जातधनो वा वैश्वानरोऽग्निः पतत्रि पतनशीलं पक्षिजातमित्वरं गमनशीलं सरीसृपादिकं स्थाः स्थावरं वृक्षादिरूपं च जगत् । स्थावरं
> जंगमं च यज्जगदित्यर्थः । श्वात्रं क्षिप्रमेवाकृणोत् । अजनयत् ' तथा च
> यास्कः । स पतत्रि चेत्वरं स्थावरं जंगमं च यत्तत्क्षिप्रमग्निरकरोज्जातवेदाः ।
> नि. ५-३ । इति ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The Vaiśvānara Agni who, served by the gods (होता (*hotā*) the Hotṛ), was the first, that is the chief, Hotṛ, and whom the sacrificers, choosing him (वृणानाः (*vṛṇānāḥ*)), anoint (समांजन् (*samāṃjan*) means "they anoint") with ghee. Jātavedas, that is, he who has born wisdom or born wealth, Vaiśvānara Agni, quickly (श्वात्रं (*śvātraṃ*) means "quickly") made, that is, produced, the winged class of birds (पतत्रि (*patatri*)), the moving (इत्वरं (*itvaraṃ*)) creatures, serpents and the like, and the stationary (स्थाः (*sthāḥ*)) world, in the form of trees and the like; that is, the world which is both stationary and moving. Accordingly Yāska (Ni. 5-3) says that Agni Jātavedas quickly made what both flies and moves, and what is stationary and moving.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- यः (*yaḥ*)—which Vaiśvānara Agni
- देवजुष्टः (*devajuṣṭaḥ*)—served by the gods
- प्रथमः (*prathamaḥ*)—most chief
- होता (*hotā*)—the accomplisher of oblations
- आसीत् (*āsīt*)—was
- यं (*yaṃ*)—whom
- वृणानाः (*vṛṇānāḥ*)—the sacrificers who worshipped
- अज्येन (*ajyena*)—with ghee
- समांजन् (*samāṃjan*)—refined
- जातवेदाः सः (*jātavedāḥ saḥ*)—that same Agni, of born wisdom
- पतत्रि (*patatri*)—the class of birds
- इत्वरं (*itvaraṃ*)—the creatures that move about on the ground
- स्थाः (*sthāḥ*)—the trees and the like that do not move
- जगत् (*jagat*)—the whole world
- श्वात्रं (*śvātraṃ*)—swiftly
- अकृणोत् (*akṛṇot*)—made

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The Vaiśvānara Agni who is served by the gods, is the most chief, and is the accomplisher of oblations, whom the sacrificers worshipped, refining him with ghee—that same Agni quickly made the whole world, including the flying birds, all the creatures that walk on the ground, and the trees and the like.

##### English translation
Who propitiated by the gods was the first offerer of oblations, whom his worshippers anoint with clarified butter—he, Agni Jatavedas, quickly

### Printed p. 548

made that which can fly, that which can walk, that which is stationary, that which is moveable.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

श्वात्रं (*śvātraṃ*)—Śvātra means quickly, swiftly. In this matter Yāska has stated the etymology: श्वात्रमिति क्षिप्रनामाशु आतनं भवति (*śvātramiti kṣipranāmāśu ātanaṃ bhavati*) (Ni. 4-7).

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> तं । त्वा । अहेम । मतिभः । गीभिः । उक्षैः । सः । यज्जियः । अभवः ।  
> रोदसिप्राः ॥ ५ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> हे जातवेदो जातप्रज्ञाग्ने यद्यस्त्वं भुवनस्य त्रैलोक्यस्य मूर्धन्
> मूर्धनि रोचनेनादित्येन सहातिष्ठः स्थितवानसि तं वैश्वानराग्निं त्वा त्वां मतिभिरर्चनियाभिर्गिभिः स्तुतिभिरुक्थैः शस्त्रश्चाहेम । प्रपद्यामहे ॥ हि गताविति धातुः ॥
> सवैश्वानरस्त्वं रोदसिप्रा द्यावापृथिव्योः पूरयिता यज्ञियो यज्ञार्हश्चाभवः।
> भवसि ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

O Agni Jātavedas, that is, Agni of born wisdom, you who have stood at the head (मूर्धन् (*mūrdhan*)) of the world, that is, of the three worlds, together with the shining one (रोचनेन (*rocanena*)), the sun: you, that Vaiśvānara Agni, we approach (अहेम (*ahema*) means "we resort to") with worshipful thoughts (मतिभिः (*matibhiḥ*)), with praises (गीर्भिः (*gīrbhiḥ*)), with recitations (uktha) and with śastras. That Vaiśvānara you are the filler of heaven and earth (रोदसिप्राः (*rodasiprāḥ*)) and are worthy of sacrifice (यज्ञियः (*yajñiyaḥ*)).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- जातवेदः (*jātavedaḥ*)—O omniscient one
- अग्ने (*agne*)—O Agni
- यत् (*yat*)—you who
- भुवनस्य (*bhuvanasya*)—of the whole world
- मूर्धन् (*mūrdhan*)—at the top
- रोचनेन सह (*rocanena saha*)—together with the resplendent Āditya
- अतिष्ठः (*atiṣṭhaḥ*)—stand
- तं त्वा (*taṃ tvā*)—you, who are of the form of Vaiśvānara Agni
- मतिभिः (*matibhiḥ*)—with meditations
- गीर्भिः (*gīrbhiḥ*)—with praises
- उक्षैः (*ukṣaiḥ*)—with śastras and the like
- अहेम (*ahema*)—I worship
- सः (*saḥ*)—you who are of the form of Vaiśvānara
- रोदसिप्राः (*rodasiprāḥ*)—the satisfier of heaven and earth
- यज्ञियः (*yajñiyaḥ*)—worthy of worship
- अभवः (*abhavaḥ*)—you are

### Printed p. 549

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O omniscient Agni, you who are together with the resplendent Āditya at the top of the whole world, such you, who are of the form of Vaiśvānara Agni, we worship with meditations, with praises and with the mantras of the śastras and the like. You, who are of the form of Vaiśvānara, are the satisfier of heaven and earth, and worthy of worship.

##### English translation
Inasmuch as you abide, Agni Jatavedas, on the brow of the universe together with the sun, we have come to you with praises, with prayers : you are adorable, the satisfier of heaven and earth.

> उत् 5 यन् ।  
> मायां । ऊं इति । तु । यज्ञियानां । एतां । अपः । यत् । तूर्णिः । चरति ।

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> अग्निर्वैश्वानरोऽग्निर्नक्तं रात्रौ भुवो भूतजातस्य मूर्धा शिरोवत्प्रधानभूतो भवति । रात्रौ सर्वप्राणिनामालोकस्य तदधीनत्वात् । ततो रात्रेरनंतरं
