##### Gist of the bhāṣya

By this Ṛk they state the decision of the question that was put about the Vaiśvānara under discussion. O Mātariśvan, that is, Vāyu of the middle region, who breathes in the mother, the atmosphere: for as long as the well-winged nights cover the face of the dawn, that is, its appearance called light, the word न (*na*) being a filler; for so long the Brahman, the Hotṛ, the lower, the inferior one, sits down to perform the hotṛ's act of this divine hotṛ, the Vaiśvānara Agni, approaches the sacrifice and bears the hotṛ's work in his mind. Yāska says accordingly (Ni. 7-31): the word for "as much as" and for the face of the dawn has the sense of "visible" or "appearance", the word is used in the sense of "now", as in the phrase इहेव (*iheva*) **NOTE**; as the well-winged nights cover, Mātariśvan, so long the Brahman, the hotṛ who is lower than the hotṛ of this Agni, coming to the sacrifice and sitting down, bears it; and the hotṛ's muttered prayer becomes that of the Vaiśvānara fire.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- मातरिश्वः (*mātariśvaḥ*)—O Agni, who has the form of Vāyu
- यावन्मात्रं (*yāvanmātraṃ*)—as long as
- सुपर्ण्यः (*suparṇyaḥ*)—the nights that have a good manifestation
- उषसः प्रतीकं (*uṣasaḥ pratīkaṃ*)—the face of the dawn
- वसते (*vasate*)—cause to be covered
- तावत् (*tāvat*)—for so long
- अवरः ब्राह्मणः (*avaraḥ brāhmaṇaḥ*)—the hotṛ who is on the earth
- होतुः (*hotuḥ*)—to perform the act of the Agni who accomplishes the offering
- निषिदन् (*niṣidan*)—sitting down
- यज्ञं (*yajñaṃ*)—the sacrifice
- आयन् (*āyan*)—approaching
- उप दधाति (*upa dadhāti*)—obtains the knowledge of his act

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Agni, who have the form of Vāyu, for as long as the nights that have a good manifestation cause the face of the dawn to be covered, for so long the hotṛ who is on the earth sits down to perform the act of the Agni who accomplishes the offering, approaches the sacrifice and obtains the knowledge of his own duty.

##### English translation
As long, Matarishvan, as the swiftly-moving (nights) cover the face of the dawn, (so long) the Brahman, the inferior sitting down (to perform the work) of the Hotri, approaching the sacrifice supports (the ceremony).

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

The explanation of this by Yāska is as follows:

यावन्मात्रमुषसः प्रत्यक्तं भवति प्रतिदर्शनमिति वास्तुपमानस्य संप्रत्यर्थे प्रयोग इहेव निधेहीति यथा सुपर्ण्यः सुपतना एता रात्रयो वसते मातरिश्वन ज्योतिर्वर्णस्य तावदुपदधाति यज्ञमागच्छन् ब्राह्मणो होतास्याग्नेर्होतुरवरो नीषीदन् ॥ (*yāvanmātramuṣasaḥ pratyaktaṃ bhavati pratidarśanamiti vāstupamānasya saṃpratyarthe prayoga iheva nidhehīti yathā suparṇyaḥ supatanā etā rātrayo vasate mātariśvana jyotirvarṇasya tāvadupadadhāti yajñamāgacchan brāhmaṇo hotāsyāgnerhoturavaro nīṣīdan ‖*)

(Ni. 7.31)

An example of one more Ṛk has been given in this matter. In the preceding Ṛk Agni and Vāyu are praised. In this Ṛk Agni alone is praised. Mātariśvan (Vāyu) is asked by a man whether the Brahman, the human hotṛ who takes part in the sacrifice, can bear, that is, can know, the knowledge which Agni, the hotṛ of the gods, has (the understanding of the performance of the sacrifice). That man has given this reply: O Mātariśvan, for as long as (for how long) the birds with good wings hold the dawn, for so long the Brahman, the human hotṛ, who sits in the sacrificial hall near the sacrificial fire, in a place lower than Agni, bears it

### Printed p. 574

(that is, by the grace of Agni he knows it to some extent).

The word न (*na*) in this Ṛk does not have the sense of comparison. It has the sense of "now" (संप्रत्यर्थ (*saṃpratyartha*)). It is to be understood in the way that, although the word इह (*iha*) has the meaning "here", the sentence इहैव निधेहि (*ihaiva nidhehi*) has the meaning "put it right now". Therefore the sentence यावन्मात्रमुषसो न प्रतीकं (*yāvanmātramuṣaso na pratīkaṃ*) means: for how long, that is, for what length of time (only a short time), the time of dawn at the end of the night spreads, for that length of time only. The sentence सुपर्ण्यः सुपतना एता रात्रियो वसते मातरित्वन् (*suparṇyaḥ supatanā etā rātriyo vasate mātaritvan*) means: O Mātariśvan, birds with good wings, flying, hold the time of dawn. Here birds means nights. The word सुपर्ण्य (*suparṇya*) that indicates this has the meaning of various kinds of wings; it indicates the meaning of the various (good) colours of the dawn time. Therefore सुपर्ण्यः (*suparṇyaḥ*) means that when at the last part of the night the dawn rises, that dawn has various or beautiful colours. The extent of this dawn time is very small. Since after the dawn time the sun rises very quickly, the dawn time is very small in extent. The meaning is: for a very short time only. The human hotṛ is lower than Agni, the divine hotṛ. Therefore the Brahman, the human hotṛ, sitting in a place lower than the Agni established on the sacrificial altar, performs the hotṛ's act only for a very short time, by the grace of Agni, who is of special wisdom: this is the main meaning. By this the smallness of man and the greatness of Agni become evident. Since it is said in this Ṛk that the Brahman, the human hotṛ, sitting on the sacrificial altar, performs the hotṛ's act praising Agni, the divine hotṛ, it is clearly evident that here the terrestrial Agni is praised as Vaiśvānara Agni, and not Āditya.

होतृजपस्त्वनग्निर्वैश्वानरियो भवति देव सतविरेतं त्वा वृणतेऽग्निं होत्राय सह पित्रा वैश्वानरेणेतीममॆवाग्निं सवितारमाह सर्वस्य प्रस. वितारं मध्यमं वोत्तमं वा पितरं ॥ यस्तु सूक्तं भजते यस्यै हविर्निरुप्यतेयमेव सोग्निर्वैश्वानरः । निपातमेवैते उत्तरे ज्योतिषी एतेन नामधेयेन भजेते भजेते ॥ (*hotṛjapastvanagnirvaiśvānariyo bhavati deva sataviretaṃ tvā vṛṇate 'gniṃ hotrāya saha pitrā vaiśvānareṇetīmamèvāgniṃ savitāramāha sarvasya prasa. vitāraṃ madhyamaṃ vottamaṃ vā pitaraṃ ‖ yastu sūktaṃ bhajate yasyai havirnirupyateyameva sognirvaiśvānaraḥ | nipātamevaite uttare jyotiṣī etena nāmadheyena bhajete bhajete ‖*)

(Ni. 7-31)

The muttered prayers and the like that the hotṛ recites in the sacrifice address and praise Vaiśvānara himself, not Agni. The mantra-japa is देवसवितरेतु त्वा वृणतेऽग्नि होत्राय सह पित्रा वैश्वानरेण (*devasavitaretu tvā vṛṇate 'gni hotrāya saha pitrā vaiśvānareṇa*). The sentence "O shining god Savitṛ, the hotṛ has chosen you for the praise, that is, Agni, together with your father Vaiśvānara"

### Printed p. 575

needs explanation. Here the seer has called Agni Savitṛ. Here Savitṛ (the word savitṛ) means the cause of the origin of all things (or of beings). In this sense this word is used here. He has addressed as father Vāyu, who stands in the middle region, or the Ādiśa **NOTE**, who stands in the highest (heavenly) region.

That Vaiśvānara to whom the sūkta is addressed, for whom the oblation is offered (the deity towards whom the offering is made), is this terrestrial Agni.

There is an old well-known story of the churning of fire. As it says there: सर्वमिदमंधंतम आसीत् । अथ मातरिश्वाकाशे सूक्ष्ममग्निमपश्यत् । तममथ्नात् । मथित्वा जानयदिति । (*sarvamidamaṃdhaṃtama āsīt | atha mātariśvākāśe sūkṣmamagnimapaśyat | tamamathnāt | mathitvā jānayaditi |*) Formerly the whole world was covered with pitch darkness. Then Mātariśvan noticed the Agni in subtle form in the sky and churned him. Afterwards he brought that Agni to the earth so as to suit the sacrifice. This well-known story is told in the Ṛgveda in the Ṛks

अन्यं दिवो मातरिश्वा जभारामथ्नादन्यं परि श्येनो अद्रेः । (*anyaṃ divo mātariśvā jabhārāmathnādanyaṃ pari śyeno adreḥ |*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-93-6)

आ दूतो अग्निमभरद्विवस्वतो वैश्वानरं मातरिश्वा परावतः (*ā dūto agnimabharadvivasvato vaiśvānaraṃ mātariśvā parāvataḥ*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-8-4)

and in other Ṛks too: there is a description in praise of Agni that only after Mātariśvan had brought him did Agni shine in the sacrificial house.

मातरिश्वा—मातरिश्वा वायुर्मातर्यंतरिक्षे श्वसिति मातराश्वनितीति वा। (*mātariśvā—mātariśvā vāyurmātaryaṃtarikṣe śvasiti mātarāśvanitīti vā|*) Since he breathes in the atmosphere or moves, the name Mātariśvan has come to Vāyu. In the Ṛk Kha. Saṃ. 1-96-4 **NOTE** they explain this word as Agni, and in 1-141-3 as the sacrificer. But except in one or two such places, everywhere else Mātariśvan means Vāyu.

अन्यं मातरिश्वा दिव आ जभार (*anyaṃ mātariśvā diva ā jabhāra*): thus the supramundane manifestation and the worldly origin of Agni, who is the self of the sacrifice, are described in many ways. The manifestation of Agni, who is the banner of the sacrifices, the means for the vidatha, the father of the sacrifices and the like, and the king of the adhvaras (see the descriptions in the Ṛks Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-3-3; 3-11-2; 4-2-3 and others), took place first, in the form of lightning, in Vāyu; this is praised in the Ṛk-saṃhitā in

### Printed p. 576

त्वमग्ने प्रथमो मातरिश्वन आविर्भव सुक्रतूया विवस्वते । (*tvamagne prathamo mātariśvana āvirbhava sukratūyā vivasvate |*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-31-3)

स जायमानः परमे व्योमान्या विरग्नि रभवन्मातरिश्वने । (*sa jāyamānaḥ parame vyomānyā viragni rabhavanmātariśvane |*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-143-2)

and in other such Ṛks. There are many Vedic sentences that this Vāyu brought Agni, who was hidden in a very distant region, for the sake of Bhṛgu and Manu, the sacrificers, and helped them. For example:

द्विजन्मानं रयिमिव प्रशस्तं रातिं भरद्भगवे मातरिश्वा । (*dvijanmānaṃ rayimiva praśastaṃ rātiṃ bharadbhagave mātariśvā |*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-60-1)

यॆं मातरिश्वा मनवे परावतो देवं भाः परावतः । (*yèṃ mātariśvā manave parāvato devaṃ bhāḥ parāvataḥ |*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-128-2)

ऐनं नयन्मातरिश्वा परावतो देवेभ्यो मथितं परि । (*ainaṃ nayanmātariśvā parāvato devebhyo mathitaṃ pari |*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-9-5)

आ दूतो अग्निमभरद्विवस्वतो वैश्वानरं मातरिश्वा परावतः (*ā dūto agnimabharadvivasvato vaiśvānaraṃ mātariśvā parāvataḥ*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-8-4)

ईळेन्यं प्रथमं मातरिश्वा देवास्त्रक्षुर्मनवे यजत्रं । (*īḷenyaṃ prathamaṃ mātariśvā devāstrakṣurmanave yajatraṃ |*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-46-9)

In many such Ṛks it is well known from the Veda that Mātariśvan, for the benefit of the sacrificers Bhṛgu and Manu, brought to the earth the Agni who was hidden in a distant region, and did good to all the people on the earth.

### Printed p. 577

## Sūkta 89 (Maṇḍala 10)

In the Ṛgveda no other deity has the importance that Agni and Indra have. Even among these two, if one examines the number of sūktas and Ṛks, the first place falls to Indra. About a quarter of all the mantras of the Ṛgveda-saṃhitā praise Indra alone. Therefore, since it is necessary to know the subject of Indra in detail and critically, we explain it here. On the question who Indra is, the seer Gṛtsamada gave the right answer earlier, in the 12th sūkta of Ṛ. Saṃ. 2.12. Stating that briefly here, the matters found in the Ṛgveda concerning Indra are set forth.

O people, he who, as soon as he was born, became foremost among the gods, firm of mind and radiant, and by deeds such as the slaying of Vṛtra honoured and protected all the gods, and through the strength of whose body Heaven and Earth both were seized with fear, he, joined with the greatness of a strength that takes the form of armies, is Indra.

O people, he who made the trembling earth stand firm, who made the mountains that roamed everywhere with wings bend to his command and remain steady, who fashioned the wide atmosphere, who held back and fixed the heavenly world, he is Indra.

O people, he who slew the cloud and made the seven flowing rivers, the Gaṅgā and the others, flow, who released the cows held in the barrier of the Asura named Vala, who created the fire in the form of lightning in the middle region of the clouds, and who remains unconquered in battles, he is Indra.

O people, that Indra by whom this whole perishable world was made to stand firm, who made the destroyer, the vile Asura, lie in the cave that is hell, and conquered the enemy he had taken aim at, and who, as a hunter brings down a deer, brought the rich possessions of the enemy under his own control, he is Indra.

That Indra, of whom, as the one terrible to the enemy, people ask "Where is he?", of that Indra those who know say that he is not in one place only. That same Indra, becoming a terror to the enemy, strikes all around the cattle, horses and the like that belong to the enemy and sustain him.

### Printed p. 578

O people, place faith in such a great-souled Indra.

O people, he who provides wealth in one and the same manner to the rich man and to the poor man, to the one who begs of him, and to the praising priest; who has fine cheeks, and who is the protector of the sacrificer who holds the pressing-stone in his hand and has pressed the Soma juice, he is Indra.

O people, he under whose rule, as the inner controller of all, are the horses, the cows, the villages and all the chariots, who, having slain Vṛtra, created the sun and Uṣas, who, having split the cloud, is the impeller of the waters, he is Indra.

O people, he whom the army of the gods and the army of men, sounding together, call for protection, whom enemies too, the superior and the inferior, call, and whom the two charioteers who have mounted a chariot like Indra's chariot call separately, he is Indra.

O people, he without whom people cannot win victory, and therefore those engaged in battle call him for protection; who is the representative of the whole world, and who made the unmoving mountains and the like move, he is Indra.

O people, he who killed with his thunderbolt the people who bore great sin, were numerous and were filled with arrogance, who gives no encouraging help to one who does not know the Self, who is the destroyer of the enemy who works ruin, he is Indra.

O people, he who searched for and at last found the Asura named Śambara, who had hidden himself in the mountains and lived there for forty years, and who killed that powerful, murderous Dānava, he is Indra.

O people, he who, with seven rays, a shedder of rain and mighty, freed the seven rivers, the Gaṅgā and the others, from Ahi so that they might flow, and who, with the thunderbolt in his hand, killed the Asura named Rauhiṇa who was climbing to the heavenly world, he is Indra.

To this Indra Heaven and Earth both bow in humility, and through the strength of this Indra the mountains tremble. He who is a drinker of the Soma juice, firm of body, with arms equal to the thunderbolt, who holds the thunderbolt in his hand, he is Indra.

### Printed p. 579

O people, he who protects the sacrificer who presses the Soma juice, who protects the one who cooks the purodāśa and the like, who protects those who compose for protection, who protects the praisers, and for whom the hymn, the Soma juice and the purodāśa and other foods are a cause of increase, he is Indra.

O Indra, you who, unconquered, give food and strength in abundance to the sacrificer who presses the Soma juice and cooks the purodāśa and the like, are you not indeed one whose nature is truth? We, who are dear to you and are endowed, by your grace, with auspicious sons, grandsons and the rest, recite the hymn on all days.

**The origin of Indra; his mother and father, and his wife.**

Although Indra's greatness is described in a most excellent and poetic style, Indra is nowhere described as a supreme god without birth. As has been observed on many occasions earlier, Indra's mother and father are specified. And the manner of Indra's origin too has been praised very extensively in many places. For example, in some of the mantras quoted below the matter of Indra's birth is stated.

"O Indra, on the very day you were born you drank the juice of the Soma plant that grew on the mountain slope and showed your great delight in it. Your mother, who bore you and was young, gave you that Soma juice to your satisfaction in the house of your father, who possesses greatness. This same Indra, as soon as he was born, approached his mother and found the Soma juice in her breast." (3-48-2, 3)

"O Indra, as the atmosphere looked for, your father is exceedingly strong of body. The begetter of Indra, who roars in the atmosphere and is steady like the earth, is a most skilful performer of work. Indra has the utmost devotion to his father and also to his mother." (4-17-4).

"This (womb) too is the same ancient door through which the gods were born of old. Let the fully grown embryo come out through this door; let Indra, who is born from it, not needlessly harm his mother." (4-18-1)

Knowing that Indra's birth would reveal a fault, Indra's mother hid him. Exceedingly powerful, he arose of his own accord as a most attractive bearer of weapons, and at once pervaded both Heaven and Earth. (4-18-5)

### Printed p. 580

Indra, who is exceedingly powerful, firm of body, of unassailable strength, valiant and robust, his mother brought forth, as a cow bears a calf, so that he might move about freely of his own accord and display his strength. (4-18-10)

When Indra of great strength was born, his mother warned him out of affection for her son: "O son, none of these gods helped you; all of them abandoned you." Then Indra said: "O Viṣṇu, since there is need to slay the Asura Vṛtra, be one who takes on a form and a strength that pervade all the worlds." (1-18-11) **NOTE**

"O Indra, who made your mother a widow? Who wished to slay you, whether you were asleep or moving about? Who was the god near you when your father was seized by the foot and harmed?" (4-8-12).

"The valiant father begot in battle a son whose strength was fit to destroy enemies; the radiant woman bore a radiant son." (7-20-5)

"O Indra, as soon as you were born you drank Soma to gain your strength. Your mother made your greatness manifest." (7-98-3)

"To display your unassailable strength you were born with a terrible form, and showing your wrath you also made known your proud valour and showed your self-confidence. When Indra's mother, endowed with wealth, bore Indra, the Maruts tended and nourished this mighty Indra so that he might grow and flourish." (10 73-1)

The god who begot this Indra, of terrible form and unassailable strength, has the greatest power in the whole universe. (11-20-1) **NOTE**

"O Indra, as Uṣas pervades the whole world, so when you too stood pervading all Heaven and Earth, the mother, divine in nature and of great form, bore you, the lord of the gods, who are the best of the people of the world." (80-24-1) **NOTE**

"As we knew before, this Indra is the son of Niṣṭigrī." (Sāyaṇa has explained Niṣṭigrī as Aditi.) (10-101-12) **NOTE**

### Printed p. 581

Although in the Purāṇas and elsewhere Indra is well known as one of the Ādityas and as the companion of Varuṇa (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-85-4), in other parts of the Ṛk-saṃhitā he is hardly ever described in this way, that is, as one of the Ādityas. In 4-26-1 identity with Manu and Sūra is shown. In the mantras 8.8-2-1 and 4, and 10-89-2, he is denoted by the word Sūra. In 2-30-1 he is described by the epithet Savitṛ. **NOTE**

In the Atharvaveda the description of Indra's power is given in the passages quoted below, as follows.

एकाष्टका तपसा तप्यमाना जजान गर्भं महिमानमिंद्रं । तेन देवा अपहंत शत्रून् हंता दस्यूनामभवच्छचीपतिः ॥ (*ekāṣṭakā tapasā tapyamānā jajāna garbhaṃ mahimānamiṃdraṃ | tena devā apahaṃta śatrūn haṃtā dasyūnāmabhavacchacīpatiḥ ‖*)

(A. Pe. 3-10-12) **NOTE**

Having practised powerful austerity, Ekāṣṭakā bore Indra, who possesses greatness. With the help of this Indra the gods conquered their enemies. Indra, the lord of Śacī, became the slayer of the Dasyus.

In the Ṛk that follows this, Ekāṣṭakā is specified as the mother of both Indra and Soma and as the daughter of Prajāpati. In the Atharvaveda Indra's mother is addressed (6.38), but her name is not given. The Mahābhārata states that Indra is one of the sons born to Kaśyapa from Dākṣāyaṇī, the daughter of Dakṣa, who has the other name Aditi. (Ā. Pa.) In Atharvaveda 8-58-4 he is called the son of Truth (सूनुं सत्यस्य (*sūnuṃ satyasya*)).

In another place it is stated that Indra was created by the gods for the destruction of enemies. (3.49-1) घनं वृत्राणां जनयंत देवा (*ghanaṃ vṛtrāṇāṃ janayaṃta devā*). (2-13.5; 3-51-8)

In the Puruṣa-sūkta it is stated that Indra, together with Agni, was born from the mouth of the Puruṣa. (मुखादिंद्रश्चाग्निश्च (*mukhādiṃdraścāgniśca*)).

(10-90-13)

In another place of the Ṛk-saṃhitā it is stated explicitly that Indra is one of the gods begotten by Soma.

(9-96-5)

Such a valiant Indra won heaven by the power of his austerity.

(10-167-1)

In the Śatapatha and other Brāhmaṇas the story of Indra's origin is set out in different ways. For example, the account of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa is as follows.

### Printed p. 582

ता ना एताः प्रजापतेरधि देवताः असृज्यंत अग्निरिंद्रः सोमः परमेष्ठी प्राजापत्यः । ताः सहस्रायुषो जज्जिरे । ता यथा नद्यै पारुं परापश्येदेवं स्वस्यायुषः पारं पराचख्युः ॥ (*tā nā etāḥ prajāpateradhi devatāḥ asṛjyaṃta agniriṃdraḥ somaḥ parameṣṭhī prājāpatyaḥ | tāḥ sahasrāyuṣo jajjire | tā yathā nadyai pāruṃ parāpaśyedevaṃ svasyāyuṣaḥ pāraṃ parācakhyuḥ ‖*)

(Śa. Brā. 11-1-6-14)

Agni, Indra, Soma and Pārameṣṭhī Prājāpatya are all gods created by Prajāpati. All of them were born with a thousand years of life. Just as a man can see the far bank of a river, in the same way all of them were able to see beyond the limit of their own span of life. So it says. The account of the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa states the matter of Indra's origin in this way:

प्रजापतिर्देवासुरानसृजत । स इंद्रमपि ना सृजत । तं देवा अब्रुवन् । इंद्रं नो जनयेति । सोऽब्रवीत् । यथाहं युष्माग्स्तपसासृक्षि । एवमिंद्रं जनयध्वमिति । ते तपोऽतप्यंत । त आत्मन्निंद्रमपश्यन् । तमब्रुवन् । जायस्वेति । सोऽब्रवीत् । किंभागधेयमभि जनिष्य इति । ऋतून्त्संवत्सरं । प्रजाः पशून् । इमान्लोकानित्यब्रुवन् । तं वै माहुत्याप्रजनयतेत्यब्रवीत् । तं चतुर्होत्रा प्राजनयन् । (*prajāpatirdevāsurānasṛjata | sa iṃdramapi nā sṛjata | taṃ devā abruvan | iṃdraṃ no janayeti | so 'bravīt | yathāhaṃ yuṣmāgstapasāsṛkṣi | evamiṃdraṃ janayadhvamiti | te tapo 'tapyaṃta | ta ātmanniṃdramapaśyan | tamabruvan | jāyasveti | so 'bravīt | kiṃbhāgadheyamabhi janiṣya iti | ṛtūntsaṃvatsaraṃ | prajāḥ paśūn | imānlokānityabruvan | taṃ vai māhutyāprajanayatetyabravīt | taṃ caturhotrā prājanayan |*)

(Tai. Brā. 2-2-3-3, 4).

Prajāpati created the gods and the Asuras. Only Indra he did not create. Then they addressed Prajāpati with the prayer, "Create Indra for us." Then he said to the gods, "In the way that I, by the power of my austerity, made all of you come into being, in the same way you too, as the fruit of the hardship of austerity, create Indra." Then all those gods practised austerity. Then they found Indra within themselves. Afterwards they told him to take a share of the oblation. Then Indra said, "For what purpose must I come forth outwardly?" Then they said, "You must be born for the nourishment of the seasons, and for the protection of the year, of all beings and of all the worlds." But in another place of this same Brāhmaṇa there is a somewhat different account of Indra's origin. That account is as follows:

प्रजापतिरिंद्रमसृजतानुजावरं देवानां । तं प्राहिणोत् । परेहि । एतेषां देवानामधिपतिरेधीति । तं देवा अब्रुवन् । कस्य मसि । वयं वै त्वच्छेयाग्ंसस्य इति । सोऽब्रवीत् । कस्य मसि वयं वै त्वच्छे याग्ंसस्य इति मा देवा अवोचन्निति । अथवा इदं तर्हि प्रजापता दर आसीत् । यदस्मिन्नादिश्ये । तदेनमब्रवीत् । एतन्मे प्रयच्छ । अथा- (*prajāpatiriṃdramasṛjatānujāvaraṃ devānāṃ | taṃ prāhiṇot | parehi | eteṣāṃ devānāmadhipatiredhīti | taṃ devā abruvan | kasya masi | vayaṃ vai tvaccheyāgṃsasya iti | so 'bravīt | kasya masi vayaṃ vai tvacche yāgṃsasya iti mā devā avocanniti | athavā idaṃ tarhi prajāpatā dara āsīt | yadasminnādiśye | tadenamabravīt | etanme prayaccha | athā-*)

### Printed p. 583

हमेशेषां देवानामधिपतिभविष्यामाति.... ... ततो वा इंद्रो देवानामधिपतिधवर् ॥ (*hameśeṣāṃ devānāmadhipatibhaviṣyāmāti.... ... tato vā iṃdro devānāmadhipatidhavar ‖*)

(Śrī. Ba. 2. 2. 10 2. 2) **NOTE**

After creating all the gods, Prajāpati created Indra last and made him the lord over the remaining gods. Then the gods addressed Indra: "Who are you? When we are all superior to you, how can you be lord over all of us?" Then Indra explained this situation and begged Prajāpati to furnish him with the power of Prajāpati, which gives the fitness to be lord over all the gods. Afterwards he obtained their lordship. So it says in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā.

इंद्रो वै देवानामानुजावर आसीत्स प्रजापतिमुपाधावत्तस्मा एतग्ं षोडशिनं प्रायच्छत्तमगृह्णीत ततो वै सोग्रं देवतानां पठैत् (*iṃdro vai devānāmānujāvara āsītsa prajāpatimupādhāvattasmā etagṃ ṣoḍaśinaṃ prāyacchattamagṛhṇīta tato vai sograṃ devatānāṃ paṭhait*)

(Tri. Sa.: 6.6.-2.) **NOTE**

Indra was the youngest of all the gods. Then he went to Prajāpati, and with the intention of obtaining his help and of attaining lordship over the gods, he offered the Ṣoḍaśin. Then Prajāpati showed him favour. As a result Indra obtained the supreme fitness and became lord of the gods. Moreover, in another part of this same Taittirīya Saṃhitā this same matter is stated somewhat differently, in this way.

तेनेंद्रं प्रजापतिरयाजयत्तको वा इंद्र इंद्रोऽभवत् (*teneṃdraṃ prajāpatirayājayattako vā iṃdra iṃdro 'bhavat*)

(Śrī. Saṃ. 7-2-10-2) **NOTE**

Prajāpati made Indra perform a sacrifice, through the offering of rice and the like according to the season. As a result Indra obtained Indra-hood. Likewise it is stated that by the power of the sattra called Pañcadaśarātra he obtained both the power to destroy the Asuras and the power to become lord of the gods.

(Kṛ. Saṃ. 7-3-6-1) **NOTE**

A passage of the Yajus-saṃhitā states that Indra and Agni are twins, that they have the same father but different mothers.

(6-5-2)

In 10.55-1 the sons of Indra's brother are mentioned. It can be said that Heaven and Earth are these sons of the brother. In 6.55-5 Pūṣan is specified as Indra's brother.

### Printed p. 584

The birth of Indra in infancy as a warrior, showing a warrior's valour, is described. Its description is as follows.

"As soon as he was born, Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra, took up his weapon and asked, 'Who are the warriors famed as most valiant?'"

(8-45-4; 8-66-1)

"O Indra, you are by nature without enemies and are aged," so a devotee praises Indra and shows his devotion.

(1-102-8; 1.176-1; 10-133-2)

"O Indra, greatly delighted, unite with your wife, and obtain your satisfaction through union with her." The passage where Indra's wife is mentioned in this way describes the occasion of Indra's enjoying amorous beauty. (समु पत्न्यामदः (*samu patnyāmadaḥ*)).

(1.92-5, 6)

In this time of such domestic pleasure a perplexing situation sometimes arises. On the one side the oblation in the form of Soma juice that the sacrificers offer at the time of the sacrifice is most attractive. The seer describes Indra's dilemma, that Indra often falls into doubt as to which of these two he should accept and which he should give up. It is like this:

"O Indra, the housewife is the house; she is the dwelling of the man. Therefore let your horses carry you to the place where your housewife is. But as soon as we offer the oblation in the form of Soma, let Agni come to you to give you the invitation." (3-534) **NOTE**

"O Indra, brother, set out. Please come here. Both places are attractive to you. When your chariot halts, your horses are unyoked."

(3 53.5)

"O Indra, you have drunk the Soma; now set out for your house. In your house there is an attractive wife, and you have excellent domestic happiness. Wherever your chariot halts, there you should unyoke the horses." (3.53-6)

The name Indrāṇī is mentioned in many places. But she is not stated directly to be Indra's wife. Yet from that naming it can be said freely that she is Indra's wife.

(1 22.12; 2-32.8; 5-46.8; 10.86 .11, 12)

### Printed p. 585

In these places she is praised together with Agnāyī, the wife of Agni, and Varuṇānī, the wife of Varuṇa, and she too is invited with them to the sacrifice. But in the mantras 10-86-11 and 12 there is some special explanation concerning her.

"I have heard that among all these goddesses Indrāṇī is the most fortunate, for she has no death resulting from it," it says.

A passage of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa states explicitly that Indrāṇī is Indra's wife and that she has the most excellent adornment of hair, which takes on all forms.

(Pa. Ba. 14-2-1-8) **NOTE**

The account describing the good fortune of Indrāṇī is as follows—

इंद्राणी देवी सुभगा सुपत्नी । उदग्‌ंशेन पतिविद्यॆ जिगाय । त्रिग्‌ंशदस्या जघनं योजनानि । उपस्थ इंद्रग् स्थविरं बिभर्ति ॥ (*iṃdrāṇī devī subhagā supatnī | udagṃśena patividyè jigāya | trigṃśadasyā jaghanaṃ yojanāni | upastha iṃdrag sthaviraṃ bibharti ‖*)

(Tai. Brā. 2-4-2.7)

What was stated above is that Indrāṇī, endowed with good fortune, is a giver of happiness to her husband. The Kāṭhaka passage is of another kind.

इंद्रो वै विलिष्टेंगां दानवीमकामयत । सोऽसुरेष्वचरत् स्त्रीव स्त्रीषु भवन् पुमान् पुंसु । स निर्युतिगृहीत इवामन्यत । स एतमैंद्रानैर्युतमपश्यत् ॥ (*iṃdro vai viliṣṭeṃgāṃ dānavīmakāmayata | so 'sureṣvacarat strīva strīṣu bhavan pumān puṃsu | sa niryutigṛhīta ivāmanyata | sa etamaiṃdrānairyutamapaśyat ‖*)

(Kā. Saṃ 13-5) **NOTE**

Indra fell in love with a Dānava woman named Viliṣṭeṅgā. Then, joining the Asuras himself, he behaved among women like a woman and among men like a man. Then, as if seized by Nirṛti, he recognised himself, that is, his bondage, and to counter it he accepted an oblation. Besides this, in the Atharvaveda:

येनानि चक्रे आसुरी इंद्रं देवेभ्यस्परि । तेनानि कुर्वे त्वामहं यथा तेऽसामि सुप्रिया ॥ (*yenāni cakre āsurī iṃdraṃ devebhyaspari | tenāni kurve tvāmahaṃ yathā te 'sāmi supriyā ‖*)

(A. Ve. 7.38-2) **NOTE**

"O Indra, you must love me. To do so, with the help of this herb I make you mine," and with its help that woman drew Indra, who was among the gods, to her own side, it says. In this way different Vedic passages give different accounts concerning Indra's wife.

### Printed p. 586

**The epithets showing Indra's physical and mental qualities**

The epithets that describe Indra's extraordinary qualities are very abundant. First, the description of his youth and strength. This Indra is exceedingly young, and yet ancient, exceedingly powerful and skilful in action.

(1.130.7; 2-22.4; 6-29-3; 8-24.9, 12; 8-58.7; 8-81-3)

Occasions describing Indra's warrior qualities are also very many: that he has the heroic strength of a warrior, is resplendent, ageless, conquers all, has boundless wisdom, has unassailable heroic strength and vigour, and bears the thunderbolt.

(1-4-8; 1-16-9; 1-30-6, 15; 1-61-1; 1-81-2, 7; 1-84-2; 1-100-12;
1-102.6; 1 165-6; 2.21-1, 2, 3; 3-30-3; 3-32-7; 3-45-3; 3-46.0;
6-18-4; 7.20.4; 7-22-5; 8-81-8; 8.84-7; )

In Indra's body there is heroic strength, in his shoulders strength, in his hand the thunderbolt, and in his head wisdom.

(2.16-2)

Indra can take on many kinds of forms. All those forms are exceedingly beautiful, and have the golden colour of the sun. (10-102-3)

The seers who saw the Ṛk-saṃhitā have described this special beauty of Indra by showing many kinds of similes. The words Suśipra and Śiprin are the chief among these. These words mean one with fine cheeks or nose. This is Indra's personal quality.

(1-9-3; 1-29-2; 1-81-4; 1-101-10; 3-32-3; 3-36-10; 8-32.4, 24.
8-33.7; 8-55.4; 10-105-5; 3-30-3; 8-17.4; 8-81-4)

In 8-65-10 it is described how Indra, having obtained strength as a result of drinking Soma, savours the sweetness of the Soma drink by smacking his lips. Epithets such as Hariśipra, Harikeśa and Hariśmaśru are also exceedingly many. That is, they mean one with golden cheeks, one with golden hair, one with a golden beard.

(10-96-4, 9, 12; 10-96-5, 8; 10-23-4).

When he is greatly delighted, his beard bristles and moves.

(2-11-17; 10-23-1.)

### Printed p. 587

(In 6-46-3 Indra is also described as thousand-faced.)

The whole form of this Indra is golden. In many places his form is described as Harivarpas and as of golden form.

(10-96-1; 8-25-3; 1-7-2).

But in some other places he is also stated to be of iron form, that is, one with a body made of steel.

(C.-286-3; C.0-96-4, 8). **NOTE**

His arms are spread far and wide. (पृथू करस्ना बहुला गभस्ती (*pṛthū karasnā bahulā gabhastī*)).

(6-19-3; 8-32-10; 8.70-1)

A mantra not in the Ṛk-saṃhitā, in the Sāma-saṃhitā, praises Indra's long arms and attractive form and describes them in this way.

इंद्रस्य बाहू स्थविरौ युवानावनाधृष्ट्य सुप्रथितावसह्यौ । तौ युंजीत प्रथमौ योगे आगते याभ्यां जितमसुराणां सहो महत् ॥ (*iṃdrasya bāhū sthavirau yuvānāvanādhṛṣṭya suprathitāvasahyau | tau yuṃjīta prathamau yoge āgate yābhyāṃ jitamasurāṇāṃ saho mahat ‖*)

(Sā. Ve. 2-1219) **NOTE**

When the occasion arises for Indra to display his valour, let him employ the arm that formerly destroyed the great strength of the Asuras and won victory, the arm that is powerful, youthful, of unassailable strength, of a delightful form, and unconquerable. So it says.

But Indra's forms are endless. By his mere will he can take on all the forms he wishes, it says in many places—

(3-38-4; 3.48.4; 3-213.8) **NOTE**

रूपरूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव तदस्य रूपं प्रतिचक्षणाय । इंद्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते युक्ता ह्यस्य हरयः शता दश ॥ (*rūparūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva tadasya rūpaṃ praticakṣaṇāya | iṃdro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate yuktā hyasya harayaḥ śatā daśa ‖*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-47-18)

**Indra's chariot and horses**

Indra, seated in his golden chariot, holding in his hand a golden whip (cāvuṭi), sets out on his journey. That chariot has a thousand supporting pillars.

(6-29-2; 8-1-24; 8-25-16)

This chariot of Indra has a speed greater than the speed of the mind.

(10-12-2)

### Printed p. 588

**NOTE**

### Printed p. 589

Indra is described as sometimes the charioteer, and at other times the friend, of the god Vāyu, the two travelling seated together in the same chariot. This description shows to an extraordinary degree the relation between Indra and Vāyu, and the speed of Indra's chariot.

(4-46-2; 4-48-2; 7-91-6)

Indra's horses, by the power of praise, come of themselves to the chariot and are yoked. (ब्रह्मणा ते ब्रह्मयुजा युनज्मी हरी (*brahmaṇā te brahmayujā yunajmī harī*)).

(3-35.4; 1-82-6; 2-18-3; 8-1-24; 8.17-2; 8 2-27; 8-45-39 : 8.86-9)

The purport is that as soon as the prayer in the form of praise from the sacrificers who perform the sacrifice has been offered, Indra at once yokes the horses to the chariot in order to come to their sacrifice. Since praises themselves are the cause of the yoking of the horses to the chariot, the idea is that the yoking of the horses takes place through the power of praise. Thus, of the many Saṃhitā passages that describe the powerful chariot and horses of Indra, who travels through the earth, the atmosphere and all the regions, only a few have been set out above as examples.

**Indra's thunderbolt and other implements**

It is well known that Indra's great thunderbolt was made by Tvaṣṭṛ, the divine craftsman. It is also said that Tvaṣṭṛ made it for Indra himself (त्वष्टास्मै वज्रं स्वर्यं ततक्ष (*tvaṣṭāsmai vajraṃ svaryaṃ tatakṣa*)).

(1-32-2; 1-61-6; 1-85-9; 5.31-4; 6-17-10; 10-48-3)

But in some places alone it is stated explicitly that it was made by Kāvya Uśanas and given to Indra for the slaying of the Asuras. (यं ते काव्य उशना................ततक्ष वज्रं (*yaṃ te kāvya uśanā................tatakṣa vajraṃ*)).

(1-12-12; 5-34.2)

On the creation of the thunderbolt and Indra's taking it up, a passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa states as follows—

देवा वै प्रथमेनाह्नेंद्राय वज्रं समभरंस्तं द्वितीयेनाह्नासिंचंस्तंतृतीयेनाह्ना प्रायच्छंस्तं चतुर्थेऽहन्वाहरत् ॥ (*devā vai prathamenāhneṃdrāya vajraṃ samabharaṃstaṃ dvitīyenāhnāsiṃcaṃstaṃtṛtīyenāhnā prāyacchaṃstaṃ caturthe 'hanvāharat ‖*) (Ai. Brā. 4-1)

The gods provided Indra with the thunderbolt for the proceedings of the first day. On the second day they consecrated it. On the third day they handed it over to him. On the fourth day Indra employed that thunderbolt given by the gods. So it says. Moreover,

"The thunderbolt lies covered with water in the ocean that is in the atmosphere."

(8-108-9)

### Printed p. 590

In this account the natural order of the origin of the thunderbolt weapon is described. **NOTE** This thunderbolt is stated in some places to be of gold (1-57-2; 1-85.9; 8-57-3; 10-23-3), and in some places to be golden-hued mixed with green (10-96-3); in still other places it is stated to be of iron (आयसः (*āyasaḥ*)), that is, made of steel.

(1-52-8; 1-80-12; 1-81-4; 1-121-9; 8-85-3; 10-48-3; 10-96-3; 10-113-5)

Some passages hold that it has four edges. (4-22-2) (चतुरश्रिः (*caturaśriḥ*)) But there are also passages stating that it has a hundred edges (शताश्रि (*śatāśri*)). (6-17-10) The meaning is one with a hundred edges. It is also described as having a hundred joints. (शतपर्वन् (*śataparvan*))

(8-80-6; 8-6-6; 8-65-2; 2-78-3)

There are also some occasions where it is said to have a thousand joints.

(1-80-12; 1-85-9; 33-34-2; 6-17-10) **NOTE**

भीमा इंद्रस्य हेतयश्च तभृष्टीरयस्मयिः (*bhīmā iṃdrasya hetayaśca tabhṛṣṭīrayasmayiḥ*)

(A. Pe. 4-37-5) **NOTE**

The weapons of Indra, having a hundred points and made of iron, are praised in the Atharvaveda as exceedingly terrible. In place of आयस्मयिः (*āyasmayiḥ*) the same description is found elsewhere with the variant reading हिरण्ययाः (*hiraṇyayāḥ*).

(A. Pe. 8-5-19)

As a bull rubs its horn, Indra rubs his weapon and sharpens it (for the destruction of enemies). (शिशीते वज्रं (*śiśīte vajraṃ*)).

(1-53-1)

As the Āditya, stationed in the atmosphere, shines with his divine radiance, so the thunderbolt placed in Indra's hand shines. (दिवे न सूर्यः (*dive na sūryaḥ*))

(8-52-2)

There are also some occasions on which Indra is described as a deity who carries arrows and a bow.

(8-45-4; 8-66-6, 11; 10-103-2; 10.103-3)

Indra's arrows have three joints and sharp edges. They are adorned with feathers in the thousands, and are of gold.

(8-66-7; 8-66-12)

Indra is also described as a bearer of the goad. (दीर्घस्ते अस्त्वंकुशः (*dīrghaste astvaṃkuśaḥ*))

### Printed p. 591

"O Indra, let your goad, which helps to provide wealth for the sacrificer who offers you the oblation, be long.

(8-17-10)

In the Atharvaveda too this same matter is stated in this way.

यस्ते अंकुशो वसुदानो बृहन्निंद्र हिरण्ययः । तेनाजनीयते जायां मद्यं धेहि शचीपते ॥ (*yaste aṃkuśo vasudāno bṛhanniṃdra hiraṇyayaḥ | tenājanīyate jāyāṃ madyaṃ dhehi śacīpate ‖*)

(A. Ve. 6-82-3) **NOTE**

"O Indra, I am very eager to obtain a wife. With the help of your goad, which provides wealth and is of gold, provide me with a wife." This is the occasion on which the sacrificers pray to Indra. Moreover,

O Indra, as a goat stretches out its forefoot and seizes the branch of a creeper, so you too stretch out your goad and draw to yourself the thing you wish for. You bear such power.

(10-134_6)

A mantra whose purport is, "O Indra, I bring and offer to you this long goad, with the help of which you destroy powerful Asuras," also conveys the same idea.

(10-44-9)

In the Atharvaveda the description and praise of Indra's net (jāla) is as follows.

अंतरिक्षं जालमासीज्जालदंडा दिशो महीः । तेनाभिधाय दस्यूनां शक्रः सेनामपातयत् ॥ (*aṃtarikṣaṃ jālamāsījjāladaṃḍā diśo mahīḥ | tenābhidhāya dasyūnāṃ śakraḥ senāmapātayat ‖*)

(A. Ve. 8-8-5)

(A. Pe. A-8-5) **NOTE**

The atmosphere is Indra's net, and the great directions are the poles of this net. Casting this net that spreads over all directions, Indra seized the enemies in the form of Dasyus and made them fall down.

बृहद्धि जालं बृहतश्यक्रस्य वाजिनीवतः । तेन शत्रुनभि सर्वान्न्युब्ब यथा न मुच्यातै कमश्चन एषां ॥ (*bṛhaddhi jālaṃ bṛhataśyakrasya vājinīvataḥ | tena śatrunabhi sarvānnyubba yathā na mucyātai kamaścana eṣāṃ ‖*)

(A. Ve. 8-8-6)

The net of Indra, the giver of food, whose form is great, is very extensive. When it is cast and spread, all the enemies are caught. Not one of them can escape from it.

### Printed p. 592

बृहिर्ज्वलं बृहत इंद्र उरुण सदुसिल्घस्य शतवीर्यस्य । ईन सहस्रमयुतं न्यर्बुदं जघान शक्रो दस्यानामभिधाय सेनया ॥ (*bṛhirjvalaṃ bṛhata iṃdra uruṇa sadusilghasya śatavīryasya | īna sahasramayutaṃ nyarbudaṃ jaghāna śakro dasyānāmabhidhāya senayā ‖*)

(Ā. Ve. Ā.A-2) **NOTE**

O Indra, of great form, your net, you being valiant, is exceedingly extensive. You possess together the strength of a hundred enemies. You can face thousands of enemies at once. Indra, together with his followers, caught in his net all the Dasyu people, numbering thousands, ten thousands and ten crores, struck them all with his weapon and killed them.

अयं लोको जालमासीच्छ क्रस्य महतो महान् । शेनाहमिंद्रजालेनामूंस्तमसाभिदधामि सर्वान् ॥ (*ayaṃ loko jālamāsīccha krasya mahato mahān | śenāhamiṃdrajālenāmūṃstamasābhidadhāmi sarvān ‖*)

(A. Pe. 8-8-8)

This world is the net of Indra, whose form is great. With the help of that net I make all the enemies be caught in the pitch darkness.

**Indra's regard for Soma-drinking** **NOTE**

As soon as he is invited by the sacrificers to drink Soma, Indra comes ready, seated in his chariot. And there the food for his horses too is ready. And as soon as he arrives, the oblation in the form of Soma is made ready in abundance for his drinking and offered.

(Śi-25-7) **NOTE**

(3-35-7)

As soon as this Soma is drunk he obtains exceeding delight, and from it he obtains not only the enthusiasm needed for battle but also strength useful for many other extraordinary deeds, such as the upholding of Heaven and Earth. All kinds of strength and enthusiasm increase.

(2.12-2)

Of the many passages that state the manner of Indra's worship, only the purport of some is stated here. This Soma juice produces imperishable vigour. As the sun pervades with his rays the atmosphere and all the other regions, may this Soma juice make strength pervade Indra's whole body; so the seer has prayed.

(2-15-1, 2 : 3.19-1; 2.20-1; 3-26-3; 3-40-1 : 3-42-1; 6-23-1, 5, 6 :
6.28-1; 6-29-4; 7-22.1; 7-29.1; 8-3-1; 8-81-5, 6; 10-104-1)

### Printed p. 593

All the gods run up eagerly to the share of the Soma juice that is to be offered to Indra.

(8-2-18)

"Together with Indra, the other gods and Agni have drunk. All the gods have obtained satisfaction. But Indra's satisfaction is the greatest."

(1-104-9; 1-125-5; 2-14-1; 7-33-2; 8-2-4)

Among all the other gods, Indra's Soma-drinking is the most extraordinary. इंद्र इत् सोमपा एकः.......अंतर्देवान् मर्तांश्च । (*iṃdra it somapā ekaḥ.......aṃtardevān martāṃśca |*) (8-2-4). Among the gods and the like, Indra alone is the true Soma-drinker. Therefore he alone is the truly valiant one.

(8-4-12; 8-6-40)

Since Indra's mother provided him with Soma on the very day of his birth, the point is clear that Soma is the life-giver of Indra. (सद्यो यज्जातो आपिबो ह सोमं (*sadyo yajjāto āpibo ha somaṃ*)).

(3-32-9, 10; 3-48-2; 6-40-2; 7-98-3)

It is well known that he drank the Soma of thirty Droṇa vessels in a single draught.

(8-66-4; 6-17-11; 8-7-10; Ni. 4-11)

His devotees call him to this Soma-drinking with the utmost humility and devotion, and Indra, accepting their invitation and coming, drinks in haste like a thirsty deer.

(8-4-10; 5-36-1; 8-33-2)

The belly (bellies) of this Indra is like two lakes. In his eagerness to fill it, Indra roars like a bull wandering for water in a waterless desert.

(5-36-1; 1-8-7; 1-104-9; 2-11-11; 2-14-10; 2-16-2; 3-35-6;
3.36-7, 8; 3-40-5; 3.47-1; 3.51-12; 8-12-23; 8-2-1; 8-17-5 to 8;
8.67-7; 8.81-22, 23, 24; 10.28-2; 10.43-7; 10.104-2; A. Ve. 2.5-1;
6.2-1)

Sometimes, when the sacrificers drink this same Soma juice, there is a description of the same kind. For example—

"As soon as I drink this Soma, it increases my body."

(6-47-3)

So the seer says. In another passage, stating the power of Soma-drinking—

### Printed p. 594

"We have drunk the Soma; therefore we have become free from death. No man can now harm us. O immortal Indra, by your grace we too, together with you and without fear, shall ascend to the atmosphere," he proclaims.

(La.48.3) **NOTE**

As birds fly to a tree full of leaves, and as rivers full of water go and join the ocean, so the stream of Soma juice goes and joins Indra. As, when rain falls, grain and the like grow abundantly and robustly, in the same way the sacrificers, by the offering of Soma juice, make Indra grow strong.

(19-43-4, 7) **NOTE**

As a good husband loves his wife and desires her company, so Indra is prayed to drink the Soma offered by the sacrificers, to accept the praises offered by them, and to obtain satisfaction from them.

(3.52-3; 4-32-16)

To show clearly how the power of Soma-drinking increases Indra's enthusiasm, a seer in one sūkta describes Indra's nature in this way. From it one learns in what ways Indra, satisfied by Soma-drinking, shows his favour to the sacrificer.

"I have drunk Soma fully. Therefore I shall provide the sacrificer with cattle and horses. The stream of Soma that I have drunk has produced exceeding vigour in me. As a cow runs in affection and joins her calf, the praise made by the seer has come and joined me. As a smith goes round and refines it, I too have made that praise pervade my heart. **NOTE** Even the five peoples, the Gandharvas and the rest, are insignificant before me. That is the power of Soma. Even Heaven and Earth together would not amount to half of me. I am one whose greatness exceeds the greatness of these two, Heaven and Earth. I shall establish this earth according to my resolve. The atmosphere is half of me. The other half I have let down below. I have the power to rule in the atmosphere. As the fruit of this Soma-drinking, I have the power to carry the oblation to all the gods and distribute it."

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-119-1, 389 1) **NOTE**

### Printed p. 595

Just like the Soma offered to Indra, the praises offered by the sacrificer, and praises of other kinds as well, greatly increase his vigour and energy. ब्रह्माणींद्र तवयानि वर्धना (*brahmāṇīṃdra tavayāni vardhanā*) (उक्थैर्वर्धमानाः (*ukthairvardhamānāḥ*))

(1-52-7, 1-53-8, 1-54-9, 2-55-10, 3-56-11; 3-57-12, 3-58-13.
4-59-14; 4-60-15: 4-61-16; 4-62-17; 4-63-18; 4-64-19;
4-65-20). **NOTE**

To bring about an extraordinary effect on the heroic strength stirred up by that Soma-drinking, the gods and men place the thunderbolt in Indra's hand.

**NOTE**

Moreover, the other gods too place all their strength in Indra himself.

(1-20-5 : 6.20-7 : 10-48-3 : 70-113-8 : 10-120-3 : 10 56-4 : 8.15-8)

And they seat him in the chariot and make him ready for battle.

(1-25-3 : 1.150-1 : 6.17-8:)

In many places it is described that at the time of the slaying of the Asura Vṛtra the Maruts encourage this Indra and make his strength stand firm and bring victory. That increases still further the power of Soma-drinking. (या अभजो मरुत इंद्र सोमे ये त्वामवर्धन्नभवन् गणस्ते (*yā abhajo maruta iṃdra some ye tvāmavardhannabhavan gaṇaste*)).

(3.35.7 : 3-33.4 ; 3.42.3 : 6-3.11 ; 8-3-24 ; 10-33-1, 2 ; 10-113-3).

In this connection it is necessary to state the natural relation and the companionship between Indra and the Maruts. This section shows Indra's regard for Soma. But since it also indicates how stimulating that Soma-drinking is for the slaying of Vṛtra, and what the part of the Maruts is in this, this matter too is incidental.

In 1-16 a dispute in words between Indra and the Maruts is described. **NOTE** In 1-116-8 Indra praises himself, saying that he slew Vṛtra without the help of the Maruts, by his own strength. In 7.21-6 this same praise is made by a devotee of Indra (स्वेना हि वृत्रं शवसा जघंथ (*svenā hi vṛtraṃ śavasā jaghaṃtha*)). Likewise, in 10.138-6 too he is praised with "एता त्या ते श्रुत्यानि केवला यदेकः......... (*etā tyā te śrutyāni kevalā yadekaḥ.........*)" and so on. It is stated that because of this valour all the gods fear Indra. (5.30.5). In 8-7-1 the Maruts are asked whether it was an offence that they did not help their friend Indra in a time of

### Printed p. 596

distress, and how, in such a situation, they could be worthy of trust.

In 4-18-11 Aditi, the mother of Indra, grieved that all the other gods had abandoned her son without helping him, approaches Viṣṇu and prays that he help her son. But elsewhere there is a somewhat different account of this. It is stated that when he was fighting with the Asura Vṛtra, all the other gods, afraid of his terrible form, ran away leaving Indra alone, and that Indra then, because of his friendship with the Maruts, destroyed Vṛtra with their help. (8-96-7). Sāyaṇa has stated the purport in this connection so that there is no contradiction between the earlier passages and this one. And he has supported his meaning by quoting a passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa. The passage of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa is as follows.—

इंद्रो वै वृत्रं हनिष्यन्सर्वा देवता अब्रवीदनु मोपतिष्ठध्वमुप मा ह्वयध्यमिति तथेति तं हनिष्यंत आद्रवन्नोऽवेन्मां वै हनिष्यंत आद्रवंति हंतेमान्षया इति तानभिप्राश्वसीत्तस्य श्वसथादीषमाणा विश्वे देवा अद्रवन् मरुतो हैनं नाजहुः प्रहर भगवो जहि वीरयस्वेत्येवैनमेतां वाचं वदंत उपातिष्ठंत । तदेतदृषिः पश्यन्नभ्यनूवाच वृत्रस्य त्वा श्वसथादीषमाणा विश्वे देवा आजहुर्ये सखायः । मरुद्धिरिंद्र सख्यं ते अस्त्वथेमा विश्वाः पृजना जयासीति । सोऽवेदिमे वै किल मे सचिवा इमे माकामयंत हंतेमानस्मिन्नुक्थ अभजा इति ॥ (*iṃdro vai vṛtraṃ haniṣyansarvā devatā abravīdanu mopatiṣṭhadhvamupa mā hvayadhyamiti tatheti taṃ haniṣyaṃta ādravanno 'venmāṃ vai haniṣyaṃta ādravaṃti haṃtemānṣayā iti tānabhiprāśvasīttasya śvasathādīṣamāṇā viśve devā adravan maruto hainaṃ nājahuḥ prahara bhagavo jahi vīrayasvetyevainametāṃ vācaṃ vadaṃta upātiṣṭhaṃta | tadetadṛṣiḥ paśyannabhyanūvāca vṛtrasya tvā śvasathādīṣamāṇā viśve devā ājahurye sakhāyaḥ | maruddhiriṃdra sakhyaṃ te astvathemā viśvāḥ pṛjanā jayāsīti | so 'vedime vai kila me sacivā ime mākāmayaṃta haṃtemānasminnuktha abhajā iti ‖*)

(Ai. Brā. 3-20)

Indra, wishing to kill the Asura Vṛtra, said to the gods, "O gods, follow me without leaving me, and be my helpers." Then they gave their assurance, "We shall do so," and rushed forward to kill Vṛtra. Then Vṛtra said, "These gods are rushing forward to kill me. I shall frighten them," and, letting out a powerful breath, made a terrible sound. Then all the gods, hearing that terrible sound, were frightened and ran off in all directions. But the Maruts alone did not abandon Indra. Standing right beside Indra, they encouraged him, saying, "O Indra, strike him. Show your valour." Then the seer, praising the friendship of the Maruts, recited the mantra beginning वृत्रस्य त्वा (*vṛtrasya tvā*) and praised them. (8-96-7). Then Indra said, "These Maruts alone are my true friends. They love me; therefore in the uktha-mantra offered to me I shall give them a share too."

### Printed p. 597

In the Ṛk-saṃhitā, in the mantra 1.32-14, describing this same situation, it is praised with the words अहेर्यातारं (*aheryātāraṃ*). Here too the meaning is doubtful. It is stated here that at the time of the slaying of the Asura Vṛtra a little fear arose in Indra. Out of that fear, running like a hawk, he crossed the ninety-nine river streams that he met on the way and escaped. In this way two or three kinds of purport can be stated. But that examination is unnecessary at present. The other gods who helped Indra are also praised in some places. For example—

"O Aśvins, lords of radiance, having drunk the sweet Soma together with Indra, you helped him when he was destroying the Asura Namuci, and at that time you protected him."

(10-3-4) **NOTE**

"O Indra, as parents protect their children, the two Aśvins protected Indra in time of calamity. When you drank Soma at the time of the manifestation of your valour, the goddess Sarasvatī, with all her means of protection, was beside you as helper."

(10-13 7-5) **NOTE**

This account is also stated in the Vājasaneya-saṃhitā. (10-33, 34) And in the Vājasaneya-saṃhitā commentary the commentator has quoted a story stated in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. Its form is as follows—

इंद्रसेंद्रियमन्नस्य रसग्‌ंसोमस्य भक्षग्ंसुरयासुरो नमुचिरहरत्योऽश्विनौ च सरस्वतीं चोपाधावछेपानोऽस्मि नमुचये न त्वा दिवा न नक्तग्ं हनानि न दण्णेन न धन्वना न पृथेन न मुष्टिना न शुष्केण नाद्रॆणार्थ म इदमहार्षिदिदं म आजिहर्षथेति । (*iṃdraseṃdriyamannasya rasagṃsomasya bhakṣagṃsurayāsuro namuciraharatyo 'śvinau ca sarasvatīṃ copādhāvachepāno 'smi namucaye na tvā divā na naktagṃ hanāni na daṇṇena na dhanvanā na pṛthena na muṣṭinā na śuṣkeṇa nādrèṇārtha ma idamahārṣididaṃ ma ājiharṣatheti |*)

(Pa. Brā. 12-7-3-1) **NOTE**

The Asura Namuci once carried off Indra's heroic strength, his food, his Soma and his surā. Then Indra went to the Aśvins and to Sarasvatī and said, "I have given an assurance that I shall not kill Namuci either by day or by night. Not only this, I have also given an assurance that I shall not kill him with wood, or with my hand, or with a fist, or with a dry instrument, or with a wet one. Because of this assurance he has carried off my strength. Bring it back to me." They gave him this answer.

### Printed p. 598

अस्तु नोऽप्राप्यथाहरामेशि सह न एतदथाहरतेत्यब्रवीदिति (*astu no 'prāpyathāharāmeśi saha na etadathāharatetyabravīditi*)

(12-4-3-2)

They said, "It will do if you give us too a share in that heroic strength and in the Soma and the rest." Indra agreed to that.

तावश्विनी च सरस्वती च अपां फेनेन वज्रमसिंचन्न शुष्को नार्द्र इति तेनेंद्रो नमुचेरासुरस्य व्युष्टायाग्ं रात्रावनुदित आदित्ये न दिवा न नक्तमिति शिर उदवासयत् । (*tāvaśvinī ca sarasvatī ca apāṃ phenena vajramasiṃcanna śuṣko nārdra iti teneṃdro namucerāsurasya vyuṣṭāyāgṃ rātrāvanudita āditye na divā na naktamiti śira udavāsayat |*)

(2-7-3)

Then the Aśvins and Sarasvatī anointed the thunderbolt with the foam of the waters. Then it was neither wet nor dry. Then with it Indra struck Namuci. Since he struck at dawn, when the night had passed but the sun had not yet risen, it was neither day nor night. With it he cut off Namuci's head.

तस्मादेतदृषिणाभ्यनूक्तं...... तस्य शीर्षंश्णिन्ने लोहितमिश्रः सोमोऽतिष्ठत्तस्मादबीभत्संत त एतदंधसोर्विपानमपश्यन्सोमो राज्ञामृतग्ं सुत इति तेनैनग्ं स्वदयित्वात्मन्नदधत ॥ (*tasmādetadṛṣiṇābhyanūktaṃ...... tasya śīrṣaṃśṇinne lohitamiśraḥ somo 'tiṣṭhattasmādabībhatsaṃta ta etadaṃdhasorvipānamapaśyansomo rājñāmṛtagṃ suta iti tenainagṃ svadayitvātmannadadhata ‖*)

(6-7-8-9)

As soon as Namuci's head was split, the Soma became mixed with blood. Then it became repulsive. Then they, understanding that "when King Soma is sprinkled he becomes immortal," poured it together with this Soma and drank it. This is the description. But here, in this last part, which are the two Somas, "this Soma" and "that Soma," is worth examining. For the present it is not to the point.

In the same way, in another passage of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa it is stated that when Indra's strength was impaired, the Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, and Sarasvatī caused his heroic strength to be restored.

(12-7-1980 ; 12-8-3-1) **NOTE**

Just as, with the help of the Maruts, Indra destroyed the strength of the Asuras, so also with the help of Bṛhaspati Indra destroyed the enemies of the gods who opposed him.

(8-85-15)

### Printed p. 599

In this way, delighted and stimulated by Soma-drinking, Indra goes, sometimes accompanied by the Maruts and at other times by Viṣṇu, to fight against Vṛtra

(2-15-1: 2-19-2 : 6-47-1, 2; 10-11-2-1)

With the help of these Maruts and Viṣṇu he goes to fight the Asuras who hold back the stores of water in the atmosphere so that they do not flow.

(1-22-19 ; 1-85-7 ; 4-18-11 ; 6-20-2 ; 8-89-12 ; 7-99-4, 5)

The companionship of Indra and Viṣṇu is praised in many mantras. By passages such as आ यो विनाय सचथाय दैव्य इंद्राय विष्णुः सुकृते सुकृत्तरः (*ā yo vināya sacathāya daivya iṃdrāya viṣṇuḥ sukṛte sukṛttaraḥ*) (1.156-25) the help that Viṣṇu gave to Indra is made manifest.

(6-17-10 : 8-12-26 : 8-67-10 ; 10-1-(3-2) **NOTE**

On the companionship of Indra and Viṣṇu the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa describes a situation in the form of a story, in the passages quoted below, as follows.

वृत्रे ह वा इदमग्रे सर्वमास यदृचो यद्यजूग्ंषि यत्सामानि तस्मा इंद्रो वज्रं प्राजिहीर्षत् । (*vṛtre ha vā idamagre sarvamāsa yadṛco yadyajūgṃṣi yatsāmāni tasmā iṃdro vajraṃ prājihīrṣat |*)

(Śa. Brā. 5-5-1)

In the beginning Vṛtra, the lord of the Asuras, had taken into himself the Ṛk, the Yajus and the Sāman, all of them. With the aim of bringing them out and making them shine for the world, Indra tried to hurl the thunderbolt at that Vṛtra.

स ह विष्णुमुवाच । वृत्राय नै वज्रं प्रहरिष्याम्यनुमा तिष्ठस्वेति तथेति ह विष्णुरुवाचानु त्वा स्वास्ये प्रहरेति तस्मा इंद्रो वज्रमुद्ययाम स उद्यताद्वज्राद्वृत्रो बिभयां चकार ॥ (*sa ha viṣṇumuvāca | vṛtrāya nai vajraṃ prahariṣyāmyanumā tiṣṭhasveti tatheti ha viṣṇuruvācānu tvā svāsye prahareti tasmā iṃdro vajramudyayāma sa udyatādvajrādvṛtro bibhayāṃ cakāra ‖*)

(5-5_5-2)

Then Indra said to Viṣṇu, "I intend to hurl the thunderbolt at Vṛtra in order to gather the Ṛk and the rest. You too help in this." Then Viṣṇu said, "So be it. I shall help in this work. Strike Vṛtra with the thunderbolt." On that assurance, when Indra hurled the thunderbolt at Vṛtra, Vṛtra became afraid. And he said this to Indra.

### Printed p. 600

स होवाच । अस्ति वा इदं वीर्यं तन्नु ते प्रयच्छानि मा तु मे प्रहार्षीरिति तस्मै यजूग्ंषि प्रायच्छत्तस्मै द्वितीयमुद्ययाम (*sa hovāca | asti vā idaṃ vīryaṃ tannu te prayacchāni mā tu me prahārṣīriti tasmai yajūgṃṣi prāyacchattasmai dvitīyamudyayāma*)

(5-5-5-3)

"This heroic strength is established in me. I give it to you. Do not strike me." So saying, he handed the Yajus over to Indra. Then Indra, not satisfied with that, raised the thunderbolt a second time to strike him, with the intention of seizing the rest also.

(Śa. Cā. 53-54) **NOTE**

"O Indra, I have yet one more kind of means of heroic strength. That too I offer to you. Please do not strike me." So saying, he offered the Sāmans too to Indra.

इंद्रो हि वज्रमुद्यच्छद्विष्णुरन्वतिष्ठत (*iṃdro hi vajramudyacchadviṣṇuranvatiṣṭhata*)

(5-5-5-2)

Even so, it says that when Indra raised the thunderbolt and tried to strike, Viṣṇu too stood by him.

The same kind of story is told in the Taittirīya Saṃhitā. But there it is stated that Vṛtra offered Indra three kinds of uktha in place of the powers in the form of the Ṛk, Yajus and Sāman, one each time, three times. It is stated that since Viṣṇu too helped Indra, Viṣṇu too has a share in this.

(Tai. Saṃ. 6-5-1-1) In Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-109-5, 7, 8 : 3-12-4, 6 : 10-65.2 and other places it is stated that Agni, the destroyer of Vṛtra and of solid form, joined Indra and slew Vṛtra.

### Printed p. 601

"O Indra and Agni, I have heard that when wealth is being distributed to all the praisers, you two, standing in front, proved most capable in the work of destroying the Asura Vṛtra.

(1-109-5)

The epithets Vajrabāhū, Purandarā and the like are common to the two. In one or two situations it is also stated that Varuṇa helped Indra.

"O Indra and Varuṇa, upon this Vṛtra, who has extraordinary strength, you two together hurled the radiant thunderbolt of great strength."

(3-21.4)

These Asuras, the causes of famines, are famous under many names, such as Vṛtra, Ahi, Śuṣṇa, Namuci, Pipru, Śambara and Uraṇa.

(1-12-5, 10 : 2-14-4 ; 8-32-2, 3)

If some of the situations that give information about them and describe their deeds of destruction are taken here as examples, their terrible nature becomes known. In some places the names of all of them are specified together. All of them are Dānavas. Danu is their mother. It is stated that she too, to protect her sons, sometimes takes part in battle. For example—

"At the time of the slaying of the Asura Vṛtra, his mother came to protect him from the blow of the thunderbolt, to protect her son. Then Indra weakened her strength and struck her hard on the lower part of her body. After he had struck her with the thunderbolt, the mother came to be on top; the son lay trapped below. As a cow lies together with her calf, the mother, the Dānavī, lay dead together with her son Vṛtra."

(1.32-9)

तद्वै एष एव इंद्रो य एष तपति । अथ एष एव वृत्रो यच्चंद्रमाः ॥ (*tadvai eṣa eva iṃdro ya eṣa tapati | atha eṣa eva vṛtro yaccaṃdramāḥ ‖*)

(Śa. Brā. 1-6-4-18)

10-133-2 ;) **NOTE**

As soon as Indra shows his valour and resolves, all the clouds in the atmosphere scatter and the darkness is destroyed. The sun too, regaining his natural state, sheds everywhere the radiance that gives light to the whole world.

(1-32-4 ; 1-51.4 ; 1-51.8 : 2-19-3)

On the matter described in the mantra 1-251-4, Sāyaṇa states his opinion in this way. **NOTE** Its original is:

वृत्रं यदिंद्र शवसावधीरहिमादित्सूर्यं दिव्यारोहयो दृशे (*vṛtraṃ yadiṃdra śavasāvadhīrahimāditsūryaṃ divyārohayo dṛśe*)

Explaining its purport, Sāyaṇa states:

वृत्रेणावृतं सूर्यं तस्माद्वृतात् अमूमुच इत्यर्थः (*vṛtreṇāvṛtaṃ sūryaṃ tasmādvṛtāt amūmuca ityarthaḥ*)

He has stated that the purport is that Indra caused the sun, who was enveloped by Vṛtra, to be freed. But if the original sentence is examined, it tells us that after the slaying of Vṛtra he established the sun in the atmosphere, giving that meaning. On the whole, its purport is simply that Indra became the cause of the destruction of darkness.

### Printed p. 603

In this way, the situation of a battle with Vṛtra, who is of the nature of darkness, is described in many places in the Ṛk-saṃhitā. The aim of the battle is to destroy the darkness and spread light.

(1-4-2 ; 1-32-1 ; 1-52-2 ; 1-50-1 ; 1-103-2 ; 2-11-5 ; 5-32-1 ; 1.89-7 ; 1.0-103-6). **NOTE**

And this description is poetic, full of many kinds of metaphors. Because clouds possess most wonderful forms, they are described in many ways: sometimes as mountains, at other times as the fortresses of the Asuras, and as the dense cities of the Asuras.

(9-126 ; 8-130-14 ; 8-87-6)

These moving clouds, which obstruct the light, are described as made of ayasa (iron or steel), and as made of stone. And these very clouds are described as the cities of the Asuras; it is stated that Indra destroyed, by hurling the thunderbolt, these very cities, which stand in the atmosphere and give shelter to the Asuras.

1-50-2 ; 1-63-7 : 1-80-3 ; 1-90-4 ; 2-10-5 ; 3-20-6 ; 3-12-6 ; 4-20-3 ; 4-30-5 ; 5.83-2 ; 7-80-7).

Indra picks out all the Asuras who lay asleep in the mountains of the atmosphere, beats them down, and hurls all of them from the atmosphere to the earth below.

(1-32-2; 1-330 7 ; 3-12-11 ; 4-20-14 ; 6-26-5)

And when they wish to spread over the whole atmosphere, he drives all of them back.

(2-12-12; 8-14-14)

One of those Asuras he treads upon and tramples with his foot. And he torments him with frost.

(1-5-6 ; 8-32-26)

With a stream of water he strikes off the head of Namuci.

(8-14-2)

Of the Asuras who are Indra's enemies, one named Uraṇa is described as having ninety-nine arms and as a monster; his deformed shape is portrayed.

Of another it is stated that he had three heads and six eyes.

(2-14.4)

(C.O-99-6) **NOTE**

These forms, too, and these imaginative descriptions are fitting for natural occurrences. It is natural that people scorched by the burning heat of the summer season should look for rain as soon as the summer is over. But there are also very many occasions when dense clouds spread over the whole atmosphere and yet

### Printed p. 604

do not pour down rain. In such circumstances it is natural that the belief arises that some Asuric power is obstructing the rain. It is likewise natural that a kind of faith arises in the divine power that destroys this Asuric power. The appearance of thunder and lightning is described as the clash, taking place in the atmosphere, of two powers, the divine and the Asuric.

Indra is the presiding deity who reflects this divine power. This power of Indra, who benefits his devotees and destroys their enemies, grants wealth to the sacrificer and others and frees them from the afflictions caused by the Asuras. The masses of clouds moving in the atmosphere are described as chariots, as the horses of the chariot, and as Indra's bearers.

It is understood that this Indra is a deity of a different nature from Parjanya. Since there are also passages where Indra and Parjanya are compared, there is full room to say that they are separate deities, each of a distinct nature. Many hymns addressed to Parjanya also show that he is a deity different from Indra.

(8-6-1)

But there are also very many passages that state the identity of Indra and Sūrya.

**The description of Indra's greatness**

It may be said that, throughout the Ṛk-saṃhitā, the epithets that show the highest position among all the deities are most numerous in praise of Indra. These also show Indra's universal sovereignty. Only a selection of them has been made, and their purport is stated here.

**In the first Maṇḍala:**

Indra has established the sun in the atmosphere so that it is seen even at the farthest distance.

(1-2-3)

O Indra, you bear in your arms the thunderbolt made of steel, and you have established the sun in the atmosphere.

(8-52-8)

(C-953-12) **NOTE**

In the passage quoted above, that is, in stating the purport of mantra 6.47.16, one point calls for a little discussion. In the sixteenth mantra विधमानद्विट् (*vidhamānadviṭ*) is an epithet of Indra and tells of his nature. The word विधमान (*vidhamāna*) means "one who is increasing," that is, one who is endowed with wealth and the like and with mental comforts. But is Indra one who cultivates enmity toward those who are endowed with wealth? Is there no distinction between friend and foe in this? The question naturally arises. Therefore Sāyaṇa, in this context, has explained असुन्वतां विधमानानां (*asunvatāṃ vidhamānānāṃ*) as enemy of the selfish who, having gained increase of wealth, do not even offer oblations in sacrificial rites such as the yāga

### Printed p. 623

and the like. How? विधमानद्विट् (*vidhamānadviṭ*) applies in general to all the gods. It is made clear by this that the gods do not **NOTE** the progress of men. The meaning of the next mantra supports the same view. The scholar Wilson states as follows:

"He is also represented in the same hymn as of a capricious temperament, neglecting those who serve him, and favouring those who pay him no adoration; a notion somewhat at variance with a doctrine, previously inculcated that the ceremonial worship of Indra is able to atone for the most atrocious crimes." **NOTE**

(Quoted by Muir. Original Sanskrit Text. Vol. v. p. 111).

The purport of these sentences is as follows. It may be said that the meaning given to विधमानिद्विट् (*vidhamānidviṭ*) by the English commentators is natural. For immediately after this mantra, the sentence in the next mantra, "Indra acts as he pleases. Indra is ready to leave the sacrificer who offers oblations and go to those who do not offer them," supports the above purport. There is a complete contradiction between what is described in the mantras that give the sense that any sins are destroyed if an oblation is offered in the sacrifice to Indra (1-34-4) and what is said in the present mantras. This is the opinion of the same scholar Wilson. For this contradiction to be removed, विधमानानां वर्धमानानां असुन्वतां द्विट् (*vidhamānānāṃ vardhamānānāṃ asunvatāṃ dviṭ*), as said by Sāyaṇa and the Nirukta-writers, must be understood to mean "an enemy of all who are prospering without offering oblations." That fits the context.

**Some apparent inconsistencies in the description of Indra's nature, as they appear to a gross view, and their resolution.**

To those who have no acquaintance with the Ṛk-saṃhitā, either through study of the original or through translation, it is natural that some contradictory elements should appear in the above description of Indra's nature. But that is natural indeed. If it is examined only from the gross point of view, there is no doubt that inconsistencies appear in the above accounts. The description of Indra as the supreme deity, the regulator and supporter of the universe, stands opposed to the other ordinary descriptions of qualities. For example: in the drinking of Soma and in other dealings, wishes and the like such as ordinary human beings have are described in Indra. At times even desire for sensual objects seems to be intense. Such a description does not fit with Indra's extraordinary, supramundane, spiritual great qualities, by which he guides the whole universe. There are also occasions where such opposed descriptions occur in a single sūkta. But when one examines the matter here from the spiritual point of view, it becomes clear that such a nature is only natural. How? All the elements of the universe may be seen to have a twofold nature: one eternal, the other non-eternal; one sensory, the other spiritual; one ordinary, the other extraordinary; in this way this duality is plainly present in every human being. There is no inconsistency in the ordinary qualities natural to the universe and the extraordinary, supramundane, divine qualities, which belong to him because he transcends the universe, being found together. Even if one supposes that wishes and similar qualities show a terrestrial nature in Indra, it is established that, in relation to modern culture, the description is not one of desire for sensual objects. The wish for the Soma-juice, in the drinking of Soma and similar acts in which Indra procures immortality, is a supramundane and divine wish, and it is certain that it is no fault. Since these opposed qualities are described by one and the same seer, it is not right to say that such words of the seer are inconsistent. Some such occasions may be examined. For example:

"Indra established the heaven in the empty region. He stood pervading all the heaven and earth. He supported the earth and made it spread out widely. All these extraordinary deeds Indra did by the power of drinking the Soma-juice."

(2-15-2)

### Printed p. 628

O Indra, of most marvellous valour, maker of the atmosphere, creator of the earth, drink the Soma that produces the highest delight in you.

(8-2.6-4)

As explained earlier, in the Ṛks beginning with 8-78-5 and others, Indra's drinking of the Soma-juice, the valour produced by it, and the supramundane acts which Indra performs as the fruit of that valour are all celebrated.

"By this drinking of Soma, which produces a most intense and most excellent delight, Indra's valour grew, and by its power Indra conquered all the worlds and became the lord, the ruler of the whole universe." (8-92-6)

From passages of this kind it cannot be said that Indra's wish to drink Soma is a desire for sensual objects, that the valour produced by it is merely worldly valour, or that such descriptions point to elements opposed to Indra's divine qualities. Even when examined from the spiritual point of view, there is no doubt that these descriptions describe Indra's divine qualities.

**Some passages describing the mutual relation of Indra and Varuṇa**

In the early maṇḍalas of the Ṛk-saṃhitā the sūktas addressed to Indra are more numerous. In the last maṇḍalas the sūktas addressed to Varuṇa are in greater number. For this reason some English scholars have held the opinion that at the beginning of the composition of the Ṛk-saṃhitā greater importance was attached to Indra than to Varuṇa, and that at the end greater reverence was shown to Varuṇa than to Indra. There is no proper basis for this opinion, and it may be said to be a mistaken opinion. It was explained earlier, and will be stated again later, that the Saṃhitā passages themselves declare that all the practical differences such as Indra and Varuṇa are different manifestations of one and the same principle, and that these names are not classes of deities with a difference of principle. (इंद्रं मित्रं वरुणमग्निमाहुः (*iṃdraṃ mitraṃ varuṇamagnimāhuḥ*)) Even so, to establish that there is no room for such a difference even in the description of the manifestations of the one principle, some occasions on which these two deities are described, whether together or individually, may be examined.

In the sūktas 1-17, 4-41; 4-42; 6-68; 7.82; 7.83, 7-84; 7.85 and others, equal reverence is shown to Indra and Varuṇa both. At the very beginning, Indra and Varuṇa are both indicated as the sovereigns who support the whole world.

इंद्रावरुणयोरहं सम्राजोरव आ वृणॆः । ता नो मृळात ईवृशॆ ॥ (*iṃdrāvaruṇayorahaṃ samrājorava ā vṛṇèḥ | tā no mṛḷāta īvṛśè ‖*)

(1-2-7)

### Printed p. 629

गंतारा हि स्थोऽवसे हवः विप्रस्य मावतः ! दर्तारा चर्षणीनां ॥ (*gaṃtārā hi stho 'vase havaḥ viprasya māvataḥ ! dartārā carṣaṇīnāṃ ‖*)

(1.17-2)

In such passages no superiority or inferiority is shown for either deity. Epithets such as धृतव्रत (*dhṛtavrata*) are also common to both, and indicate the equal part of both in the governance of the universe.

(6-68 10)

Just as Indra is prayed to hurl the radiant thunderbolt against the enemy, so Varuṇa too is prayed.

(6.7.5)

But in many passages this power applies to Indra alone. In 7-82-2 Varuṇa is praised with the epithet सम्राट् (*samrāṭ*) and Indra with the epithet स्वराट् (*svarāṭ*). (सम्राळन्यः स्वराळन्य उच्यते (*samrāḷanyaḥ svarāḷanya ucyate*)).

(u-46-1: 1-61-9 and other mantras may be seen) **NOTE**

In this same sūkta and in other sūktas too, the individual deeds and qualities of Indra and Varuṇa are described separately.

O Indrāvaruṇa, when you created all the beings of the world and displayed your power, Mitra shone peacefully together with Varuṇa, and the terrible Indra together with the Maruts.

(7-82-5)

Varuṇa conquers the destroying enemy. Indra, with the help of the Maruts alone, drives far away enemies of great number.

(7-8-6)

Indra shows his delight in destroying enemies in battle. For Varuṇa, as the one who holds to his vows, the duty is the keeping of the law.

(6-83-9)

May Varuṇa's anger be far from us and not injure us. May Indra make for us a wide space. **NOTE**

(2-a4-2) **NOTE**

The one, Varuṇa, bears many kinds of vital powers. The other, Indra, utterly destroys endless armies of enemies.

(2-85:a) **NOTE**

### Printed p. 630

While all this is a description of their individual actions, some of the descriptions of certain chief joint undertakings of the two, well organised and mutually helpful, may be examined next.

(7-85-2)

O Indrāvaruṇa, you two together by your power removed the obstruction that was on the waters and made them fit to flow. You made the sun, the illuminer of the world, lord of the atmosphere. As the fruit of the delight arising from Soma-drinking you made all the banks of the river fertile. Be kind and fulfil the purpose of our sacrificial rite.

(7-82-3)

O Indrāvaruṇa, by your great power you have created all the beings of the world.

(7-82-5)

All the other gods too fill Indrāvaruṇa, who dwell in the highest region of the atmosphere, with valour and splendour. (7-82-2)

In the same way, in some other mantras Indra and Viṣṇu are praised together.

Indra and Viṣṇu, both unobstructed and great, stand in splendour on the lofty region of the clouds that are like peaks, as if mounting on tamed horses and climbing to high places. To Indra and Viṣṇu, powerful and valiant, offer your nourishing food in the form of Soma.

(1-155-1)

O Indra and Viṣṇu, through Agni, the granter of desires, you always provide to the human sacrificer the food and other things that he is to receive in the form of the fruit of the sacrifice. The sacrificer worships the shining and united coming of you both, whose works are the granting of desires and the like.

(1-155_2)

He distributes great manly power for heaven and earth, for the sake of giving living beings the capacity of procreation and for the enjoyment of pleasures. This power, established in the orb of the radiant Āditya, every man obtains, through the grace of Viṣṇu, as that which bears the name of sons, grandsons and the like.

(1-1235-3 ; 7.99.4) **NOTE**

The companionship of Indra and Agni is also praised in many places. (1-105 ; 1.109), for example:

### Printed p. 631

O Indra and Agni, you have made your auspicious name known as ever joined together. And as slayers of Vṛtra you were united even at the time of the slaying of Vṛtra. Therefore, O Indra and Agni, bestowers of what is wished for, sit together on the sacrificial altar and drink the flowing Soma-juice of your share.

(C-103-3) **NOTE**

O Indra and Agni, who hold the thunderbolt in your hands, bring wealth for us and give it to us. Protect us, who perform the sacrifice, by your heroic deeds.

By those rays of Indra in the form of the sun, by which our fathers, grandfathers and others together reached the world of Brahmā, may those same rays that are visible to our eyes favour us also.

(1-109-6 ; 3-12 ; 5-86 ; 6-59)

In the same way, joint descriptions and praises such as Indra and Vāyu, Indra and Pūṣan, and Indra and Soma are numerous.

(3-46 to 8) Indranāyaṇa ; (6-27) Indrapūṣan ; (6-22 ; 6-104) Indrasomā. **NOTE**

What is described in the mantras in which the word असिंद्र (*asiṃdra*) is used deserves attention. This word is used on many occasions.

(1-133-1 ; 4-23-7 ; 5-2-3 ; 6-18-16 ; 10-27-6 : 10-98-2)

अनिंद्र (*aniṃdra*) means one who is not a worshipper of Indra. By this word may be understood either non-Āryas who did not worship Indra and the other gods, or the demoniac powers that are hostile to Indra. **NOTE**

In the twelfth sūkta of the second maṇḍala the description of Indra's great qualities is most excellent. Only some of them may be examined in the present context. They describe Indra's power of governing the universe.

As soon as the all-wise Indra was born, he surpassed by his great power all the other gods. O men, know him to be Indra, at whose power and might heaven and earth trembled. (2-12-1)

O men, he who made the trembling earth stand firm, who made the agitated mountains immovable, who created the vast atmosphere and supported the heaven, know him to be Indra. (2-12-2)

"I, whose self is divine, have obtained, with the help of the Ādityas and the other gods alone, a most powerful strength, an unconquerable state and unobstructed valour

### Printed p. 632

and therefore I shall not cause any breach in the excellent states of the Ādityas, the Vasus and the Maruts, who are adopted sons." These words of Indra (10.48 11) show an occasion on which Indra indicates his gratitude toward the other gods.

I shall conclude this section by stating the purport of some of the laudatory passages saying that Indra alone accomplished extraordinary deeds that the other gods could not.

Indra alone, who has surpassed men and does not desire the help of others, possesses a strength greater than that of all living beings. And he possesses a strength that cannot be conquered by anyone.

All the other gods too make manifest Indra's excellent seat and valour, and their own humility. **NOTE**

May our praise addressed to Indra be a good poem, with no kind of untruthfulness in it. A most severe calamity befalls the one who does not offer Soma-juice to Indra. But the devotee who worships Indra by offering Soma obtains abundant wealth together with great light.

There is no deity equal to Indra. Therefore there is no possibility at all of there being any deity with qualities like his. **NOTE**

This Indra alone conquered all the gods in battle. And even the most ancient gods, recognising Indra's power, showed their humility before him and acknowledged his lordship. (6-1-6)

Varuṇa, Sūrya and all the remaining gods too bow to the law laid down by Indra and discharge their duties.

Indra alone conquered all the jewels equal to those of the gods Mitra, Aryaman and Varuṇa (10-89-8, 9). From passages of this kind it is understood that Indra has greater power than all the gods named in them. **NOTE**

### Printed p. 633

**The account of the slaying of Vṛtrāsura**
