#### Ṛk 1

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> स॒हस्र॑तीर्षा॒ पुरु॑षः सहस्रा॒क्षः स॒हस्र॑पात् ।  
> स भूमिं॑ वि॒श्वतो॑ वृ॒त्वात्य॑तिष्ठद्दशांगु॒लं ॥ १ ॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> सहस्रशीर्षा ! पुरुषः । सहस्रअक्षः । सहस्रपात् ।  
> सः । भूमिं । विश्वतः । वृत्वा । अति । अतिष्ठत् । दश अंगुलं ॥ १ ॥

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> सर्वप्राणिसमष्टिरूपो ब्रह्मांडदेहो विराडाख्यो यः पुरुषः सोऽयं
> सहस्रशीर्षा । सहस्रशब्दस्योपलक्षणत्वादनंतैः शिरोभिर्युक्त इत्यर्थः । यानि सर्वप्राणिनां शिरांसि तानि सर्वाणि तद्देहांतःपातित्वात्तदीयान्येवेति सहस्रशीर्षत्वं ।
> एवं सहस्राक्षित्वं सहस्रपादत्वं च । स पुरुषो भूमिं ब्रह्मांडगोलकरूपां
> विश्वतः सर्वतो वृत्वा परिवेष्ट दशांगुलं दशांगुलपरिमितं देशमत्यतिष्ठत् ।
> अतिक्रम्म व्यवस्थितः । दशांगुलमित्युपलक्षणं । ब्रह्मांडाद्बहिरपि सर्वतो व्याप्यावस्थित इत्यर्थः ।

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The Puruṣa who is the aggregate of all beings, whose body is the cosmic egg and who is called Virāṭ, is "of a thousand heads". Since the word for thousand is only indicative, the meaning is that he has endless heads. All the heads of all beings are his own, because they fall within his body; this is his thousand-headedness, and in the same way his thousand eyes and thousand feet. That Puruṣa, having encompassed on all sides the earth, which is the globe of the cosmic egg, stood beyond it, having gone past a space measured by ten fingers. The measure of ten fingers is only indicative: the meaning is that he stands pervading everywhere, even outside the cosmic egg.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- पुरुषः (*puruṣaḥ*)—the primal Puruṣa
- सहस्रशीर्षा (*sahasraśīrṣā*)—he who is joined with countless heads
- सहस्राक्षः (*sahasrākṣaḥ*)—he who has countless eyes
- सहस्रपात् (*sahasrapāt*)—he who has countless feet
- सः (*saḥ*)—this Puruṣa
- भूमिं (*bhūmiṃ*)—the earth in the form of the globe of the cosmic egg (the whole universe)
- विश्वतः (*viśvataḥ*)—all around
- वृत्वा (*vṛtvā*)—having encompassed
- दशांगुलं (*daśāṃgulaṃ*)—by ten fingers beyond that
- अत्यतिष्ठत् (*atyatiṣṭhat*)—he stands, having surpassed it

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The primal Puruṣa has countless heads, and has countless eyes and feet. This Virāṭ Puruṣa, having encompassed the universe, which has the form of the cosmic egg, from all directions, stands established, having surpassed it by ten fingers.

### Printed p. 718

##### English translation
Purusha, who has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, investing the earth in all directions, exceeds (it by a space) measuring ten fingers.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

By such epithets as सहस्रशीर्षा पुरुषः (*sahasraśīrṣā puruṣaḥ*) the Supreme Person is praised and described in this Ṛk. It is said that the Puruṣa has a thousand heads, a thousand eyes and a thousand feet. Here the word thousand does not mean merely a thousand; thousand means endless in number. सहस्रशब्दस्कोपलक्षणत्पादनंतैः शिरोभिः युक्तः । यानि सर्वप्राणिनां शिरांसि तानि सर्वाणि तद्देहांतःपातित्वात्तदीयान्येव इति सहस्रशीर्षत्वं । (*sahasraśabdaskopalakṣaṇatpādanaṃtaiḥ śirobhiḥ yuktaḥ | yāni sarvaprāṇināṃ śirāṃsi tāni sarvāṇi taddehāṃtaḥpātitvāttadīyānyeva iti sahasraśīrṣatvaṃ |*) The Lord is the inner controller in all beings. Therefore the heads of all the endless beings are the Lord's own heads. Therefore the word thousand here gives the sense of endless. So Sāyaṇa has explained. Head, eye and foot indicate the Lord's will, seeing, and activity in the form of movement. This is described in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad thus.

विश्वतश्चक्षुरुत विश्वतो मुखो विश्वतो हस्त उत विश्वतस्पात् । सं बाहुभ्यां धमति संपतत्रैर्दार्वाभूमी जनयन् देव एकः ॥ (*viśvataścakṣuruta viśvato mukho viśvato hasta uta viśvataspāt | saṃ bāhubhyāṃ dhamati saṃpatatrairdārvābhūmī janayan deva ekaḥ ‖*)

(Prai. U. 3-3) **NOTE**

The Supreme Lord has eyes extended everywhere and a head turned everywhere. Likewise, spreading his arms and his feet into thousands of regions, he gives life to the world. Therefore all the heads, eyes, arms and feet in the universe are his alone. He, the one without a second, is the maker of the whole world.

सर्वाननशिरोग्रिवः सर्वभूतगुहाशयः । सर्वव्यापी स भगवांस्तस्मात् सर्वगतः शिवः ॥ (*sarvānanaśirogrivaḥ sarvabhūtaguhāśayaḥ | sarvavyāpī sa bhagavāṃstasmāt sarvagataḥ śivaḥ ‖*)

(Kvi. U. 3-11) **NOTE**

This all-pervading Supreme Lord, dwelling in the heart of all, makes the heads, the necks and all the faces of all his own. The Lord of countless heads is the one denoted here by the word Puruṣa.

### Printed p. 719

1) यत्पूर्वोऽस्मात्सर्वस्मात्सर्वान्पाप्मन औषत्तस्मात्परुषः (*yatpūrvo 'smātsarvasmātsarvānpāpmana auṣattasmātparuṣaḥ*) (Bṛ. U. 1-4.1)

2) अस्यां पुरि शेते तस्मात्सुरुषः (*asyāṃ puri śete tasmātsuruṣaḥ*) (Śa. Brā. 13-6-2-1)

By giving such etymologies, the sense of the word Puruṣa has been explained in the introduction. The word पूः (*pūḥ*) means body. The sense is that he is established in all bodies, those of gods, men, animals and the rest. Explaining this same matter, the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad describes him as एको देवः सर्वभूतेषु गूढः (*eko devaḥ sarvabhūteṣu gūḍhaḥ*) (Śve. U. 6-11) **NOTE**.

Thirdly: पुर उषति प्रकाशयतीति पुरुषः! दाहप्रकाशयोरेकाधिकरणत्वात् । (*pura uṣati prakāśayatīti puruṣaḥ! dāhaprakāśayorekādhikaraṇatvāt |*). The word उषति (*uṣati*) has been explained earlier as "burns (sin)". Since the meaning "illuminates" is also possible for this word, in the present context the etymology can also be given that he is called Puruṣa because he illuminates the whole body that has the form of the world. For burning and illuminating have one and the same locus. **NOTE** For this very reason the epithet सहस्राक्षः (*sahasrākṣaḥ*) also is found. How? Thus—

य एष वैश्वानरो विश्वरूपः प्राणोऽग्निरुदयते । तदेतदृचाभ्युक्तं । विश्वरूपं हरिणं जातवेदसं परायणं ज्योतिरेकं तपंतं । सहस्ररश्मिः शतधा वर्तमानः प्राणः प्रजानामुदयत्येष सूर्यः ॥ ( (*ya eṣa vaiśvānaro viśvarūpaḥ prāṇo 'gnirudayate | tadetadṛcābhyuktaṃ | viśvarūpaṃ hariṇaṃ jātavedasaṃ parāyaṇaṃ jyotirekaṃ tapaṃtaṃ | sahasraraśmiḥ śatadhā vartamānaḥ prāṇaḥ prajānāmudayatyeṣa sūryaḥ ‖ (*)

(Praśna. 1-8) **NOTE**

Agni, who is the Self of all, who has all forms and is the life of the world, rises. Those who know the truth know the Supreme Brahman, who has all the forms of the world, who is omniscient, of golden form, the highest refuge, the one light for the whole world, self-luminous. This Supreme Brahman, who shines in the form of fire and in the form of the sun, joined with countless rays, showing his own nature in many ways, shines as the life of all creatures. Therefore the word thousand denotes everything. How the sense "everything" belongs to the word thousand is shown thus—

सहस्रस्य प्रमासि । सहस्रस्य प्रतिमासि सहस्रस्योन्मासि साहस्रोऽसि सहस्राय त्वेति सर्वं वै सहस्रं सर्वमसि सर्वस्मै त्वेत्येतत् ॥ (*sahasrasya pramāsi | sahasrasya pratimāsi sahasrasyonmāsi sāhasro 'si sahasrāya tveti sarvaṃ vai sahasraṃ sarvamasi sarvasmai tvetyetat ‖*)

(Śa. Brā. 8-7-4-11)

O Agni, you are one who has the measure of a thousand. You are the counterpart of a thousand and have a multiplier of a thousand. Thousand means everything. Therefore you alone are every measure and every counter-measure: thus the sense of the word thousand is explained. The matter described by the words विश्वतो वृत्ता (*viśvato vṛttā*) **NOTE**

### Printed p. 720

is also this very one. This same matter is explained in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad thus—

सर्वतः पाणिपादं तत्सर्वतोऽक्षिशिरोमुखं । सर्वतः श्रुतिमल्लोके सर्वमावृत्य तिष्ठति ॥ (*sarvataḥ pāṇipādaṃ tatsarvato 'kṣiśiromukhaṃ | sarvataḥ śrutimalloke sarvamāvṛtya tiṣṭhati ‖*)

(Śve. U. 3-16)

The hands and feet of the Lord are spread everywhere. His eyes, head and faces are extended on every side. His ear too is all-pervading. This principle of the Lord stands pervading everything in the world. Such a Supreme Person not only pervades the whole world but has surpassed it. In अत्यतिष्ठद्दशांगुलं (*atyatiṣṭhaddaśāṃgulaṃ*) there is praise of the Lord, who is greater than the world and is the master of the whole world. In the present context it is most necessary to consider what दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) means in अत्यतिष्ठद्दशांगुलं (*atyatiṣṭhaddaśāṃgulaṃ*) and what the purport of अत्यतिष्ठत् (*atyatiṣṭhat*) is.

दशांगुलपरिमितं देशमत्यतिष्ठदतिक्रम्य व्यवस्थितः । दशांगुलमित्युपलक्षणं । ब्रह्मांडाद्बहिरपि सर्वतो व्याप्यावस्थित इत्यर्थः । (*daśāṃgulaparimitaṃ deśamatyatiṣṭhadatikramya vyavasthitaḥ | daśāṃgulamityupalakṣaṇaṃ | brahmāṃḍādbahirapi sarvato vyāpyāvasthita ityarthaḥ |*)

(Sā. Bhā.) **NOTE**

He stands, having surpassed a region measured by ten fingers. The ten fingers are merely indicative. Sāyaṇa has explained that the purport is that he stands pervading everywhere, even beyond the cosmic egg. The commentary of Maṅgalācārya also gives the same purport.

स एतादृशः परमेश्वरः ब्रह्मांडशरीरवान् भूमिं भूशब्दोपलक्षितभूर्भुवःस्वराज्यत्रैलोक्यमित्यर्थः । अत एव विश्वतः समंततः सर्वं जगदिति यावत् वृत्वा आवृत्य अधिष्ठाय । दशांगुलानि मायंते यस्मिन् कर्मणि तद्दशांगुलं अत्यतिष्ठत् अतिक्रम्य स्थितवान् । औपचारिकमिदं वचः परिमातुमशक्यत्वात् सर्वतोऽधिकं व्याप्य तिष्ठतीति भावः ॥ (*sa etādṛśaḥ parameśvaraḥ brahmāṃḍaśarīravān bhūmiṃ bhūśabdopalakṣitabhūrbhuvaḥsvarājyatrailokyamityarthaḥ | ata eva viśvataḥ samaṃtataḥ sarvaṃ jagaditi yāvat vṛtvā āvṛtya adhiṣṭhāya | daśāṃgulāni māyaṃte yasmin karmaṇi taddaśāṃgulaṃ atyatiṣṭhat atikramya sthitavān | aupacārikamidaṃ vacaḥ parimātumaśakyatvāt sarvato 'dhikaṃ vyāpya tiṣṭhatīti bhāvaḥ ‖*)

By the word भूमिं (*bhūmiṃ*) the three worlds Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ and Svaḥ are intended. Therefore the purport that he pervades everything is consistent. The word दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) is only a figurative word. Since measuring is not possible, the use of this word merely indicates endlessness. Maṅgalācārya explains that the purport is that he stands beyond everything, even apart from the world. It is the opinion of Mahīdhara and Rāmānuja that दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) indicates the lotus of the heart. Whether this opinion is right needs to be examined here.

### Printed p. 721

What is the meaning of अत्यतिष्ठत् (*atyatiṣṭhat*)? One meaning is to stand having surpassed; another is, because he is greater than all, to exercise lordship over everything. How this second meaning is possible and what its basis is, one must see by noting in what sense its use has been made elsewhere.

यो जनान् महिषा इवातितस्थौ पवीरवान् । उतापवीरवान् युधा ॥ (*yo janān mahiṣā ivātitasthau pavīravān | utāpavīravān yudhā ‖*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-60-3)

In this Ṛk, whose purport is that this king crushes his opponents and shows his power over them, the verb अतितस्थौ (*atitasthau*) means that (among the enemies) he throws down all and shows his authority over them. Likewise,

प्र नू स मर्तः शवसा जना अति तस्थौ व ऊती मरुतो यमावत । अर्वद्भिर्वाजं भरते धना नृभिरापृच्छ्यं क्रतुमा क्षेति पुष्यति ॥ (*pra nū sa martaḥ śavasā janā ati tasthau va ūtī maruto yamāvata | arvadbhirvājaṃ bharate dhanā nṛbhirāpṛcchyaṃ kratumā kṣeti puṣyati ‖*)

(Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-64-13)

O Maruts, the man whom you protect with your protections surpasses other people by his valour and exerts his power over them: in this Ṛk too the same meaning is stated for the verb अतितस्थौ (*atitasthau*). In this sense this usage occurs not only in the Ṛk-saṃhitā but also in Brāhmaṇas such as the Śatapatha. For example—

सायवस कं त्वं वैश्वानरं वेत्थेति दिवमेव राजन्निति होवाचोमिति होवाचैष वा अतिष्ठा वैश्वानर एतग्ं हि वै त्वमतिष्ठां वैश्वानरं वेत तस्मात्त्वग्ं समानानतितिष्ठसि यो वा एतमतिष्ठां वैश्वानरं वेदाप पुनर्मृत्युं जयति सर्वनायुरेति ॥ (*sāyavasa kaṃ tvaṃ vaiśvānaraṃ vettheti divameva rājanniti hovācomiti hovācaiṣa vā atiṣṭhā vaiśvānara etagṃ hi vai tvamatiṣṭhāṃ vaiśvānaraṃ veta tasmāttvagṃ samānānatitiṣṭhasi yo vā etamatiṣṭhāṃ vaiśvānaraṃ vedāpa punarmṛtyuṃ jayati sarvanāyureti ‖*)

(Śa. Brā. 10-6-1-9)

"O Sāyavasa, whom do you know as Vaiśvānara?" In answer to this question he replied, "O king, I know Vaiśvānara as the world of heaven." It is true. That same Vaiśvānara is the lord of all; because you know the nature of that same Vaiśvānara, you too exercise authority over those equal to you. The one who knows this principle conquers death: thus for the word अतिष्ठाः (*atiṣṭhāḥ*) the same purport as above has been given.

It has been said above that some hold the opinion that the word दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) indicates the heart. Whether this is right must now be examined.

### Printed p. 722

यद्वा नाभेः सकाशाद्दशांगुलमतिक्रम्य हृदि स्थितः। नाभित इति कुतो लभ्यते कतम आत्मा इत्युपक्रम्य सोऽयं विज्ञानमयः प्राणेषु हृद्यंतर्जोतिरिति श्रुतेः विज्ञानात्मनः हृद्यवस्थानं कर्मफलोपभोगाय ॥ (*yadvā nābheḥ sakāśāddaśāṃgulamatikramya hṛdi sthitaḥ| nābhita iti kuto labhyate katama ātmā ityupakramya so 'yaṃ vijñānamayaḥ prāṇeṣu hṛdyaṃtarjotiriti śruteḥ vijñānātmanaḥ hṛdyavasthānaṃ karmaphalopabhogāya ‖*)

(Mahīdhara-bhāṣya)

Beyond the measure of ten fingers from the navel, the Puruṣa is situated in the heart. On the authority of the śruti passage that this knowing Self is an inner light in the heart of beings, in order to enjoy the fruit of action, the sense "heart" must be stated here too: so the commentary of Mahīdhara Ācārya states. Following this same view, Rāmānujācārya too has stated the purport:

नाभेरूर्ध्वं द्वादशांगुलमतिक्रम्यातिष्ठत् । हृत्पद्मे इति यावत् ॥ (*nābherūrdhvaṃ dvādaśāṃgulamatikramyātiṣṭhat | hṛtpadme iti yāvat ‖*)

(Rāmānuja-bhāṣya)

The Self is situated in the lotus of the heart, above the navel, beyond a measure of twelve fingers.

But in the present context it seems not quite proper to say that दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) is a word indicating the heart. There are many reasons to reject the view that it indicates the heart. For example, in describing this Puruṣa who is situated in the heart, the word दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) is not always used. Ordinarily the usage आंगुष्ठ मात्रः (*āṃguṣṭha mātraḥ*) is found.

अंगुष्ठमात्रः पुरुषः..................हृदये सन्निविष्टः । (*aṃguṣṭhamātraḥ puruṣaḥ..................hṛdaye sanniviṣṭaḥ |*)

(Śau. U. 4-12; 6-17) **NOTE**

This kind of description is the commoner. Moreover, the Puruṣa praised in the Puruṣa-sūkta is the all-pervading Puruṣa, not the Puruṣa who is within the heart. Since there are such descriptions as "the earth is his feet, the atmosphere his head, the sun his eye", this is a description of the Puruṣa who pervades the universe. Therefore, when it says अत्यतिष्ठत् (*atyatiṣṭhat*), the purport that, having pervaded from the earth the atmosphere, he surpassed that too, is natural, rather than that, having pervaded from the earth up to the heart, he surpassed the ten fingers. Support for this purport can be shown from a śruti passage. For example—

मूर्धानमुपदिशन्नेष ना अतिष्ठा वैश्वानर इति............मुख्यमाकाशमुपदि. शन्नुवाचैष वै बहुला ॥ (*mūrdhānamupadiśanneṣa nā atiṣṭhā vaiśvānara iti............mukhyamākāśamupadi. śannuvācaiṣa vai bahulā ‖*) **GLOSS**

(Śa. Brā. 10-6-1-11)

### Printed p. 723

By such descriptions, having shown that the Supreme Person, in the form of Agni Vaiśvānara, has covered the worlds such as the atmosphere, the vastness of this pervasion is explained. Moreover, the passages in which whatever vast limbs the cosmic egg has are all compared with the limbs of the human body, which is the epitome of the cosmic egg, and described accordingly, also make this matter clear. In this comparison there are three kinds.

1. Comparing the limbs in the form of the cosmic egg with the whole body of man. (Chā. U. 5-18; Mai. U. 6-7) **NOTE**

2. Or comparing them only with the head of man. (Śa. Brā. 9-3-1-3 to 6; Bra. Sū. Bhā. 1-2-31, 32) **NOTE**

3. Or comparing them only with the eye of man. (Bṛ. U. 2-2-2)

In a comparison of this kind the limit is stated as प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*). This limit is of a measure suited to the context concerned. By the word दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*), which indicates a measure, it must be understood that here the measure of the human body is what is specified. How? Thus—

तं ना अंगुलिभिर्मिमीते । पुरुषो वै यज्ञस्तेनेदग्ं सर्वं मितं तस्यैषावमा मात्रा यदंगुलयः ॥ (*taṃ nā aṃgulibhirmimīte | puruṣo vai yajñastenedagṃ sarvaṃ mitaṃ tasyaiṣāvamā mātrā yadaṃgulayaḥ ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 10-2-12)

He measures the sacrificial altar by the measure of fingers. Since the sacrifice has the form of the Puruṣa, everything connected with the sacrifice is measured by that very measure of the Puruṣa. Therefore, if in the present context दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) denotes the measure of the Puruṣa (man), it does not denote the complete body. The body of a man is more than ten fingers. Nor is it the measure of the eye; the eye is not of the measure of ten fingers. Therefore here the measure of ten fingers must denote the measure of the head.

In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa (10-6-11-11) **NOTE** and in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (5-12-18), Aśvapati Kaikeya, describing the nature of this Supreme Person who is the Self of the universe, has shown the comparison with the human body, the epitome of that cosmic egg. According to that description, the earth, which is the support of the Puruṣa, is compared to the feet. Likewise his wealth in the form of water is compared to the stomach inside the body, the sky that shows his abundance to the Self within, the wind of manifold movement to the vital breath of the body, the sun of great radiance to the eye of the body, and the heaven that is the means of his lordship to the head. The last section of this part helps in determining the purport of दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) in the present context.

### Printed p. 724

तान्नोवाच्यते वै खलु यूयं पृथगिवे ममात्मानं वैश्वानरं विद्वांसोऽन्नमत्थ यस्त्वेतमेवं प्रादेशमाश्रमभिविमानमात्मानं वैश्वानरमुपास्ते स सर्वॆषु लोकेषु सर्वॆषु भूतेषु सर्वॆष्वात्मस्वन्नमत्ति ॥ (*tānnovācyate vai khalu yūyaṃ pṛthagive mamātmānaṃ vaiśvānaraṃ vidvāṃso 'nnamattha yastvetamevaṃ prādeśamāśramabhivimānamātmānaṃ vaiśvānaramupāste sa sarvèṣu lokeṣu sarvèṣu bhūteṣu sarvèṣvātmasvannamatti ‖*) (Chā. U. 5-18)

You eat food knowing only the separate forms of this Self of the universe. But those who worship this Vaiśvānara Self, who is of the measure called प्रादेश (*prādeśa*), eat, pervading all worlds, all beings and all selves, the Self everywhere: so it is said.

स एषोग्निर्वैश्वानरो यत्पुरुषः स यो हैतमेवमग्निं वैश्वानरं पुरुषविधं पुरुषेंतः प्रतिष्ठितं वेद..................वैश्वानरो हिनस्ति ॥ (*sa eṣognirvaiśvānaro yatpuruṣaḥ sa yo haitamevamagniṃ vaiśvānaraṃ puruṣavidhaṃ puruṣeṃtaḥ pratiṣṭhitaṃ veda..................vaiśvānaro hinasti ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 10-6-1-11)

This Vaiśvānara fire is none other than the Supreme Person. Worship of him is itself worship of the Supreme Person: thus there is praise of the Supreme Person who is of प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*) measure.

In this description two points become clear. One is that, in this section, having explained the comparison with the human body, the epitome of the cosmic egg, the measure of ten fingers denotes only the head of the Puruṣa. The second is that the Puruṣa is the possessor of parts, endowed with parts of seven kinds (sapta).

प्रादेशमात्रमिव ह वै देवाः सुविदिता अभिसंपन्नाः (*prādeśamātramiva ha vai devāḥ suviditā abhisaṃpannāḥ*) (Śa. Brā. 10-6-1-10)

In this Puruṣa of प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*) measure all the gods are united and one. (The commentators have said that प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*) means 10 or 12 fingers.) This is the greatness of the Lord. Explaining this same sentence of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, Śaṅkarācārya has said in the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya thus.

संपत्तिनिमित्ता वा स्यात्पादेशमात्रश्रुतिः । कुतः । तदाहि ; समानप्रकरणं वाजसनेयिब्राह्मणं द्युप्रभृतीन्पृथिवीपर्यंतांस्त्रैलोक्यात्मनो वैश्वानरस्यावयवानध्यात्ममूर्धप्रभृतिषु चुबुकपर्यंतेषु देहावयवेषु संपादयत्पादेशमात्रसंपत्तिं परमेश्वरस्य दर्शयति । (*saṃpattinimittā vā syātpādeśamātraśrutiḥ | kutaḥ | tadāhi ; samānaprakaraṇaṃ vājasaneyibrāhmaṇaṃ dyuprabhṛtīnpṛthivīparyaṃtāṃstrailokyātmano vaiśvānarasyāvayavānadhyātmamūrdhaprabhṛtiṣu cubukaparyaṃteṣu dehāvayaveṣu saṃpādayatpādeśamātrasaṃpattiṃ parameśvarasya darśayati |*) (Bra. Sū. Śaṃ. Bhā. 12-31) **NOTE**

This description is made because everything is contained within his own limit of प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*). The heaven, the atmosphere and the earth, all these worlds, are contained within this प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*). The purpose of this section is the description of the Lord, who possesses the combined wealth of all the worlds and of all the gods:

### Printed p. 725

thus the purport of this section is explained. Why is there for this all-pervading Supreme Person the contraction to a mere प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*)? Thus—

द्युप्रभृतिपृथिव्यंतप्रदेशसंबधिन्या मात्रया परिच्छिन्नत्वं अनवच्चिन्नस्य परमात्मनो वैश्वानरस्य कथं उपपद्यत इत्यत्राह-अनवच्चिन्नस्यैव परमात्मनः उपासनाभिव्यक्त्यर्थ० ॥ (*dyuprabhṛtipṛthivyaṃtapradeśasaṃbadhinyā mātrayā paricchinnatvaṃ anavaccinnasya paramātmano vaiśvānarasya kathaṃ upapadyata ityatrāha-anavaccinnasyaiva paramātmanaḥ upāsanābhivyaktyartha0 ‖*) (Bra. Sū. Rā. Bhā. 1-2.30) **NOTE**

If the question arises whether the limitation called प्रादेश (*prādeśa*) is proper for Īśvara, who is thus undivided, endless and unlimited, the answer given is that this description in the form of a limitation is not ultimate truth. It is only a means of worship.

Explaining the प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*) nature of the Vaiśvānara Puruṣa described in the passages of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa cited above, Śaṅkarācārya has stated its purport and the aim of this description in the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya thus.

1. मूर्धादिचुबुकांतेषु पुरुषावयवेषु पुरुषविधत्वं कल्पितं तदभिप्रायेणेदमुच्यते—पुरुषविधं पुरुषेन्तः प्रतिष्ठितं वेद इति ॥ (*mūrdhādicubukāṃteṣu puruṣāvayaveṣu puruṣavidhatvaṃ kalpitaṃ tadabhiprāyeṇedamucyate—puruṣavidhaṃ puruṣentaḥ pratiṣṭhitaṃ veda iti ‖*) (Śa. Bhā. 1-2-28) **NOTE**

The description that this Supreme Self is within the Puruṣa, in the form of a Puruṣa, is a description only of the region from the head of the Puruṣa down to the chin.

2. अतिमात्रस्यापि परमेश्वरस्य प्रादेशमात्रत्वं अभिव्यक्तिनिमित्तं (*atimātrasyāpi parameśvarasya prādeśamātratvaṃ abhivyaktinimittaṃ*) (Śa. Bhā. 1-2-29)

This residence within a region is adopted **NOTE** only for the sake of the description, which is the manifestation of the Supreme Lord who is to be described.

3. प्रादेशमात्रहृदयप्रतिष्ठॆन वायं मनसानुस्मरते तेन प्रादेश मात्र इत्युच्यते । ...... .... । नचेह परमेश्वरगतं किंचित्परिमाणस्तिम यद्धृदयसंबंधाद्व्यज्यते । प्रादेशमात्रत्वेन वायमप्रादेशमात्रोऽप्यनुस्मरणीयः प्रादेशमात्रश्रुत्यर्थवत्ताय्कॆ । (*prādeśamātrahṛdayapratiṣṭhèna vāyaṃ manasānusmarate tena prādeśa mātra ityucyate | ...... .... | naceha parameśvaragataṃ kiṃcitparimāṇastima yaddhṛdayasaṃbaṃdhādvyajyate | prādeśamātratvena vāyamaprādeśamātro 'pyanusmaraṇīyaḥ prādeśamātraśrutyarthavattāykè |*) (Śa. Bhā. 1-2-30)

It is the opinion of Bādari that this reference to residence in a region is only for the sake of constant remembrance. This description is for meditating, with the help of the mind, on this Supreme Lord who is established in the heart. But if the true state is examined, the Supreme Person is not an object of such a limitation. He is not प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*) at all.

### Printed p. 726

4. The purport of the bhāṣya on the thirty-first sūtra of 1-2 has been stated above. **NOTE**

5. आमनंति चैनं परमेश्वरमस्मिन् मूर्धचुबुकांतराळे जाबालाः । पुनरामनंति कतमच्चास्य स्थानं भवतीति । भ्रुवोघ्र्णस्य च यः संधिः स एष द्युलोकस्य परस्य च संधिर्भवतीति ...... .... ॥ (*āmanaṃti cainaṃ parameśvaramasmin mūrdhacubukāṃtarāḷe jābālāḥ | punarāmanaṃti katamaccāsya sthānaṃ bhavatīti | bhruvoghrṇasya ca yaḥ saṃdhiḥ sa eṣa dyulokasya parasya ca saṃdhirbhavatīti ...... .... ‖*) (Śa. Bhā. 1.2-32)

The place of this Supreme Lord is between the mūrdha (head) and the chubuka (chin). That is, the exact place is between the bhrū (brow) and the ghrāṇa (nose). This place is the junction between the world of heaven and the highest world beyond it. While explaining the sense **NOTE** of the sentence of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad cited above, Śaṅkarācārya has given an alternative meaning for the word प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*).

1. यस्तेतमेवं यथोक्तावयवैद्युमूर्धादिभिः पृथिवीपादान्तैर्विशिष्टमेकं प्रादेशमात्रं प्रादेशैः द्युमूर्धादिभिः पृथिवीपादान्तरध्यात्मं मीयते ज्ञायत इति प्रादेशमात्रं । (*yastetamevaṃ yathoktāvayavaidyumūrdhādibhiḥ pṛthivīpādāntairviśiṣṭamekaṃ prādeśamātraṃ prādeśaiḥ dyumūrdhādibhiḥ pṛthivīpādāntaradhyātmaṃ mīyate jñāyata iti prādeśamātraṃ |*) (Bhā. U. Śa. Bhā. 5-18) **NOTE**

The region from the head of the body to the foot reflects the region that lies in the interval between heaven and earth. This knowledge of the region is a means to knowledge of the Self.

2. मुखादिसु ना करणेष्वत्तत्वेन मीयत इति प्रादेशमात्रः (*mukhādisu nā karaṇeṣvattatvena mīyata iti prādeśamātraḥ*)

The face, with its upper and lower jaws, has its own extended space, which gives entry to food; this central region of space is therefore the प्रादेश (*prādeśa*). It is a reflection of the all-pervading space.

3. द्युलोकादिपृथिव्यंतप्रदेशपरिमाणो वा प्रादेशमात्रः (*dyulokādipṛthivyaṃtapradeśaparimāṇo vā prādeśamātraḥ*)

The interval between the world of heaven and the earth may be called प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*). Or,

4. प्रकर्षेण शास्त्रेणादिश्यंत इति प्रादेशा द्युलोकादय एव तावत्परिमाणः प्रादेशमात्रः । (*prakarṣeṇa śāstreṇādiśyaṃta iti prādeśā dyulokādaya eva tāvatparimāṇaḥ prādeśamātraḥ |*)

The very measure that the śāstras state regarding the world of heaven and the rest is प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*). Or,

5. शाखांतरे तु मूर्धादिचिबुकप्रतिष्ठ इति प्रादेशमात्रं कल्पयंति । (*śākhāṃtare tu mūrdhādicibukapratiṣṭha iti prādeśamātraṃ kalpayaṃti |*)

Some śāstras state that the region from the head to the chin is प्रादेशमात्र (*prādeśamātra*).

### Printed p. 727

Of these meanings, the third meaning is the one that explains the purport of the word दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) in the present context. But there is no room for the question whether the interval between the world of heaven and the earth is really only of ten fingers. This must be understood as a mere symbol. Such symbols reflect the principle of the universe in many contexts. For example, the sacrificial altar, its measure, and the fact that the altar reflects the vastness of the universe are all described by technical terms of this symbolic kind. The measure of the altar, which reflects the universe itself, also follows the measure of the finger. The altar and the Puruṣa are of equal measure. By whatever measure the body of the Puruṣa is measured, the altar too is to be measured by that same measure. How? Thus—

तं ना अंगुलिभिमिर्मिते । पुरुषो वै यज्ञस्तेनेदग्ं सर्वं मितं तस्यैषावमा मात्रा यदंगुलयस्तद्यास्यावमा मात्रा तामस्य तदाप्पोति तय्यैनं तन्निमाते । (*taṃ nā aṃgulibhimirmite | puruṣo vai yajñastenedagṃ sarvaṃ mitaṃ tasyaiṣāvamā mātrā yadaṃgulayastadyāsyāvamā mātrā tāmasya tadāppoti tayyainaṃ tannimāte |*) (Śa. Brā. 10-2-1-2)

He measures the altar with the fingers. Since the sacrifice reflects the Puruṣa and is of equal measure with him, it is to be measured by the very measure by which he is measured. The smallest measure for measuring the Puruṣa is the measure of the finger. Therefore the altar too is to be measured by that same measure. This is the method of measuring the sacrificial Puruṣa.

The creation of the universe, and the sacrifice that imitates this creation, are both praised as acts of measuring, that is, acts of measure. For example—

कासीत्पमा प्रतिमा किं निदानमाज्यं किमासीत्परिधिः क आसीत् । छंदः किमासीत्पउगं किमुक्थं यद्देवा देवमयजंत विश्वे ॥ (*kāsītpamā pratimā kiṃ nidānamājyaṃ kimāsītparidhiḥ ka āsīt | chaṃdaḥ kimāsītpaugaṃ kimukthaṃ yaddevā devamayajaṃta viśve ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-130-3)

When the Viśvedevas offered the sacrifice addressed to Īśvara, the Supreme Self, the measure of this sacrifice is indicated by the questions that are asked: What was the measure? What was the image? What was the first cause? What was the ghee? What was the enclosing boundary? What was the metre? and so on. Many passages also state that the measure of the Puruṣa is the measure of the sacrifice. For the earthly sacrifice, the measure of the earthly Puruṣa; for the sacrifice that is the universe, the measure of the Supreme Person.

Just as all the principles of the cosmic egg are described as reflected in the limbs of the human body, which is its epitome, so too the measure of the face of the Supreme Person, the chief of the universal sacrifice, is reflected in the measure of the face of man. This measure of the face

### Printed p. 728

is of ten fingers. If this is interpreted with reference to the Self of the universe, then the purport of दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) becomes the interval between the earth and the world of heaven. Therefore, for अत्यतिष्ठद्दशांगुलं (*atyatiṣṭhaddaśāṃgulaṃ*) the purport can be stated that, pervading the whole interval between heaven and earth that is indicated by the measure of ten fingers, the Puruṣa has displayed his lordship in the whole universe; or the purport can also be taken that, pervading the whole interval between heaven and earth indicated by the measure of ten fingers, he stands established, having surpassed even that. Bhaṭṭabhāskara, explaining this matter in the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka section, has stated that both these meanings are possible, thus.

दशांगुलं दशांगुलप्रमाणावच्छिन्नं । दश अंगुलयः प्रमाणं अस्य इति । अत्र सामर्थ्यात् हृदयाकाशपरिग्रहः। हृदयाकाशस्यैव दशांगुलमित्याख्येति केचित् । हृदयं दहरं गगनं पुरुष इति पर्यायः ॥ (*daśāṃgulaṃ daśāṃgulapramāṇāvacchinnaṃ | daśa aṃgulayaḥ pramāṇaṃ asya iti | atra sāmarthyāt hṛdayākāśaparigrahaḥ| hṛdayākāśasyaiva daśāṃgulamityākhyeti kecit | hṛdayaṃ daharaṃ gaganaṃ puruṣa iti paryāyaḥ ‖*) (Tai. Ā. Bhā. 2-12-1) **NOTE**

Because it is of a measure of ten fingers, there is a usage that indicates the measure of ten fingers. This explanation tells the nature of the space of the heart. According to some, the use of दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) ordinarily occurs only when the space of the heart is meant. Heart, dahara, gagana and puruṣa are all synonymous names: this is one kind of explanation of the purport. Secondly—

यद्वा । सर्गप्रकरणमिदं । अतो विकारजातं भूम्यादिकं सर्वं वृत्वा पदेनैव घनमावृत्य शशांगुलमतितिष्ठति दशांगुलादधोऽधिष्ठानं न करोति आत एव भूमेर्दशांगुलादधोऽंकुरादेरनुत्पत्तिः । सर्वगसिसृक्षोपधानमूल तत्वेऽपि पुरुषस्य कारणात्मकत्वात् सर्वकार्यदेशवाप्यैव स्वप्रयोजनसंपादनात् तदेव तस्य सर्वगतत्वमिति दशांगुलात्परतो न व्याप्ोति प्रयोजनाभावादिति केचित् ॥ (*yadvā | sargaprakaraṇamidaṃ | ato vikārajātaṃ bhūmyādikaṃ sarvaṃ vṛtvā padenaiva ghanamāvṛtya śaśāṃgulamatitiṣṭhati daśāṃgulādadho 'dhiṣṭhānaṃ na karoti āta eva bhūmerdaśāṃgulādadho 'ṃkurāderanutpattiḥ | sarvagasisṛkṣopadhānamūla tatve 'pi puruṣasya kāraṇātmakatvāt sarvakāryadeśavāpyaiva svaprayojanasaṃpādanāt tadeva tasya sarvagatatvamiti daśāṃgulātparato na vyāpoti prayojanābhāvāditi kecit ‖*) (Trai. Ā. Bhā. 3-12-1) **NOTE**

After the root nature has undergone modification and been transformed in the form of the world, it plants its foot and stands planted on the ground, so as to occupy a space of only ten fingers. **NOTE** Thus another kind of purport has been given. But the view explained above states in a reasoned manner the spiritual purport of दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*).

**The main purport**

In this Ṛk three main matters are set forth. The first: what is the meaning of the word पुरुष (*puruṣa*)? Who is the Puruṣa? What does the word पुरुष (*puruṣa*) used in this Ṛk indicate? These matters must be examined. For the word पुरुष (*puruṣa*) in ordinary language

### Printed p. 729

means one of the three genders. That is, among the masculine, feminine and neuter genders, the word पुरुष (*puruṣa*) is the word that indicates the masculine. Trees, mountains and the like, which do not move and are without consciousness, belong to the class called the neuter gender. Among animals and human beings, who have the power to move, two kinds of class (group) are seen: one male and the other female. These classes themselves are indicated by the masculine and feminine words. So that the increase of progeny may go on without break, Parameśvara himself has devised this twofold difference in all living beings. From the union of these females and males (or animals) offspring arise, and the work of creation goes forward. But if one asks whether Parameśvara, who devised the difference of female and male, has a definite gender, female or male, then Parameśvara has no such difference of gender. He can assume any form he pleases. Since all things moving and unmoving, and the whole world as well, are a part, that is, the very form, of the Paramātman, there is no thing at all apart from the Paramātman, that is, apart from Brahman. All that exists is one thing alone (that same Parabrahman or Paramātman, Parameśvara and so on); it may be called by whatever gender one wishes, which means that it has no definite gender at all. According to the occasion, devotees, as they please, attribute images of various genders to that supreme thing and worship it. Durgā, Cāmuṇḍā and the like are feminine words (or images); Prajāpati, Rāma, Kṛṣṇa and the like are masculine words (or varieties of image); the Parabrahman, which is without change and beyond the reach of the senses such as the eye, is a word of neuter gender. Since all these point to one and the same supreme thing, that supreme thing may be called by any gender or word. In the present Ṛk it is indicated by the word पुरुष (*puruṣa*). This Parameśvara is also indicated by names such as Ādipuruṣa and Virāṭpuruṣa, whose body is the cosmic egg itself. Therefore the word पुरुष (*puruṣa*) in this Ṛk means Parameśvara alone.

Secondly: the Parameśvara denoted by the word पुरुष (*puruṣa*) spoken of above is described here as सहस्रशीर्षा (*sahasraśīrṣā*), सहस्राक्षः (*sahasrākṣaḥ*), सहस्रपात् (*sahasrapāt*), that is, one who has thousands of heads, thousands of eyes, thousands of feet. Here the word सहस्र (*sahasra*) does not have the numerical meaning "thousand". It means endless, innumerable. That is, the word सहस्रशीर्षा (*sahasraśīrṣā*) must not be explained only as "one with a thousand heads"; one must say "one who has thousands, or innumerable, uncountable, endless heads". In the same way it is to be understood that he has endless eyes and endless feet. As is commonly within our experience, a man has only one head, two eyes and two feet. Some animals have more than two legs. But if one asks whether it is possible to have a thousand or an endless number of heads, it is possible only in the case of Parameśvara. The human beings in the world

### Printed p. 730

and all the other creatures and all the multitudes of living beings are parts of Parameśvara; that is, since Parameśvara himself is present in the form of all living beings, within their bodies, in the form of consciousness, the heads and so on of those innumerable beings are all heads of Parameśvara. Since the heads, eyes and feet of these multitudes of living beings are countless, Parameśvara is described here as having endless heads, endless eyes and endless feet. This is the explanation of the commentator Sāyaṇa.

But here another important matter has to be examined. It is described in the Śruti and other texts that Parameśvara has no definite form in the unmanifest state and that he is all-pervading. That being so, the question naturally arises what is meant by saying that this Paramātman has heads, eyes and feet in countless numbers. As within our experience, that is, as we have them, the Paramātman does not have heads, eyes and feet. If we had no eyes we could not see anything; without ears we could not hear; without feet we could not move about. The case of the Paramātman is not so. Even though he has no eyes and the like, he can see, he can know, he can move about. He has no need of the senses such as the eye. Since he is of the nature of consciousness, he does not have to grasp the nature of things through the senses. Without limbs he can perform the work of all the limbs. Therefore it is to be understood that the words सहस्रशीर्षा (*sahasraśīrṣā*) and so on said here are not used to describe that the Paramātman has thousands or countless heads and other organs, but that those words are used in order to convey, at least to some small extent, his boundless power and capacity in the language that is in use among us.

Thirdly: the principle set forth in the sentence स भूमिं विश्वतो वृत्वा दशांगुलं अत्यतिष्ठत् (*sa bhūmiṃ viśvato vṛtvā daśāṃgulaṃ atyatiṣṭhat*) is very profound. In this sentence the word भूमि (*bhūmi*) does not indicate only the earth or world in which we live. This word भूमि (*bhūmi*) explains the general meaning that indicates the earth in which we live and, like it, the innumerable other earths or cosmic eggs in the universe, that is, the entire universe. Therefore भूमि (*bhūmi*) means the universe. In order to tell in easy language a matter that is within our experience, the universe, which is beyond experience, has been described by the word भूमि (*bhūmi*), which can be known by experience. In the same way the meaning of the word दशांगुलं (*daśāṃgulaṃ*) also includes an upalakṣaṇa, that is, a general meaning. दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) does not mean a measure of ten fingers. The intention is that दशांगुल (*daśāṃgula*) means ten parts, or much more. It has been said before that this Paramātman at the time of creation himself transformed into the world of the moving and the unmoving and entered it in the form of the inner controller. From this, this world

### Printed p. 731

or universe, all the moving and unmoving things in it, the many worlds and cosmic eggs, all these came to be the Paramātman. Here a doubt arises. When the Paramātman himself has been transformed in the form of all the cosmic eggs, do the cosmic eggs exist alone, without the Paramātman? No, it is not so. Before creation, only a small part of the Paramātman (Parabrahman), who was in the unmanifest form, was transformed into the world and the rest. The greater part remained as it was. Even now it is so. That is, the world and the rest that are seen by the eye are only some parts of the Paramātman. The part that remains in the unmanifest form is far greater. It is not seen by our eye. Therefore at the time of creation the Paramātman exists in two kinds of forms, in the manifest forms such as the world and in the unmanifest form. The part that is in the form of the world and the rest is small; the part that is in the unmanifest form is large. In order to indicate this meaning, the word अत्यतिष्ठत् (*atyatiṣṭhat*) is used here, to convey the meaning that even though he has enveloped the earth (world, universe) that is visible to the eye (having been transformed into the form of the world and the rest), the greater part of him, the unmanifest form, still remains in excess. An example may be given to make this matter clear. The water of the sea, heated by the sharp rays of the sun, is transformed into clouds in the form of vapour. Afterwards the water in the clouds falls on the earth in the form of rain, flows as rivers and again joins the sea itself. This matter is within the experience of all. Here the sea may be compared to the Paramātman and the clouds to the world and the rest. When the water of the sea is transformed into clouds, all the water of the sea does not become clouds; only some small part does. The greater part of the sea remains as it is without becoming clouds. In the same way, even when the Paramātman has been transformed in the form of the world and the rest, the greater part of the Paramātman, the unmanifest form, remains as it is, that is, in the unmanifest state. Therefore the intention is that the world and the rest, which are forms of the Paramātman, are in a small part, while the unmanifest form that surpasses all these worlds and the rest is in the greater part. This very matter is explained later in the latter half of the third Ṛk of the present sūkta, पादोऽस्य विश्वा भूतानि त्रिपादस्यामृतं दिवि (*pādo 'sya viśvā bhūtāni tripādasyāmṛtaṃ divi*). It will be explained in that context.

#### Ṛk 2

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> पुरु॑ष ए॒वेदं सर्वं॒ यद्भू॒तं यच्च॒ भव्यं॑ ।  
> उ॒तामृ॑त॒त्वस्येशा॑नो॒ यदन्ने॑नाति॒रोह॑ति ॥ २ ॥

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> पुरुषः । एव । इदं । सर्वं । यत् । भूतं । यत् । च । भव्यं ।  
> उत । अमृतत्वस्य । ईशानः । यत् । अन्नेन । अतिरोहति ॥ २ ॥

### Printed p. 732

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> यदिदं वर्तमानं जगत्तत्सर्वं पुरुष एव । यच्च भूतमतीतं जगद्यच्च
> भव्यं भविष्यज्जगत् तदपि पुरुष एव । यथास्मिन्कल्पे वर्तमानाः प्राणिदेहाः
> सर्वेऽपि विराट्टुरुषस्यावयवाः तथैवातीतागामिनोरपि कल्पयोर्द्रष्टव्यमित्यभिप्रायः । उतापि चामृतत्वस्यॆ देवत्वस्यायमीशानः स्वामा ! यद्यस्मात्कारणादन्नेन प्राणिनां भोग्येनान्नेन निमित्तभूतेनातिरोहति स्वकीयां कारणावस्थामतिक्रम्य परिदृश्यमानां जगदवस्थांप्राप्नोति तस्मात्पाणिनां कर्मफलभोगाय
> जगदवस्थास्वीकारान्नेदं तॆस्य वस्तुत्वमित्यर्थः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Everything that is the present world is Puruṣa alone. What has been, the past world, and what is to be, the future world, that too is Puruṣa alone. As the bodies of the living beings now existing in this kalpa are all limbs of the Virāṭ Puruṣa, so the same is to be seen in the past and the coming kalpas; this is the meaning. Further, this Puruṣa is the lord of immortality, that is, of divinity. Because, with food as the occasioning cause, food that is to be enjoyed by living beings, he passes beyond his own causal state and attains the world-state that is seen, therefore, for the sake of the enjoyment of the fruits of their actions by living beings, he accepts the state of the world; hence this is not his own reality. This is the meaning.

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- इदं सर्वं (*idaṃ sarvaṃ*)—all this world that is visible to us (the whole present world)
- पुरुष एव (*puruṣa eva*)—that primal Puruṣa himself (it is his very part)
- यत् भूतं (*yat bhūtaṃ*)—whatever existed in the past
- यच्च भव्यं (*yacca bhavyaṃ*)—whatever will come into being hereafter (all that world is a part of Īśvara and is not something other)
- उत (*uta*)—and
- अमृतत्वस्य (*amṛtatvasya*)—of freedom from death
- ईशानः (*īśānaḥ*)—he alone is the lord
- यत् (*yat*)—by what cause
- अन्नेन (*annena*)—by food, which is the means of enjoyment of living beings
- अतिरोहति (*atirohati*)—he grows (therefore he has a greater majesty than he now appears to have)

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

The whole world that is visible to us, that is, the whole world of the present time, is a part of that primal Puruṣa. The world that was in the past is he, and what will come to be hereafter is he also; that is, it is not something other than a part of Īśvara. He is the lord of immortality. By the food that is the means of enjoyment for living beings he appears to grow. But his own nature is beyond the reach of the senses.

##### English translation
Purusha is verily all this (visible world). all that is, and all that
is to be ; he is also the lord of immortality ; for for he mounts beyond
(his own conditon) for the food (of living beings).

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

That the whole world is full of Īśvara, that Īśvara is the lord of the entire world, that the distinctions of time such as past, present and future are all his power: such praise of the greatness of the supreme Puruṣa is given in this Ṛk.

### Printed p. 733

इदं वर्तमानं जगत् सर्व० पुरुष एव । अतीतं जगत्, भविष्यज्जगत् तदपि पुरुष एव । (*idaṃ vartamānaṃ jagat sarva0 puruṣa eva | atītaṃ jagat, bhaviṣyajjagat tadapi puruṣa eva |*). The whole world is a particular limb of Puruṣa. That there is no second independent principle apart from Puruṣa is told by the sentence पुरुष एवेदग्० सर्व० (*puruṣa evedag0 sarva0*). Śaṅkarācārya, explaining this very point in his commentary, has said सत्यं नेश्वरादन्यः संसारी (*satyaṃ neśvarādanyaḥ saṃsārī*) (Bra. Sū. Śa. Bhā. 1-1-5) **NOTE**: Īśvara alone is the eternal one whose nature is being. He himself undergoes change in the form of saṃsāra. Apart from him there is no other transmigrating being. But in the world there are many varieties. There are many multitudes of living beings. All of them have individual freedom. That being so, there is room also for the question whether it is right that Īśvara alone is the transmigrating being and that there is no second principle apart from him. To such objections an answer has been given in the commentaries and other works on the authority of Śruti passages. The Sūrya-Ātman who is described by सूर्य आत्मा जगतस्तस्थुषश्च (*sūrya ātmā jagatastasthuṣaśca*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-115-1), him Śaṅkarācārya has indicated as Īśvara. He himself is indicated by the names Brahmā, Indra and so on.

स ना आयमात्मा सर्वेषां भूतानामधिपतिः सर्वेषां भूतानां राजा तद्यथा रथनाभौ च रथनेनौ चाराः सर्वे समर्पिता एवमेवास्मिन्नात्मनि सर्वाणि भूतानि सर्वे देवाः सर्वे लोकाः सर्वे प्राणाः सर्व एत आत्मानः समर्पिताः । (*sa nā āyamātmā sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāmadhipatiḥ sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ rājā tadyathā rathanābhau ca rathanenau cārāḥ sarve samarpitā evamevāsminnātmani sarvāṇi bhūtāni sarve devāḥ sarve lokāḥ sarve prāṇāḥ sarva eta ātmānaḥ samarpitāḥ |*) (Bṛ. U. 2-5-15)

This Paramātman is the overlord of all beings. He is the king of all beings. As all the spokes are gathered together in one place in the wheel of a chariot, so in this Paramātman all beings, all gods, all vital breaths and all selves are gathered together as one. This matter was told briefly before, when the special matter of the Ṛk रूपं रूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव (*rūpaṃ rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-47-18) was given. In the present place a detailed explanation of it is very necessary, and therefore this point will be made clear by citing the Upaniṣadic and other passages. How the Śruti passages describe that the world, made up of all the unmoving and the moving, is full of Īśvara and is not something other than a part of Īśvara will be examined.

इयं पृथिवी सर्वेषां भूतानां मधु अस्यै पृथिव्यै सर्वाणि भूतानि मधु यश्चायमस्यां पृथिव्यां तेजोमयोऽमृतमयः पुरुषो (*iyaṃ pṛthivī sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ madhu asyai pṛthivyai sarvāṇi bhūtāni madhu yaścāyamasyāṃ pṛthivyāṃ tejomayo 'mṛtamayaḥ puruṣo*)

### Printed p. 734

यश्चायमध्यात्मं शारीरस्तेजो मयोऽमृतमृतमयः पुरुषोऽयमेव स योऽयमात्मेदममृतमिदं ब्रह्मेदं सर्वं । (*yaścāyamadhyātmaṃ śārīrastejo mayo 'mṛtamṛtamayaḥ puruṣo 'yameva sa yo 'yamātmedamamṛtamidaṃ brahmedaṃ sarvaṃ |*) (Bṛ. U. 2-5-1)

This earth is honey for all beings. All beings are honey for this earth. This Puruṣa, full of radiance and full of immortality, is present within all bodies. This very Paramātman who pervades the earth is the Parabrahman, the inner controller of all, all-pervading, the cause of all. He alone is the Self of all.

इमा आपः सर्वेषां भूतानां मधु ................. यश्चायमध्यात्मं रैतसस्तेजोमयः पुरुषोऽयमेव स योऽयमात्मेदमम्म तमिदं ब्रह्मदं सर्वं ॥ (*imā āpaḥ sarveṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ madhu ................. yaścāyamadhyātmaṃ raitasastejomayaḥ puruṣo 'yameva sa yo 'yamātmedamamma tamidaṃ brahmadaṃ sarvaṃ ‖*) (Bṛ. U. 2-5-2)

Water is honey for all beings. All beings are honey for this water. This Puruṣa, full of radiance and full of immortality, is in the form of semen. This very Paramātman who pervades water is the Parabrahman, the inner controller of all, all-pervading, the cause of all, full of immortality. He alone is the Self of all.

अयं वायुः................ यश्चायमस्मिन्वायौ तेजोमयोऽमृतमयः ........... यश्चायमध्यात्मं प्राणः ............ योऽयमात्मेदं ब्रह्मदं सर्वं । (*ayaṃ vāyuḥ................ yaścāyamasminvāyau tejomayo 'mṛtamayaḥ ........... yaścāyamadhyātmaṃ prāṇaḥ ............ yo 'yamātmedaṃ brahmadaṃ sarvaṃ |*) (Bṛ. U. 9-5-3) **NOTE**

This Parabrahman, the inner controller of all and all-pervading in the form of air, has entered all bodies in the form of the vital breath. He alone is the Parabrahman who is the Self of all.

अयमादित्यः.................. यश्चायमध्यात्मं चाक्षुषः ............ आत्मेदममृतमिदं ब्रह्मदं सर्वं । (*ayamādityaḥ.................. yaścāyamadhyātmaṃ cākṣuṣaḥ ............ ātmedamamṛtamidaṃ brahmadaṃ sarvaṃ |*) (Bṛ. U. 2-25-4) **NOTE**

This Paramātman, who is honey for all beings in the form of the sun, is in all beings in the form of the eye. He alone is the Parabrahman who is the Self of all.
